News.title: US officials 'secretly flew diplomat out of UK' after indecent image allegations
News.content:
US officials 'secretly flew diplomat out of UK' after indecent image allegations

Metropolitan Police was made aware of an investigation last month - however reports suggest that US officials may have acted despite having no powers of arrest in Britain

View 3 Images View of the US embassy in London (Image: AFP/Getty Images)

An American diplomat was 'secretly flown out of the UK' after being accused of possessing indecent images of children.

‌



US officials allegedly raided the diplomat's flat last month in London before taking him to an American airbase, in a move which may further strain relations between London and Washington.

‌



American personnel have no powers of arrest in Britain and, The Sun reported, there was no formal request for the man to be extradited. UK ministers are understood to be in contact with the US embassy over the incident.

‌



Metropolitan Police have confirmed that the force was made aware of the investigation into the man last month and that it is 'liaising' with US authorities over the matter.

View 3 Images The New Scotland Yard sign and building, the headquarters of the the Metropolitan Police (Image: Andrew Aitchison / Getty)

A Government spokesperson said: “We expect all foreign diplomats in the UK to abide by our laws, in the same way we expect all UK diplomats to do so when posted overseas.

‌



“As a US investigation is ongoing, it would not be appropriate to comment further at this stage.”

The man’s seizure is reported to be related to an investigation into another individual in the US.

A spokesperson for the Metropolitan Police said: “On Tuesday August 25, US authorities made us aware of an investigation they are conducting into suspected offences in London relating to indecent images of children.

‌



“We continue to liaise with them regarding this matter.”

During his visit to Ireland, Donald Trump has expressed support for a united Ireland, adding to already mounting tensions between Britain and the US.

The 47th US president claimed Irish unification was inevitable as he spoke to reporters alongside Taoiseach Micheál Martin, adding it “may as well happen now”.

‌



View 3 Images Donald Trump was on hand to observe the Irish Open at his golf course in Doonbeg (Image: Photo by Richard Heathcote/Getty Images)

In another sign of difficult UK-US relations, Mr Trump also cast doubt on Britain’s willingness to defend the Falkland Islands should Argentina attempt an invasion.

The incident comes two months after then-deputy prime minister David Lammy said he would raise with the US government the case of an American fighter pilot who avoided a trial under English law for strangling a woman in Cambridge.

‌



Captain Jacob Wulfson was tried at a court martial on a US airbase, despite his alleged crime taking place while he was off-duty, and was jailed for six months after being convicted of strangulation.

He was acquitted of charges of sexual assault and aggravated sexual contact.

Downing Street said at the time it was “very concerning” that Capt Wulfson’s case had not been dealt with by the Crown Prosecution Service.

Article continues below

The Press Association has contacted the US embassy for comment.

News.title: Homeowner speaks out after rental booking descends into 'out of control' party with 100 people
News.content:
Homeowner speaks out after rental booking descends into 'out of control' party with 100 people

The owner of the home said only two people were on the booking but, despite this, more than 100 people descended on the short-term rental property before chaos ensued

View 2 Images The carnage was captured on a doorbell camera (Image: 7News)

The owner of a rental home has spoken out after more than 100 people turned up at his property - and a brawl broke out which ended in a stabbing.

‌



The out of control party had to be broken up by police in Melbourne, Australia.

‌



The huge crowd arrived - despite only two people being on the booking - at the short-term rental property on Belvedere Drive in Pakenham about 9.30pm Friday, September 11. But even after they were moved on, there were more problems for police to deal with.

‌



Just before 10pm on Friday night, a brawl involving the same group broke out at Pakenham Railway Station. Police say a 26-year-old man, who trying to break up the fight, was then stabbed in the arm.

View 2 Images There was further disorder at Pakenham Railway Station in Melbourne (Image: 7News)

‌



Paramedics soon arrived and he was taken to hospital with non life-threatening injuries.

The group involved in the brawl fled when officers arrived, and despite a thorough search, no arrests have been made.

Anwar Sadat, who owns the home where the party was hosted, told 7News he believed he had rented the property to two adults, who had agreed there would be no partying.

Article continues below

“I said, like, make sure you don’t do any party. And he said, yes, no, they will not have any parties,” he said.

Anyone who witnessed the incident, has CCTV or dashcam footage or with information is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or submit an online confidential report at www.crimestoppersvic.com.au.

A spokesperson for Airbnb has told the Mirror that, despite reports, the property was not rented out via their platform.

News.title: Man dies in West Lothian 'shooting' as police probe nearby car fire
News.content:
Man dies in West Lothian 'shooting' as police probe nearby car fire

Dozens of police officers raced to Armadale, West Lothian, where a 35-year-old man died in a suspected shooting, with police also investigating a car that was set on fire nearby

View Image Police in Armadale after a man died (Image: Daily Record)

A man has died following a suspected shooting in West Lothian with a car set on fire in nearby.

Dozens of police officers along with other emergency services rushed to Armadale shortly before midday today following reports that a man was injured at a property on Harestanes Road.

It has now been confirmed by police that a 35-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene with his next of kin aware.

Detectives have said a line of inquiry is that a firearm may have been involved in the incident.

UK temperatures to soar to 25C on Monday as another heatwave on the cards READ MORE :

NATO military aircraft scrambled over Europe as urgent warning issued in Poland READ MORE :

Meanwhile, the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service confirmed they received a report of a vehicle set ablaze on Northrigg, a rural road leading to a nearby farm behind the scheme in question. The fire was put out by crews and there were no reports of injuries.

Police said enquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances of both incidents. Officers are keeping an open mind but are investigating them as linked, reported the Daily Record.

Forensic officers and detectives could be seen at one property on Harestanes Road, with nearby Brown Street also taped off, examining the area and taking photographs as part of their investigation this evening.

Evidence also appears to have been bagged up by forensic officers, while a heavy emergency service presence remains in the area. An air ambulance was deployed from Glasgow and spotted on FlightRadar24 travelling to Armadale before going back to the city.

Detective Superintendent Michelle Findlay, of the Major Investigations Team, said: “Our thoughts are with the family of the man who has died in this incident. Officers remain in the area and anyone with concerns or any information can approach them or call us on 101, quoting incident number 1361 of Saturday, 12 September, 2026.”

The statement from the police read: "Around 11.50am on Saturday, 12 September, Police Scotland received a report of a man injured at an address on Harestanes Road in Armadale.

"Emergency services attended and the 35-year-old was pronounced dead at the scene. His next of kin is aware. Enquiries are at an early stage and a post-mortem will take place in due course. However, a line of enquiry is that a firearm may have been involved in the incident.

"Around 12pm on Saturday, 12 September, officers received a report of a car on fire nearby in the Netherhouses area, near to Armadale. The fire was put out by the Scottish Fire and Rescue Services and there were no reports of injuries. "Enquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances of both incidents. Officers are keeping an open mind but they are being investigated as linked."

News.title: Manchester incident recap: Teen suffers 'possible life changing injuries' in 'substance attack'
News.content:
A police cordon is in place by the Arndale shopping centre in Manchester city centre after a boy in his mid-teens had an "unknown substance" thrown at him

A teenager has suffered a "potentially life-changing" injury after an "unknown substance" was thrown at him in Manchester city centre.

Police, fire crews and colleagues from the North West Ambulance service are outside the Arndale shopping centre opposite the Printworks with a large cordon in place.

Officers rushed to the scene at 6.10pm where they established a substance which has not yet been identified was thrown following an argument.

A statement from Greater Manchester Police read: "The victim, a male in his mid-teens has received an injury that has been described as not life-threatening but potentially life-changing. A 19-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of assault and remains in custody."

News.title: Man becomes first arrested for 'concealing his identity' hours after face covering ban
News.content:
Man becomes first arrested for 'concealing his identity' hours after face covering ban

Hampshire Police used newly introduced powers during rival demonstrations in Portsmouth, where three people were arrested and hundreds of protestors were kept apart

View 3 Images Men wearing balaclavas at a recent protest in Dover (file image)

A man became the first person to be arrested on suspicion of concealing his identity just hours after a new ban came into force.

The restriction took effect at 10am on Saturday, with police warning those attending rival demonstrations in Portsmouth not to wear face coverings used to conceal their identity. Hampshire Police said it would use new powers under the Crime and Policing Act 2025 to “allow peaceful protest and prevent violence”.

During the protest, three people were arrested, including a 76-year-old man from Southampton on suspicion of wearing or using an item to conceal his identity at a protest.

View 3 Images A new face-covering restriction was in force during the march (Image: James Veysey/Shutterstock)

Portsmouth protesters face arrest for wearing masks as more rallies planned READ MORE :

A 33-year-old man from Portsmouth was also arrested on suspicion of obstructing a highway, while a 16-year-old boy, also from Portsmouth, was arrested on suspicion of violent disorder in relation to a similar protest at Eastney Marina last Sunday.

The measures came amid wider concerns over masked demonstrations, after around 300 protesters blocked access to the Port of Dover last week. Groups from South Coast Patriots had called for a peaceful march through Portsmouth city centre on Saturday afternoon, while a counter-protest was also organised by Stand Up To Racism.

Around 300 people joined the counter-protest, with both sets of demonstrators kept apart by police when they arrived at Guildhall Square.

A separate order also allowed officers to require people to remove masks and other items being used to conceal their identity. Hampshire Police and Crime Commissioner Donna Jones said: “I’m pleased that today’s protests in Portsmouth took place without major issue.

“Thankfully, we didn’t see repeated scenes of Sunday night with assaults on police officers and criminal damage to police vehicles and people’s property.”

View 3 Images The counter protest was organised by Stand Up To Racism (Image: Jonathan Brady/PA Wire)

She thanked officers for their work and their impartial use of the power to ask people to remove face coverings.

The warning came after a 42-year-old man became the first person to be arrested as part of a probe into violent disorder in Portsmouth last weekend where crowds gathered at Eastney Marina overnight on Sunday after a dinghy arrived in the area having crossed the English Channel.

Hampshire Police said official vehicles were damaged and a small number of officers were injured at the scene, before around 200 people were dispersed at around 4am on Monday.

Speaking on Friday, Assistant Chief Constable Paul Bartolomeo said: “It is important to stress that this power will apply to any groups that attend the protest and will be enforced equally and impartially. Let me be clear, these powers are not being implemented to prevent protest but they are being used to help prevent crime and disorder, while making communities feel safer.”

Hampshire Police said several of its vehicles, alongside those of the coastguard and Border Force, were damaged during the previous weekend’s disruption, while a small number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries. No-one in attendance was seriously injured.

News.title: Seven-hour RNLI sea drama as six people rescued from yacht in gale-force winds
News.content:
Seven-hour RNLI sea drama as six people rescued from yacht in gale-force winds

Crew from Red Bay RNLI rushed to the rescue of a 46ft yacht that got into difficulty off the coast of Cushendall, Northern Ireland, in harsh weather conditions

View Image The dramatic rescue of six people from the yacht (Image: RNLI)

Six people were rescued from a yacht after a dramatic seven-hour rescue operation by the RNLI in brutal gale-force conditions at sea.

‌



The crew of Red Bay RNLI launched after the crew of a 46ft yacht got into difficulty off the coast of Cushendall, Northern Ireland, and sent out a Mayday while on a passenger from Oban in Scotland to Portugal.

‌



Belfast Coastguard received the emergency message from the stricken vessel which had lost all power and steering after making contact with a fish farm in Red Bay in 60-knot winds, becoming trapped..

‌



The RNLI lifeboat under Coxswain Paddy McLaughlin and with five crew members onboard, launched at 3.22am this morning and made its way the short distance to the scene. The inshore lifeboat from Red Bay RNLI also launched to assist.

UK temperatures to soar to 25C on Monday as another heatwave on the cards READ MORE :

NATO military aircraft scrambled over Europe as urgent warning issued in Poland READ MORE :

Weather conditions were difficult throughout the call-out, with force nine gusting winds, driving rain, and the darkness of night.

‌



Once on scene, the RNLI crew found that all onboard were safe but trapped due to the yacht having got entangled on the fish cages, reported BelfastLive.

Given the difficult weather and sea conditions, the Coxswain made the decision that the safest course of action was for the sailors to remain onboard the yacht and for the lifeboat to stand by until daylight broke at 7:30am.

At 9:30am, the lifeboat crew successfully freed the yacht from the fish farm and brought the sailors safely to Glenarm, where they arrived at 10am and were assisted by Larne Coastguard.

Article continues below

Speaking following the call out, Mr McLaughlin said: "This was a challenging call out in difficult weather conditions, but we were delighted to bring the sailors to safety, and we would like to wish them well.

"We would also like to commend our colleagues in the Coastguard and thank our crew who responded quickly in the middle of the night, launched our lifeboats in darkness and made their way to the scene in what were gale force conditions, and for then spending seven hours at sea.

"This shout was a great example of the selfless and dedicated efforts of volunteers who used their skills and training to bring six people to safety in what was a challenging operation."

News.title: Putin makes chilling warning of 'war' over peacekeeping force in Ukraine
News.content:
Putin makes chilling warning of 'war' over peacekeeping force in Ukraine

Vladimir Putin made it clear that Russia would see the sending of a peacekeeping force to Ukraine as meaning war, with some European leaders pledging their commitment to the plan

View 2 Images Vladimir Putin has threatened Europe with war over a peacekeeping force (Image: Alexander Kazakov/Pool Sputnik K)

Vladimir Putin made a chilling warning to Europe of "war" over a peacekeeping force as Russian strikes killed eight people and injured dozens more in Ukraine.

‌



The Russian leader did not mince his words when speaking at a summit of the BRICS group of emerging economies in India, when asked about the involvement of western European countries in Ukraine.

‌



He said: “Now they’re talking about how they’re considering sending troops into Ukraine. That means a war with Russia."

‌



Some European leaders have pledged their commitment to a potential peacekeeping force, a prospect that Moscow has repeatedly described as unacceptable.

View 2 Images Putin with the Russian delegation at the BRICS summit (Image: Kristina Solovyova/Pool Sputnik)

UK temperatures to soar to 25C on Monday as another heatwave on the cards READ MORE :

NATO military aircraft scrambled over Europe as urgent warning issued in Poland READ MORE :

At the same time, Putin also denied Russia posed any threat to Europe, saying “there is no such threat and never has been. We do not threaten, nor do we intend to threaten, European countries."

‌



Overnight Russian strikes killed eight civilians and wounded dozens of other people in Ukraine, local officials said today.

Ukraine is under mounting pressure from Russia’s intensifying air campaign that uses ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to pierce defences. Moscow’s attacks have targeted Ukraine’s power grid ahead of winter in what officials say is meant to demoralise civilians.

Two people were killed and one wounded when Russian drones struck a residential area in the city of Zaporizhzhia, regional head Ivan Fedorov said. One person also died and three others were wounded in strikes on Kryvyi Rih.

‌



In the Black Sea port of Odesa and the surrounding area, 35 people were wounded overnight in what regional head Oleh Kiper called a “massive attack.” Among the buildings hit was a residential high-rise, whose upper floors were completely destroyed.

Three people were killed on Saturday when cars were hit by drones in Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s partially occupied Donetsk region, along with a further two people in a Russian attack on a grocery store in the Zhytomyr region, local officials said.

Separately, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukrainian forces struck two chemical industry facilities in Russia, one in Samara and one in Perm. The governors of the regions did not immediately comment, but Russian independent online news outlet Astra reported drone attacks on chemical plants in both regions.

‌



Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has said that two incidents along Ukraine’s borders with Poland and Moldova this week were a preview of potential intensified Russian provocations at Ukraine’s border crossing points with Europe.

Two people died when Russian drones hit the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova on Tuesday night, while a “direct threat” to a Polish-Ukrainian crossing point on Wednesday night was only avoided thanks to cooperation between Warsaw and Kyiv, he said.

In an interview with Deutsche Welle today, Zelensky said he would meet Putin if both leaders were invited to the Group of 20 summit of rich and developing nations in December in Miami.

Article continues below

Putin’s foreign policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, said the possibility of Putin attending the summit had not yet been discussed. The Kremlin in the past has said that Zelenskyy can come to Moscow if he wants a meeting with Putin, a proposal Kyiv has rejected.

“If he really wants to meet with Putin, Putin has already said that he could fly to Moscow,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Saturday. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov affirmed Saturday that Russia is “ready for negotiations,” but that the so-called “special military operation,” as Moscow refers to its war in Ukraine, “will not be suspended during this period of negotiations.”

News.title: UK postal compensation rules as Royal Mail service labelled 'not good enough'
News.content:
UK postal compensation rules as Royal Mail service labelled 'not good enough'

People could be eligible for compensation under Royal Mail regulations if there are problems with first and second class postal deliveries

View 2 Images (Image: Nigel Harris via Getty Images)

Royal Mail rules mean you could be owed compensation as the government this week criticised the postal service over delays. Andy Burnham's government is facing pressure to hold Royal Mail bosses accountable for shortcomings after the organisation fell short of its first and second class delivery targets.

‌



Kate Dearden - Minister of State (Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade) - responded this week, stating: "The government has been clear that Royal Mail's quality of service has not been good enough. The Government has discussed Royal Mail's performance with the company and Ofcom, as the independent regulator, and they know there is more to do to improve stability and reliability for customers, but it is welcome that the most recently released quality of service figures, for Q1 26/27, show an improvement.

‌



"Ofcom has opened an investigation into Royal Mail's quality of service performance for 2025-26 and Royal Mail has published a quality of service improvement plan alongside a £500 million investment into frontline resourcing. The government will continue to press royal Mail for improvements in service quality."

‌



View 2 Images Kate Dearden - Minister of State (Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade) (Image: Parliament TV)

The organisation is currently being investigated by regulator Ofcom for failing to meet delivery standards, with a minister this week branding the situation 'not good enough'. The good news for customers is that Royal Mail is obliged to stick to compensation rules under certain conditions, which could see you receiving payouts for post that takes too long to arrive at its destination.

‌



Royal Mail may pay compensation to either the sender or the recipient of a delayed item posted using products under this scheme where it has not delivered or attempted to deliver the item. This could happen:

Three or more working days after the due date, except where an item is redirected using the Royal Mail Redirection Service.

Six or more working days after the due date for items redirected using the Royal Mail Redirection Service.

24 or more hours after the due date for Royal Mail Special Delivery Guaranteed by 1pm items (not posted on account)

Furthermore, a person "may also be eligible for substantial delay compensation" should their item remain undelivered, or no delivery attempt made, seven or more working days beyond the expected date.

Article continues below

The matter was put into the spotlight after John Slinger, Labour MP for Rugby, questioned the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade regarding "what steps the Government is taking to hold Royal Mail senior management accountable for statutory delivery performance targets."

The complete compensation rules can be found on the Royal Mail website.

News.title: AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC
News.content:
An artificial intelligence researcher who quit AI firm Anthropic has told the BBC that people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

Jacob Coxon told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg on Saturday about his viral resignation post in which he raised concerns about out-of-control AI.

"I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said.

His resignation comes amid growing safety concerns in the industry, including from his former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, who in an essay argued for development to slow down.

The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI models as they are developed.

Amodei said developing the technology was not in question, but the risks associated with it were "serious", and that companies and governments must be given time to address them.

The 27-year-old Coxon - who worked at OpenAI before joining Anthropic - welcomed the suggestion of a slowdown but said it would need to be co-ordinated with China to avoid "a race at an international scale".

"The people who work at these companies are completely serious when they ask for regulation because they find themselves trapped in a race. And they're scared of the outcomes of that race," he told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.

The hardest question to answer, according to Coxon, was what an AI apocalypse would look like.

One of the risks outlined in Amodei's comments was of a swarm of bots acting like a supercomputer that could take over the internet.

Coxon said this scenario could be realistic in six months to a year.

In response to Coxon's departure, an Anthropic spokesperson told BBC News: "We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks.

"To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry."

The firm has been a pioneer in studying how AI models work, the spokesperson added. It was the first to publish a framework for mitigating the risks posed by their development - and it also "aggressively" tests its models and publishes the findings to aid scrutiny and prevent incidents of "AI misalignment".

"This work is also why we believe the world would benefit from the industry adopting a lawful, verifiable way to work together to pace how we release powerful models," they said.

Industry figures have suggested comments about the perils and power of AI may be designed to generate hype. Other critics say Anthropic has been trying to trigger a regulatory push to block competition, leaving it and OpenAI with a duopoly.

Anthropic and OpenAI are reportedly preparing for potentially record-setting initial public offerings.

News.title: Dramatic insider warnings over AI fall flat with some in Silicon Valley
News.content:
Each September, a who's who of executives from across Silicon Valley descends on San Francisco's Palace Hotel to charm investors at a conference hosted by the investment bank Goldman Sachs.

This past week, between talk of growth and potential returns, tech titans found themselves addressing the abrupt resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon.

Coxon, a 27-year-old who worked at OpenAI before joining its chief rival Anthropic, said on Tuesday that people building artificial intelligence (AI) believed the technology could destroy humanity.

They are "gambling with our lives", he said, "these will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything".

Coxon is by no means the first AI insider to publicly sound the alarm. There have been a string of high-profile resignations from both Anthropic and OpenAI in recent years over apparent safety concerns, and some current Anthropic employees even echoed Coxon's post.

"We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," a team lead at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, posted on X.

While Coxon said explicitly in his posts that his warnings were "not marketing", some executives and investors in Silicon Valley have reacted with scepticism to a recent flurry of insiders sounding the alarm.

Anthropic and OpenAI are reportedly preparing for potentially record-setting initial public offerings, and some in the tech sector have suggested the latest stark comments about the dangers of AI may be designed to generate hype by signalling the power of these products.

Anthropic's boss, Dario Amodei, has come under fire for saying AI technology could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs and will "test who we are as a species".

One conference speaker, Grindr CEO George Arison, told the BBC he believed this week's comments from Coxon and others were indicative of an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic".

He called them "dangerous" and said they had prompted him to instruct some engineers at the LGBTQ+ dating app to stop using Anthropic's technology.

"It is irresponsible for us as stewards of our shareholders' money to be relying on a business that does what this company does, in terms of its public statements," he said.

"Maybe they actually believe it," Arison said. "Or you could argue they're saying it because it's a great way to gin up more investor support, because the only way to justify these valuations is to actually claim: 'I'm going to take over every industry and I'm going to take over every job, and my AI is going to be doing all that work.'"

Anthropic was valued at $965bn (Â£713bn) in its most recent fundraising round earlier this year.

The BBC has asked Anthropic for a response to the statements.

In an essay posted early on Saturday, Amodei called for a slowing of AI model development and global regulation - and said the risks associated with AI were "serious".

News.title: PM's top security adviser says Europe faces hard winter to keep pressure on Putin
News.content:
Speaking at the Yalta European Strategy forum, Powell said pressure on Putin was working "and that means we have to keep the pressure up".

He said: "What we don't want to do at this stage is take our foot off the gas - and literally, gas could be the problem as we come into the winter, where the EU is going to have real problems of shortage, and we cannot turn that into an advantage for Putin.

"It will require some real hardship and difficulties on our parts. But we will have to swallow that and we have to keep the economic, military, political and diplomatic support going for Ukraine."

Powell said things in Ukraine did "feel a bit difficult at the moment". He pointed to Russian jet drone attacks, strikes on Ukrainian businesses, the lack of Patriot air defences against ballistic missiles, and the government's budget deficit.

But he insisted "there are strong reasons for optimism". He said Trump â who has blown hot and cold over Ukraine â was "in a very different place".

"He sees that Ukraine is doing better, and therefore he is not leaning in the direction of Putin in the way that he was previously. I think that's a really big asset."

Powell said Russia was no longer claiming the US had agreed, at last year's Trump-Putin summit in Alaska, that Ukraine should give up territory and Nato membership.

"The so-called Anchorage compromise is firmly dead," Powell said. "That's gone. We can stop worrying about it. It's finished. I think that's a really important reason to be positive, because now we can look for serious ways of getting to a negotiated settlement, rather than waiting for the Ukrainian people to hand over territory the Russians have not been able to conquer."

He also pointed to Ukrainian commanders' success in holding the front line, the milestone of Russia suffering 1.5 million casualties since 2022, Ukraine's strikes deep in Russian territory and the fact "Europe has remained solid".

He said: "The strategy is to apply enough pressure to make [Putin] want to get into negotiation. And I think that the escalation we hear talk about is not a problem; it's a sign of success, because what's happening is the pressure that we are putting on Putin is finally paying off."

Putin himself has given little sign he is feeling under pressure, telling journalists earlier this month: "I have no doubt that the enemy will crumble."

Meanwhile Ukrainian authorities have begun evacuating some residents in Slovyansk and Kramatorsk, the biggest cities still under full Ukrainian control in the eastern Donbas region. The full capture of Donbas, made up of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, is a key objective for Russia.

Powell said it was "mug's game" to predict when the war might end but he said Europe had to be prepared to negotiate a settlement: "You have to be ready for one, and at some stage, where we least expect it, Putin will be ready to negotiate... It's all about getting him to be serious in that negotiation. And I think that strategy is beginning to work."

Powell, who helped negotiate the Good Friday Agreement in Northern Ireland, said it was "very important to maintain contact with Putin and the Russians".

He said: "What we don't want is miscalculation - that they don't understand where our red lines are. That's why I think it's important the CIA went to Moscow as well. I think we need to keep talking. I wrote a book called 'Talking to Terrorists'. I would certainly be in favour of talking to this terrorist as well - to try and maintain communication."

The war was "not about territory" but about "the right of Ukraine to be independent", Powell added, and "to the extent that [Putin] gains another 10km of land or loses another 40km of land, this war is already won".

He added: "That's the threat to him at home. There is a free, independent, and European Ukraine, and people in Russia are going to notice that."

News.title: Will the Thirlwall report change the debate about Lucy Letby?
News.content:
The quick take is this. The report won't change the narrative about Letby's guilt or innocence because it didn't examine that subject at all. That wasn't its remit.

Lady Justice Thirlwall said she had "approached the inquiry on the basis that Lucy Letby is guilty of the crimes of which she has been convicted".

She emphasised that it was not her role "to set about reviewing the convictions", telling the inquiry: "The Court of Appeal has done that, with a very clear result."

But there is also a longer, more complex answer.

Whatever the report's conclusions, Letby's convictions will stand. However, the inquiry hasn't operated in a vacuum. There are other parts of the legal system which will have an eye on its findings.

And the chairwoman of the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) - the only organisation with the power to send Letby's case back to the Court of Appeal - has told the BBC the CCRC will be paying close attention to Thirlwall.

Dame Vera Baird said: "We will be looking at the report with interest to assess whether it has any bearing on our review of the case."

The CCRC has given no indication of when it will make its decision.

But while questions over Letby's convictions weren't within the scope of the Thirlwall Inquiry, it didn't stop the subject making itself felt within the hearing room.

Just as the inquiry was wrapping up, the hospital's former executives applied for it to be delayed until the CCRC has made its decision.

Letters pushing for a delay were also written to the inquiry by Letby's lawyers and Sir David Davis, an MP who has campaigned on her behalf.

Sir David argued that an inquiry "predicated on the presumption that Lucy Letby's conviction is safe, when there is now a wealth of authoritative voices questioning that conviction, will only undermine the conclusions arrived at by your inquiry and potentially lead to more babies dying unnecessarily".

Lady Justice Thirlwall refused the requests to pause the inquiry. She said that she was not scrutinising Letby's actions, but those of the officials and managers who were responsible for responding to the crisis.

News.title: One dead, 102 rescued from Indonesian ferry that went missing in Java Sea
News.content:
One person has died and 102 have been rescued from a stricken Indonesian passenger ferry in the Java Sea, an official said.

A search and rescue operation was launched after contact was lost with the Virgo Transport 8 ship, which was carrying 243 people, as it encountered bad weather, Indonesia's search and rescue agency said.

The search for the remaining passengers is ongoing.

The ferry was travelling from Surabaya to the south Kalimantan city of Banjarmasin and was last reported to be about 150km south of Banjarmasin around 02:00 local time on Sunday.

Search and rescue ships and a helicopter have been deployed to the scene and all other vessels in that area of the Java Sea have been alerted to report signs of any passengers.

The incident comes after a separate ferry in Indonesia caught fire off Madura island last month, killing five.

The Indonesian archipelago has more than 17,000 islands and ferries are a common form of transport.

News.title: Diljit Dosanjh makes history under the famous Wembley arch
News.content:
On Saturday night, under the world-famous Wembley arch, five words rang out: "Punjabi Aa Gaye Wembley Oye!"

Indian megastar Diljit Dosanjh famously starts all his concerts by announcing that "the Punjabis have arrived".

But this time, it was a play on the usual catchphrase.

Dosanjh is the first ever Punjabi singer to headline Wembley Stadium, the music venue has said.

Addressing his fans, he reflected on the significance of the occasion. "This moment will go down in the history books," he said.

And as Bhangra beats blared out, fans erupted with cheers while Dosanjh launched into his biggest hits, from G.O.A.T. to Lover.

Over two decades, Dosanjh has built a huge global fanbase, topping charts and singing with the likes of Ed Sheeran.

He has even busted Bhangra moves with Jimmy Fallon, external, with the US talk show host labelling him "the biggest Punjabi artist on the planet".

His landmark concert at Wembley further cements his status as a global star.

Ahead of the show, the singer spoke exclusively to the BBC backstage, describing the moment as "a dream" for him.

News.title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England
News.content:
University applicants in England will be given clearer information about student loans before they take them out, the government has said.

Ministers said they would spell out that governments can change repayment rules and that different career choices can affect how much borrowers repay.

They agreed to some but not all of the recommendations made by MPs after an inquiry into student loans, and did not say whether they would reverse a freeze to the repayment threshold for some graduates.

The inquiry found the way loans had been presented to teenagers amounted to mis-selling, after the BBC revealed the Department for Education (DfE) had compared repayments to Â£30-a-month phone contracts.

The recent debate has centred around Plan 2 loans, which were issued in England between September 2012 and July 2023, and are still issued in Wales.

The interest rate on those loans is the Retail Prices Index (RPI) measure of inflation plus up to 3% depending on earnings, and borrowers repay at a rate of 9% of everything they earn over a repayment threshold, which is meant to rise with inflation every year. The loans are written off after 30 years.

Campaigners want a lower interest rate, a lower repayment rate and for the government to reverse a decision last year to freeze the threshold at Â£29,385 for three years in England.

Freezing that threshold means graduates start repaying their loans sooner and, once they do, they pay more than they would have done if it had risen with inflation.

MPs on the Treasury Committee called for a U-turn on that decision as part of a series of recommendations after an inquiry this summer.

The Treasury and the DfE did not say whether ministers would unfreeze the threshold in their response, but said: "We keep all aspects of the student finance system under review."

News.title: 'She's back': Fans dance, sing and cry after Céline Dion's comeback concert in Paris
News.content:
CÃ©line Dion's first concert in years delighted fans, with the Canadian singer crying as she made an emotional comeback to the stage.

It was Dion's first full concert in six years after she was diagnosed with a rare neurological disorder called stiff person syndrome, which forced her to cancel tours.

Joyful fans spilled out of the Paris La DÃ©fense Arena on Saturday night singing and dancing to her classic hits, while some were still wiping away tears.

Paris correspondent Hugh Schofield went along and reflects on getting swept up in the Dion dalliance that French fans are calling "the biggest comeback since Charles de Gaulle".

News.title: Reform receives second £36m donation in two days as crypto investor matches record
News.content:
Harborne has already donated millions to Reform and Farage, who is currently under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner over whether he should have declared a Â£5m cash gift from Harborne ahead of the 2024 election.

Farage has argued that he was under no obligation to register the "purely private" gift, as it was unrelated to his parliamentary or political activities.

The party is also facing scrutiny after a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week showed two senior Reform aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations.

The Metropolitan Police has said it is investigating, while the party denies any wrongdoing.

The force is also looking into donations given to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Farage ally George Cottrell, as well as a company controlled by Tice.

Harborne wrote on Saturday that he had "already accumulated enough wealth for the rest of my life", while Reform was a "start-up party" that lacked "the benefit of hundreds of years of patronage".

"A start-up party needs more money than can be provided by membership fees alone, to build and sustain itself and be ready for government," he said.

Harborne and Delo's donations mark the largest sums received by a UK political party since they had to begin declaring them in 2001.

Delo, who also announced his donation in a Telegraph op-ed, said he was giving the money away because he wanted a "fair fight and a level playing field". He said in April he was moving back to Britain from Hong Kong.

Addressing the recent scrutiny of Reform's finances, he said: "My conclusion from Reform's recent troubles is that they should spend less time trying to raise funds to compete on equal terms and more time preparing for government."

Last year, he was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over a breach of anti-money laundering laws at his crypto trading platform, BitMEX, to which he had pleaded guilty in 2022.

There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.

However, the Labour government has introduced a Â£100,000 cap on donations from British citizens living overseas, and plans to introduce a similar one for those who have recently returned to the UK.

There were nine donations of Â£1m or more to political parties in 2025. The largest was Â£9m given to Reform UK by Harborne.

Labour had five donations of Â£1m or more - totalling nearly Â£10m - and the Conservatives had three of Â£1m each.

Labour said Reform and Farage still had "serious questions" to answer about their finances.

Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said Reform were "drowning" in "sleaze and scandal".

She added: "It's time Farage and Reform came clean with the public, fully co-operated with the ongoing police investigations and prove they're not just in it for themselves."

Rachel Millward, deputy leader of the Green Party, told BBC News it wanted a cap on donations from individuals of Â£500,000.

She said the donations to Reform were "absolutely staggering amounts", adding: "What I am very frustrated about is the influence of extreme wealth and the super rich. What I want to see is people in politics representing the needs of their communities and ordinary people."

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart called for the government to introduce emergency legislation to cap donations.

She said: "These are eye-watering amounts of money. This is real emergency for our democracy. It presents a very clear and present threat."

Labour MP Stella Creasy and other backbenchers had proposed an amendment to the Government's Representation of the People Bill that would stop donors giving parties over Â£100,000 a year.

But the amendment was never debated in the Commons after the government said it would set up a task force to investigate the issue. The bill will be debated in the House of Lords on Monday.

Duncan Hames, Director of Policy and Programmes at campaigning charity Transparency International UK, said: "This is a watershed moment, with two billionaires pledging Â£72m to one political party in less than 48 hours.

"This situation is now completely out of control, and makes an irrefutable case for government to bring forward an annual cap on political donations, and fast."

News.title: 'Skimpflation' warning as tinned mackerel alternative hits more supermarket shelves
News.content:
A growing trend of supermarkets selling a cheaper, less nutritious alternative to tinned mackerel is an example of "skimpflation", a consumer group has said.

Princes - which supplies major supermarkets - has substituted jack mackerel, an entirely different species, for mackerel, with similar tins also being sold by Lidl.

The switch has been spurred by dwindling stocks of Atlantic mackerel after years of overfishing, with its Chilean counterpart more sustainable and a third of the cost.

"It's a real concern when manufacturers quietly downgrade everyday staples like these as shoppers can end up paying the same price for a product that delivers significantly less nutritional quality," Sue Davies, head of food policy at Which?, said.

Jack mackerel contains about half as much omega-3 and around a third as much vitamin B12 as traditional mackerel.

The shift has prompted complaints from some consumers over differences in taste and texture, as well as concerns about how clearly the replacement fish is being labelled.

Princes announced last October, external that it was changing all of its tinned mackerel products to jack mackerel, saying the species meets the Marine Stewardship Council's sustainability standards.

The firm said its jack mackerel products were "clearly identified" and had been introduced following extensive product and consumer testing, describing it as having a "milder flavour and meatier texture".

Lidl is selling jack mackerel under its house brand. Lidl GB said it was "committed to sourcing fish and seafood from responsibly managed fisheries".

Davies from Which? said: "While manufacturers face genuine supply chain pressures and sustainability challenges, they have a responsibility to shoppers to be completely upfront when they change a product's recipe."

She added: "Skimpflation - quietly changing ingredients to cut costs - has become increasingly common, but it can feel particularly sneaky as shoppers may not realise a product has changed until they get it home and eat it."

News.title: A united Ireland would be 'fantastic' says Trump during Irish visit
News.content:
The Good Friday Agreement says the secretary of state must hold a border poll if it appears likely that a majority of people in Northern Ireland would vote for Irish unification - and the circumstances of when that could happen is the subject of constant debate in Northern Ireland and the Republic.

Earlier this week, Martin said there needed to be more clarity on when a border poll can be called, while Burnham ruled out calling a referendum, describing a poll as "off the table".

Sinn FÃ©in leader Mary Lou McDonald said she acknowledged Trumps comments on a united Ireland and said the onus is on the Taoiseach to begin planning.

Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson said Trump "knows better than most that elections matter".

"Northern Ireland's constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington," he said.

Former DUP MP Ian Paisley and close friend of the Trump family said: "everyone is allowed a personal opinion even when it's wrong".

Welcoming his comments, the leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) Claire Hanna said there was something "fairly extraordinary" about Trump standing in Dublin and talking openly about Irish unity.

"When even Donald Trump has clocked that Irish unity is no longer some distant or theoretical prospect, it tells you something about just how far this conversation has shifted."

The Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Jon Burrows said while America is an "important ally," Northern Ireland's future will be decided by its people".

The Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said Trump "is not the first US President to meddle in the affairs which don't concern him".

Ireland's Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said: "Something to this magnitude can only happen where there's consent from the Irish people.

"It's something that that we have to work on and we have to work towards."

Later, while attending an event at the US Ambassador to Ireland's residence, Trump said there is "no good answer" to a question about a united Ireland.

Recalling the moment, he said: "Oh that's a nice question, I have a nice answer, I think, we'll read about it tomorrow."

News.title: Three arrests at rival protests in Portsmouth
News.content:
The new powers came into effect at 10:00 BST. Participants on both sides were not seen to be wearing any face coverings when the marches started.

The city centre protests follow disorder on 6 September, when police attended Eastney Marina as hundreds of demonstrators blocked roads in an attempt to stop coaches carrying 120 migrants, who had crossed the Channel in a dinghy, from leaving the city.

On Saturday, up to 500 anti-migrant protesters held Union and St George flags while some wearing Portsmouth Patriot branded clothing gathered outside All Saints Church on Commercial Road shortly before midday on Saturday.

The crowd chanted "stop the boats" as they marched to Guildhall Square.

About 300 people joined the counter-protest.

Both sets of demonstrators were kept apart by police when they arrived at the square.

Speaking before the march, Simon Magorian, of Stand up to Racism Portsmouth, described the demonstrations in Eastney as a "horrible spectacle".

He said: "Portsmouth is actually a good functioning multi-cultural city.

"We are now organising to have the broadest possible opposition to what we see as a fascist street movement and we're not going to allow them to get a grip on Portsmouth or any other town - this is quite terrifying."

News.title: Oscar-winning film producer Jeremy Thomas dies aged 77
News.content:
Oscar-winning producer Jeremy Thomas, whose films included The Last Emperor and Sexy Beast, has died aged 77.

The British filmmaker "passed away peacefully" surrounded by family and loved ones at his home in Oxfordshire on Friday, his publicist said in a statement.

Thomas built an international reputation over a career spanning five decades, working with directors including David Cronenberg, Nagisa Oshima, Julien Temple and Nicolas Roeg and backing independent films alongside mainstream successes.

His best known film, Bernardo Bertolucci's The Last Emperor, won nine Academy Awards, including best picture, and earned Thomas an Oscar as producer in 1988.

The critically-acclaimed biographical drama about the final monarch of China's Qing dynasty starred Joan Chen, Peter O'Toole and Vivian Wu.

Thomas repeatedly collaborated with Bertolucci, also producing The Sheltering Sky, Little Buddha, Stealing Beauty and The Dreamers.

He worked with several British directors at the start of their careers including Ben Wheatley, Jonathan Glazer, Stephen Frears and David Mackenzie.

Thomas's other credits included Oshima's Merry Christmas, Mr Lawrence - starring David Bowie - Cronenberg's A Dangerous Method, Roeg's Bad Timing and Eureka, and Matteo Garrone's Pinocchio.

He also produced Fast Food Nation, The Great Rock 'n' Roll Swindle, The Hit and adaptations of the JG Ballard books Crash and High-Rise.

After beginning as a film editor, London-based Thomas landed his first production role on the 1976 Australian film Mad Dog Morgan.

A former chairman of the British Film Institute, he won a Bafta for outstanding British contribution to cinema in 1990. Thomas received the European Film Academy's award for outstanding European achievement in world cinema in 2006 and was made a CBE in the New Year Honours in 2009.

Thomas's latest collaboration with Japanese director Takashi Miike, Bad Lieutenant:Tokyo, is due to premiere at the Toronto Film Festival on Monday.

News.title: Elderly woman found dead named by police
News.content:
An elderly woman whose death sparked a murder investigation has been named by police.

Thames Valley Police (TVP) said Jill Gant, aged 88, was found dead at an address on Appleford Drive in Abingdon, Oxfordshire at about 14:20 BST on Thursday afternoon.

Her family are being supported by specially trained officers.

A 36-year-old man from Abingdon who was arrested on suspicion of murder remains in police custody.

News.title: Battle to save the tiny, gooey snail only found in one lake in the UK
News.content:
A tiny snail found in only one lake in the UK has been dubbed as precious as an Egyptian artefact as conservationists bid to save it.

Several British zoos are setting up so-called ark populations of the glutinous snail, one of Europe's rarest species, using creatures bred in a back garden in Ceredigion.

"Beguiled by their cuteness," conservationist Ian Hughes has made it his "life-defining" mission to protect the threatened mollusc, which was once widespread in UK waters.

"There was a point where we'd got more snails in our garden than have ever been seen in the wild," he said.

News.title: Six people rescued after yacht gets tangled in fish farm
News.content:
Six people have been rescued after a 46ft yacht got into difficulty off the coast of Northern Ireland.

Red Bay Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) spent seven hours at sea in the early hours of Saturday morning off Cushendall, County Antrim.

Belfast Coastguard received a distress call from the boat, which had been travelling from Oban in Scotland to Portugal.

The yacht lost all power and steering after making contact with a fish farm in Red Bay, in 60 knots of wind, causing it to become trapped.

A lifeboat was launched at 03:22 BST, with an inshore lifeboat also launched.

In a statement Red Bay RNLI described the weather conditions as "difficult" due to "Force 9 gusting winds, driving rain and the darkness of night".

The RNLI crew observed that those on the yacht were safe and, given the difficult weather and sea conditions, the decision was made "for the sailors to remain onboard the yacht and for the lifeboat to standby until daylight broke" at 07:30.

At 09.30 the lifeboat crew "successfully freed the yacht from the fish farm and brought the sailors safely to Glenarm".

Those on the yacht stayed onboard the vessel while it was towed by the RNLI, who said there were no injuries.

The yacht is now receiving repairs.

Speaking following the call out, Paddy McLaughlin, Red Bay RNLI Coxswain said: "This was a challenging call out in difficult weather conditions, but we were delighted to bring the sailors to safety, and we would like to wish them well.

"We would also like to commend our colleagues in the Coastguard and thank our crew who responded quickly in the middle of the night, launched our lifeboats in darkness and made their way to the scene in what were gale force conditions, and for then spending seven hours at sea."

News.content:

It’s a warm Ecuadorian morning and my kayak is rapidly hurtling towards a pair of penguins sitting on some rocks. Only the length of my paddle stops me from crashing into the seabirds and as I worry that the scraping of plastic on the rocks might startle them – but they barely flinch. Welcome to the Galapagos Islands.

Such a close encounter would usually frighten an animal at home in Britain, but a four-night Galapagos Islands cruise with National Geographic Lindblad Expeditions quickly made me understand what naturalist Charles Darwin meant when he described this beautiful part of the globe as “a little world within itself.”

And the experience is extremely different to the contemporary cruises that we are used to. There was no no big terminal to welcome us, just an early morning flight from Quito, Ecuador’s capital to Baltra Island, in the centre of the archipelago, before we boarded a zodiac to transport us to National Geographic Islander II.

open image in gallery National Geographic Islander II rests in the calm Galapagos waters ( Marc Shoffman )



The first surprise was that there are no room keys. You can lock your door from the inside to enjoy the spacious suites – but with just 48 guests on board, this is more like sailing with trusted family (plus there is CCTV in the public areas and hallways). Everyone received a name badge, helping us to quickly get to know our fellow passengers, who were mainly from the United States.

There were no waterslides, ice cream shops or LED screens promoting evening shows but my 11 and 13-year-old daughters were fully engaged, happily kayaking or snorkelling among the turtles, parrot fish and manta rays in the unseasonably warm waters.

These were activities they would have approached nervously back home. Here, though, my eldest Isabelle enjoyed jumping off the side of the ship during swim stops, while her younger sister Amelie learned how to pilot a zodiac herself.

The headliner here, however, was the nature and wildlife. You need to get up early for it though.

A key feature of our trip was 5.45am wake up calls to avoid the heat and capture the wildlife at its calmest.

We quickly learned that this wasn’t the type of cruise where you lie in or pack your fancy shoes or best clothes. Everything will get wet or sandy, or sandy and wet. Guests travel from the ship to each destination on a zodiac – known as Galapagos Ubers – for either a wet landing as you disembark from the water onto a beach or a dry one onto rocks.

open image in gallery The Galapagos penguin is the only penguin found north of the equator ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

Our first early start was worth it as we visited South Plaza Island to be greeted by sleepy sea lions and the region’s unique swallow-tailed gulls – the world’s only nocturnal gulls – who had recovered from a night of hunting to avoid the scavenger frigate birds who try to steal their food by daylight.

There are a few rules in the Galapagos Islands. Guests must be accompanied by a guide, with limits of 16 per naturalist to keep crowds down. You can’t take anything from the islands even if the shells look really pretty and you must always stand six feet or two metres from the wildlife.

As days passed, it was hard not to go right up to a sea lion and rub their bellies. But the reward for keeping our distance was that the wildlife seemed unbothered by our presence.

open image in gallery Sea lions seem to pose for pictures with you in the Galapagos Islands ( Marc Shoffman )

Galapagos penguins perched proudly on the rocks of the Bainbridge Islets and sea lions laid down calmly as we passed, ready to be photographed.

Even the Galapagos land iguana looked as if they were content next to their own piece of cactus. Just days before the trip, our daughters were worried about small lizards they encountered in Miami before we headed to Quito. Now they were obsessively taking photos of giant ones.

Every stop was a photo opportunity. On Las Bachas island, rare birds such as the red-footed booby and shiny white Nazca boobies simply waddled by or nodded as they sat on eggs while we passed on strictly-followed tracks. My favourite was seeing the famous giant tortoises as they calmly ate grass at the Rancho El Manzanillo, unfazed by our gawping.

open image in gallery A Galapagos land iguana poses by cactus ( Marc Shoffman )



The main interaction between humans and wildlife comes in the form of conservation efforts, such as tracking wildlife migrations and growing new cacti. Cruise ship capacity is capped at 100 passengers. None of the animals are trapped behind glass, there are no crowds waiting for a penguin show and no gift shop. It made me wonder if I can ever go to a zoo again.

The landscape was also full of wonder. We hiked on a mix of beaches, rocky terrains and even volcanic scenery with hundred year-old black lava on Sullivan Bay.

Back on the ship, there was plenty more to learn, with attentive staff serving serving up Ecuadorian delicacies such as ceviche in a unique sweet tomato-lime broth.

open image in gallery The famous giant Galapagos tortoise are even bigger in real life ( Marc Shoffman )

Passengers mingled over dinner and drinks and during a karaoke evening where a shy lady from Missouri revealed her operatic talents while an older solo traveller surprised us all with a Japanese pop song.

Evening talks reminded us of the nature we had encountered and prepared us for the next day of adventure.

We also enjoyed helpful daytime lectures while sailing between destinations such as on smartphone camera skills – vital to get memorable snaps of the region – and, of course, there were chances to learn about Darwin.

One of the most interesting facts we were told was that he was only actually in the Galapagos Islands for five weeks and never returned.

I hope we do.

How to do it

Prices for a seven-day Galapagos Islands cruise with National Geographic Lindblad Expeditions start from £4,931 per person, with departures all year-round. All meals and tours are included. Internal flights from Quito or Guayaquil to Baltra Island are included.

Book now

The death toll from the fire that gutted a passenger ferry in the Philippines last week rose to 76 after rescue crews recovered more bodies on Saturday.

At least 13 people were still unaccounted for following the inferno that swept through the vessel on Wednesday night off southwestern Palawan province. There were 132 people on board the ferry and 43 survived the disaster. Coastguard images captured the ship's blackened interior, revealing ashes, warped metal, a destroyed car, and suspected human remains.

The ferry had sailed from the capital Manila and was 39km from its final destination of Coron, Palawan, when the fire erupted.

Although the precise cause was yet to be established, a coast guard spokesperson cited a survivor who recalled hearing an explosion, suggesting the fire likely started in the cargo hold before winds fanned it across the vessel.

The spokesperson, Commodore Noemie Cayabyab, said authorities were searching for the vessel's captain who reportedly survived the incident but was not included on the official list of survivors. A multiagency investigation would assess all angles, including any potential liability on the part of the captain and crew.

Ms Cayabyab said survivors described the fire spreading too fast for passengers to retrieve life jackets. She added that tarpaulins shielding open areas from rain “may be a possible contributing factor but we can’t determine now if they were trapped inside".

Investigators were reviewing whether emergency procedures were followed, such as sounding alarms or providing instructions.

A survivor earlier described how panicked crowds trampled him as he attempted to secure a life jacket.

"The fire quickly spread. That’s when I dropped to the ground and my back was burned," Arnulfo Nokki Villanueva recounted in a video broadcast by News5. He said that he jumped from a window. "I wanted to get a life jacket but failed to get one because people were stepping on me. People were in panic."

Philippine coast guard personnel stand next to body bags of victims of the ferry fire in Coron, Palawan province, on 12 September 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

Intense heat and heavy smoke had severely hindered rescue workers on Thursday, delaying search efforts for any trapped passengers inside the vessel.

“It’s painful to think that your child was asking for help while she was burning alive," Lira Daco said as she waited at a rescue centre in Turda for word about her missing 20-year-old daughter Cyriel.

“I don’t know how we can find out which one is my child," she added regarding the remains found inside the ship. "It’s ok if she just drowned and we can recover her body and give her a proper burial. But now we can’t recognize or hug her."

Ship records indicated that 134 people – 117 passengers and 17 crew – were aboard the vessel, which had a total carrying capacity of 306 passengers and 27 crew.

Two people listed on the manifest later informed authorities that they hadn’t boarded, the coastguard reported.

Among those saved were two Chilean tourists, confirmed Rachel Conserman, a staff member at vessel owner Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc.

Both are currently receiving hospital treatment in Coron for their injuries.

Coron is a popular tourist destination, renowned for its clear blue waters, dramatic limestone cliffs and rock formations.

Ferries serve as a widespread means of transport across the Philippine archipelago. Maritime accidents are not uncommon due to severe storms, poorly maintained craft, overcrowding and weak enforcement of safety regulations, particularly in remote island provinces.

The region previously suffered the history's worst peacetime sea disaster in 1987, when the ferry Dona Paz collided with an oil tanker in the central Philippines, claiming over 4,300 lives.

Camille Cottin is teaching me to swear in French. I’d asked the 47-year-old about the comedy series that made her famous in her native country, the name of which I’m valiantly trying not to butcher. “Do you mean Connasse?” she offers, kindly. That’s the one! In it she cut her teeth playing Parisian meanies, which was perfect preparation for Andréa Martel, the swaggering and hilariously icy celebrity wrangler in Call My Agent!, who made her globally famous. Connasse, she says, typically gave her fellow Frenchies a particular idea of her.

“We don’t have a proper translation for that word,” she explains. “It means to be a bit rogue, I suppose. But you have ‘con’ and you have ‘connasse’, and ‘con’ literally means ‘c***’.”

I practically spit out my drink. “Connasse”, she adds, puts a little twist on the word.

“It has something a bit mean about it,” she continues. “Arrogant. Despising. Pretentious. Someone with no consideration for others.”

It was a hidden camera show, which saw Cottin behaving obnoxiously towards unsuspecting members of the public. She notoriously attempted to climb the gates of Kensington Palace to woo Prince Harry for the film version of the show – though, contrary to popular belief, she didn’t actually spend two nights in a London jail as punishment. An arrest and a firm talking to, though? That was accurate. Anyway, the show’s backers knew Connasse would create waves early into its development, and asked Cottin if she’d prefer them to change the title. “They were like, ‘Are you sure? Because people will call you ‘connasse’. But I didn’t think anyone would really watch it.” Cut to its release, and Connasse’s backers were proven correct.

“For years I would be in the supermarket and people would scream ‘hey c***!’ at me.” She hoots with husky laughter. “But it’s fine. People still watch it here in France, so I’ll always hear a little ‘c***’ from time to time.”

I genuinely thought I would never work again. But then Call My Agent! started being binged, and that encouraged the producers to think, OK – why did we end this?

Cottin is great fun, like a glamorous socialite with a mouth like a sailor. She’s at home in Paris, her hair shampoo-ad glossy and her schedule all over the shop. She’s been juggling promotion for three separate projects at once: a film adaptation of Les Misérables, a film version of Call My Agent! on Netflix, and a brilliant coming-of-age comedy called Just an Illusion that this week arrives in UK and Irish cinemas. Life is nicely chaotic, as proven when her 11-year-old daughter wanders into Cottin’s room to try to borrow the iPad she’s speaking to me on. (Funnily enough, a similar thing happened the last time Cottin was in the pages of The Independent, which might suggest her daughter just really, really dislikes us.)

Just an Illusion finds Cottin in mum mode on-screen, playing the restless mother to Vincent, an 11-year-old boy growing up in the suburbs of Paris in the late Eighties. Vincent, as played by the bright newcomer Simon Boublil, pines for a classmate, hilariously discovers blue movies with his friends, and starts asking all of the big questions in life. But it’s a journey of self-actualisation that is mirrored in his parents, too. Cottin’s Sandrine longs for a life outside of domesticity, and Louis Garrel’s Yves struggles through prolonged unemployment.

“It was this moment in time where it suddenly became possible for women to try to access more from life,” Cottin says. “I think the worst thing is not being able to evolve and to have projects and to imagine something else for your existence. And I liked the fact that Sandrine rebels, but in a quiet way. It’s a quiet rebellion.”

open image in gallery Louis Garrel and Camille Cottin in ‘Just an Illusion’ ( Manuel Moutier )

She saw her own mother’s struggles in Sandrine’s, and the battles her generation waged that allowed Cottin’s generation to be free. “Adventure, travelling and existing outside the norm,” she says. “They’re all things I’ve been attracted to.” She sighs. “It’s complicated, though, being a mother and still wanting those things. It sometimes doesn’t convene so easily.” She has an older son, aged 16, too. She says acting is the closest she can get to adventure and travelling now. “It gives you the possibility to live multiple lives at once. It’s a beautiful gift.”

Just an Illusion felt real to her, she adds – up to a point, anyway. “Well, Vincent manages to seduce the girl of his dreams in the end,” she laughs. “When I was that age, all the boys I was in love with were absolutely never in love with me.”

And, I add, it takes forever to get over them, doesn’t it?

“Exactly,” she says. “And he’s always the popular guy who’s an asshole to you and bullies you, but you love him anyway. But then years later you see him in the supermarket and he’s lost all of his charisma and he’s not cool anymore, and [you realise] how much I’d prefer to be me than be with him.” It’s a tangent that suddenly becomes incredibly profound. It’s very, very French.

open image in gallery Camille Cottin in the ‘Call My Agent!’ series ( Netflix )

I tell her that Just an Illusion is being released in the UK during the same week as Netflix unveils the film version of Call My Agent!. It seems to be news to her. “Oh god, that’s so much of me!” The original show transformed her from a local success story – she was a jobbing actor bouncing between theatre and television beforehand – into an international one. Roles in the likes of House of Gucci and the Matt Damon drama Stillwater followed.

She says she’s always had a funny relationship with the show, which ended just as it took off worldwide. “This seems completely megalomaniacal to say, but it’s been seen in quite a lot of countries,” she laughs. “It was really Covid, I think, because it all takes place in the office and people were missing the office at that point.”

Covid was rough for her, personally speaking. “I genuinely thought I would never work again, and that Covid was the end of everything. But then Call My Agent! started being binged, and that encouraged the producers to think, OK – why did we end this?”

In the new film, Cottin’s Andréa has departed the agent life to direct her own movie, even at one point wooing a cameo-ing George Clooney to star in it. If the series felt as if it ended a bit abruptly, with Andréa’s agency collapsing and all the characters going their separate ways, Call My Agent! The Movie is more of a love letter – to cinema, to work, to friendship. Fanny Herrero, who wrote the show’s first three seasons but not its fourth, has also returned, and Cottin says her presence was felt.

“Season four ended up quite sad – the agency had closed, Andréa’s relationships had been torn apart, everybody went on their way alone. It was not a happy end, so it was great to have everyone back together.”

open image in gallery Camille Cottin and Vincent Macaigne in ‘Call My Agent! The Movie’ ( Netflix )

Even if Call My Agent! had finished as a series, though, it was tricky to escape overall. The premise has been remade a staggering 11 times so far – in countries as far and wide as Turkey and Indonesia – with more on the horizon. But the not-very-good British version of the show, titled Ten Percent, was swiftly cancelled in 2022 after a single series. Cottin won’t be broached on her thoughts on it, but she says that remaking a hit is an inherently risky proposition. She would know, after all – in 2019 she chose to star in a French adaptation of Phoebe Waller-Bridge’s Fleabag. She admits it didn’t work.

“We decided to do it at a time when nobody in France had seen it,” she says. “But by the time we’d done it, the original had exploded. That’s the thing with remakes: you don’t control the timeline. And it was exactly the same show only without Phoebe, who’s like the beating heart of it. And it all came from her mind. It was, you know, maybe a mistake.”

“I think remakes are great when you want to remake something that hasn’t been widely shared already,” she continues. “You have to be precious with them. Everything is global now, everyone watches in lots of different languages. So remaking a film, or a TV show – it’s dangerous.”

Coming from a woman who risked arrest by the Met all for the sake of a comedy skit, we should probably take her word for it.

‘Just an Illusion’ is in cinemas, and ‘Call My Agent! The Movie’ is streaming on Netflix

News.title: Garcia vs Benn LIVE: Fight result and reaction tonight as ‘King Ryan’ demolishes Benn in second round
News.content:
Conor Benn opens up on fatherhood, masculinity and Ryan Garcia

Conor Benn suffered a quick defeat by Ryan Garcia on Saturday, as the divisive American put away his controversial British counterpart in two rounds.

Benn was fighting for a world title for the first time as he challenged Garcia in Las Vegas, but after a bitter build-up, the “Destroyer” became the destroyed for the first time in his career.

Garcia, 28, handed Benn, 29, his first stoppage loss, retaining the WBC welterweight belt courtesy of a huge right hook in round two. The shot dropped Benn, who beat the referee’s count but was overwhelmed by the ensuing onslaught from “King Ryan”.

With that, Benn’s attention may return to middleweight, where he traded wins with Chris Eubank Jr in 2025. In fact, Benn’s fierce rival may even be next in a trilogy bout on British soil.

Follow all the fallout from Garcia vs Benn below.

Conor Benn suffered a quick defeat by Ryan Garcia on Saturday, as the divisive American put away his controversial British counterpart in two rounds.

Garcia, 28, handed Benn, 29, his first stoppage loss, retaining the WBC welterweight belt courtesy of a huge right hook in round two. The shot dropped Benn, who beat the referee’s count but was overwhelmed by the ensuing onslaught from “King Ryan”.

open image in gallery Conor Benn was stopped for the first time as he challenged Ryan Garcia ( Getty )

Benn had started with heavy pressure, as expected, while Garcia looked to counter with his trademark left hook. One such punch had Benn stumbling somewhat in the first round, but Garcia proved he is dangerous with both hands when he sealed the stoppage with his right.

“I’ve always had a right hand, but I’ve always had injuries,” Garcia said in the ring after the fight. “I’m just happy, man, I’m blessed.”

He added: “I feel very... It’s surprising, I feel at peace. In my locker room, we were playing worship music the whole time, praising my Lord and saviour Jesus Christ.

“I wanna thank Conor for a great build-up, a great match. I’m blessed to fight on this day, Mexican Independence [Weekend].

“I want to say a few words from my heart about this: I know some people don’t see me as Mexican because I don’t speak Spanish, but my heart never goes away from you guys.”

While Saturday’s main event brought plenty of hype, it also proved controversial due to each boxer’s drug-test controversies. In 2022, Benn failed two drug tests and was provisionally suspended from boxing in the UK, before he was cleared to do so in 2024. Also in 2024, Garcia failed a drug test and served a one-year ban. Both fighters maintained their innocence throughout the episodes.

Despite the manner of the build-up to Saturday’s fight, Benn was quick to congratulate Garcia after the bout, which marked Benn’s second-ever professional loss – following his points defeat by Chris Eubank Jr last April.

open image in gallery Garcia dropped Benn with a huge right hook in round two ( AP )

And after Saturday’s result, Benn’s attention may turn back to Eubank Jr, with whom he traded wins in 2025. After Eubank Jr outpointed his compatriot at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Benn returned the favour in the same venue in November.

Both bouts – between the sons of old rivals Nigel Benn and Eubank Sr – took place at middleweight, and Benn may feel his days fighting below that division are done.

Meanwhile, Garcia could be set for an all-American clash with Teofimo Lopez, who recently won the WBA welterweight title, and who tried to face off with King Ryan in the ring on Saturday.

Chris Eubank Jr was quick to react to Conor Benn’s loss to Ryan Garcia on Saturday, mocking his bitter rival after the emphatic defeat.

Benn was fighting for a world title for the first time, challenging Garcia for the WBC welterweight belt, when he suffered a second-round loss in Las Vegas.

Benn, 29, started aggressively as expected, but he walked onto a huge right hook in the second frame, as Garcia, 28, dropped the Briton badly. Benn beat the referee’s count but was quickly overwhelmed, leading the official to step in.

Conor Benn beat the referee’s count but was soon stopped anyway ( Getty )

The result marked Benn’s second-ever loss, and his first via stoppage; in April 2025, Eubank Jr outpointed Benn, who returned the favour in November.

And Eubank Jr wasted little time in reacting to Benn’s loss, tweeting: “Welcome to the ’fighting after cutting too much weight’ club… Enjoy.”

Eubank Jr was referencing the fact that Benn was fighting at welterweight for the first time in two-and-a-half years, with the “Destroyer” having boxed Eubank Jr up at middleweight in their two bouts, before outpointing Regis Prograis at a 150lb catchweight in April.

Eubank Jr, 36, was also referencing his own complaints about facing Benn at middleweight, having repeatedly claimed that super-middleweight is his preferred division at this stage of his career.

A trilogy bout between Benn and Eubank could well be next, with Benn surely likely to leave welterweight behind him for good.
