Sculptor Nathan Scott believes it is important to highlight all aspects of Canadian history. He sculpted the four newest statues in 2019, referring to them as "the unfortunate four" for what he sees as their limited achievements in office.

"I'm a proud Canadian. I love our history," he said. "It wasn't always done perfectly. It's the good, bad and sometimes there's ugliness to it, but it's who we are."

"And if we don't have history, if we try to erase it, who are we? Who are we at all?"

Nathan Scott rests his hand on his sculpture of Sir Robert Borden. Scott finished the newest statues in 2019, calling them 'the unfortunate four,' but was forced to hide them following backlash. (John Dalusong/CBC)

13 statues to go

Future changes to the project could yet win over opponents, Skinner said. They proposed changing its name, moving it to a hidden area so people don't have to see it and better collaboration with Indigenous people.

For his part, Bourgeois said the educational aspect of the project will remain important. This includes hosting educational symposia where the history and work of each prime minister will be discussed.

For now, the long-term goal remains completing the remaining 13 statues, he said.

Though Canada has had 24 prime ministers, Justin Trudeau and Mark Carney won't be included in the current project — to avoid it becoming "a little bit too political," Bourgeois said.

World.title: Time for a digital divorce? Trade war puts spotlight on Canada's relationship with U.S. big tech
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Canada's data in foreign hands: why digital sovereignty matters: Just Asking 1:05:27 Canada’s data in foreign hands: why digital sovereignty matters

Trade and political tensions between Canada and the United States have raised concerns about Canada's digital sovereignty, but what does that term mean, and how can Canada promote it?

While it may sound like jargon, experts say digital sovereignty can be defined simply.

It's about regulation, Vass Bednar, managing director of independent public policy think-tank the Canadian Shield Institute, told CBC Radio's Just Asking.

"Fundamentally, our digital sovereignty is our ability to regulate digital environments using the tools that we have," she said, including regulation of algorithms that influence what information we see online.

It's also about choice and the law, according to Michael Geist, Canada Research Chair in internet and e-commerce law at the University of Ottawa.

"It's fundamentally about both the ability to make Canadian choices … so we have alternatives to some of the larger — predominately U.S. — players, and also ensuring that Canadian law applies," he told CBC Manitoba's Information Radio last week.

The federal government also has a definition.

"Digital sovereignty means Canada stays in control of its own digital future — including its data, technology and essential online services — instead of relying on foreign companies, foreign systems or foreign laws," a government webpage reads.

"Think of it like this: Just as we want our homes, money and identities protected in Canada, we want the same protection for our digital information and services."

A mid-August X post from the U.S. Trade Representative account said a potential trade deal between Canada and the U.S. would include "digital trade alignment," which prompted expert concerns and speculation about digital sovereignty. Only days later, talks between the two countries fell apart at the last minute, reportedly over American insistence that U.S. streaming companies be exempt from Canadian content rules.

After talks broke down, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that Lake Ontario be renamed Lake America. Google and Apple Maps quickly implemented the change for American users, but some Canadians reported seeing it on their maps.

So, how American is our tech?

Right now, Canada doesn't have many alternatives to American technology companies and digital platforms.

"We are heavily dependent on the American big tech companies when it comes to our Canadian businesses and the public sector," said Shion Guha, assistant professor in information and computer science at the University of Toronto, on Just Asking.

The federal government also uses the Microsoft Office and Microsoft 365 platforms. In January, Shared Services Canada, which is responsible for providing IT services to the government, renewed its agreement with Microsoft in a deal worth $940 million over seven years.

University of Toronto assistant professor Shion Guha says Canada's public and private sectors both lean heavily on U.S. tech. (Submitted by Shion Guha)

Guha was part of a study on the federal government's AI Register which found that Microsoft was the single biggest supplier of systems, accounting for 42 of 409.

"An American big tech company is very heavily intertwined, not just with things like email or OneDrive … or Microsoft Office, but also in the types of predictive analytics and other types of AI products that the federal government has currently acquired," Guha said.

"This type of dependence on one big tech company is generally not a good thing for any kind of sovereignty."

There is precedent for switching, Bednar said, noting, "France has been a little bit ahead of the curve here."

France's Interministerial Directorate for Digital Affairs announced in April that it will remove Microsoft's Windows operating system from government computers. Open-source software Linux will replace it.

The French government also developed Tchap, an instant messaging application, and mandated its use for public sector employees, citing security and privacy concerns. The French government says over 600,000 public sector employees use the app.

The French government developed Tchap, a messaging app for public sector employees, as a way to promote security. (https://tchap.numerique.gouv.fr/)

What can Canadians do?

But if getting the Canadian government to switch platforms could be difficult, getting Canadians to change everything from their credit cards to their cloud storage to their social media and instant messaging platforms and more could be even harder.

Gander Social launched in July, marketing itself as a nicer, Canadian alternative to U.S. social media platforms. The company posted on Facebook last week, saying it's approaching 50,000 users, though Bednar pointed out that Prime Minister Mark Carney isn't among them.

WATCH | Gander wants to make social media more Canadian: Homegrown app Gander wants to make social media more Canadian | Duration 2:03 Gander, a new social media app similar to X or Bluesky, was designed for Canadians — but many are skeptical that being homegrown alone will be enough to get users to try it.

But having Canadian options doesn't mean Canadians will want them, Guha said.

"There is a certain amount of inertia in getting Canadians to switch to things, because convenience usually rules over most things," he said.

"Just because we can, or do, have Canadian alternatives — and they may provide better features, they may be good for us — doesn't mean that we can overcome the social inertia to get people to switch."

But it is one way ordinary Canadians can promote digital sovereignty, Bednar said. Though she also acknowledged it's going to require more "institutional imagination in Canada" to move forward.

Staying sovereign in the AI age

The Canadian government released its National AI Strategy in June. In it, the government pledges to develop a home-grown supercomputer, as well as "sovereign cloud, AI, cyber and quantum initiatives."

Geist said the government should take an approach that balances building Canadian AI programs with access to foreign ones.

"If a single government gets to determine whether or not you have access to those frontier models, they're really determining whether or not you've got the very best tools to counter things like cybersecurity threats," he said.

Guha said the federal government has also started referring to the data centres that help power AI and other services as "critical infrastructure."

The federal government's five principles for data centre construction, released earlier this month, require projects to "strengthen Canada's long-term digital resilience, security and compute capacity." They also say that the facilities must follow Canadian laws on cybersecurity and data protection.

"If we don't make the rules here, we will have to follow someone else's,” AI Minister Evan Solomon said at a news conference announcing the principles, which arrive amid concerns about the U.S. government using its laws to access Canadian data.

A data centre under construction at Steeles Technology Campus in Toronto. Building more data centres in Canada is one way of promoting digital sovereignty, says Michael Geist, but many Canadians have voiced opposition to having them in their communities. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

Bednar said Canada's current effort to assert its sovereignty against the U.S. is different from those of the past because of how much more of our lives exist digitally.

"Digital ... is the infrastructure of our economy," she said.

"It is just as, if not arguably more, important than manufacturing, automobiles, aluminum, steel — take your pick."

World.title: Swedish election could see far-right party join government for 1st time
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Swedes vote in an election on Sunday that will either bring a far-right party into government for ‌the first time or shift the country back towards the liberalism it has long been known for.

Sweden's centre-left opposition holds a narrow lead over the ruling right-wing bloc ahead of a Sept. 13 election for parliament, pointing to a likely change of government, several opinion polls have shown this week.

But Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, who has trailed in opinion polls throughout his four years ​in office, has been catching up in the final weeks of campaigning, with rival Magdalena ​Andersson and her Social Democrats losing ground.

Supporters of the right-wing bloc say its policies have helped curb gang violence and cut immigration dramatically, and that a victory would amount to a public endorsement of that approach and more in ​the same vein in the years ahead.

"We can unify parties, voters and issues into joint action. That's why we ⁠get things done," Kristersson, who ⁠has pledged to bring the far-right Sweden Democrats into government if his bloc wins, ‌told reporters in parliament this week.

Magdalena Andersson of the centre-left Social Democrats, left, and Ulf Kristersson of Sweden's ruling right-wing bloc are seen before a televised debate in Gavle on Wednesday. (Anders Wiklund /TT News Agency/The Associated Press)

Critics counter that the agenda is undermining civil liberties while forcing immigrants to conform more closely to Swedish cultural norms or leave the country, urged on by both carrot and stick.

"We've become a harder society, a quieter society, but also a poorer society as we've had growth far below our potential and where households see their pay checks buy ⁠less and less," Andersson told Reuters.

"Our country has based its strength on sharing in each other's achievements and that we stick together when things are hard."

Polling stations in the EU member state of 10 million people, which joined NATO after Russia's full-scale invasion ‌of Ukraine, open at 8 a.m. local with exit polls due soon after they close at 8 p.m.

People line up outside a polling station in Stockholm on Friday. (Nicklas Thegerström/TT News Agency/The Associated Press)

Electoral success for the Sweden Democrats would be welcomed by Europe's rising far-right parties, boosted by a significant win in a German state election this month by the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany.

The right has already agreed to form a four-party government led by Kristersson if they win, while Andersson's ​path to power is more uncertain.

The election could ultimately be decided by whether the Liberals surpass the 4 per cent threshold to win seats in parliament, bolstering a right wing that includes Moderates, Christian Democrats and, since ⁠being invited by Kristersson earlier this year, Sweden Democrats.

The Sweden Democrats were founded in the 1980s by far-right extremists. Veteran politician Jimmie Åkesson took over the party in 2005, but until 2018, no party would have anything to do with them.

Sweden Democrats leader Jimmie Åkesson votes in Rinkeby, a suburb of Stockholm, on Saturday. (Claudio Bresciani/TT News Agency/The Associated Press)

The party's message that decades of overly generous immigration policies are behind a surge in shooting and gang crime has struck a chord with voters in recent years.

Since 2022, the Sweden Democrats have propped up Kristersson's government in parliament — building credibility with the broader right-wing bloc, despite not holding any cabinet positions — in exchange for policy concessions on immigration and policing.

Meanwhile, the rival blocs have converged on several voter priorities, including support for ⁠Ukraine, military ⁠rearmament and relief for households hit by the cost-of-living ​crisis.

While the opposition Social Democrats, Greens, Left Party and Centre Party broadly agree on the need for higher welfare and public spending, divisions persist on many ​issues, including immigration, where Andersson's party wants ⁠a more restrictive line than some of its would-be partners.

They are also at odds over issues including a tax on billionaires and building new nuclear reactors, while the Centre refuses to support a government that includes the Left Party, increasing the challenge Andersson would face to form a cabinet.

Luring the Christian Democrats to switch camps to create a centrist government is favoured by the Centre Party, but so far looks a distant prospect.

World.title: Urgency level high as Blue Jays look to make push for playoff spot
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Vladimir Guerrero Jr. was walking to the shower area in the Toronto clubhouse after a 7-3 win over Baltimore when he stopped to look at the TV screen above the stalls.

The slugger smiled as the Minnesota Twins recorded a key late-game out in an eventual 4-3 win over Cleveland, the team Toronto is chasing in the race for the final American League wild-card spot.

It's officially scoreboard-watching season and the Blue Jays are doing their share.

Saturday's results trimmed the Guardians' lead over the Blue Jays to just one game. Toronto holds the tiebreaker between the clubs, giving each matchup a must-win feel over the next fortnight.

"It's hard not to pay attention [to other games] but we're all pretty locked in here," said Toronto right-hander Dylan Cease, who'll start Sunday's rubber game against the Orioles. "I mean we know we've got to win."

Brett Bateman and Alejandro Kirk homered to power the Blue Jays to their 10th win in 16 games. Spencer Miles opened for Toronto in a bullpen game that was capped with three outs by closer Louis Varland.

74-75 record with 13 games left

The reigning American League champions improved to 74-75 with 13 games left in the regular season. All of Toronto's opponents have sub-. 500 records.

"The urgency level has been high for a while, as has stress, as has everything," said manager John Schneider. "But that's going to be the same going forward."

Bateman — who's not known for his slugging — hit his first big-league homer in the series opener. He followed it up Saturday with a blast that landed in almost the same spot over the wall in right-centre field.

"It's like Willie Mays Hayes in 'Major League 2,"' Schneider joked, referencing a movie character known more for his speed than his power. "Yesterday on a slider and today on a fastball, it's just good swings."

The American League is so weak right now that the third wild-card team will likely face an opponent with a similar record.

As the sixth overall seed, the third wild-card team will visit the lowest-seeded division winner in a best-of-three playoff series. Entering Saturday's games, the Chicago White Sox (Central) and Houston Astros (West) were clinging to first place in their respective divisions as they hovered just over the .500 mark.

Much-needed reinforcements

The Blue Jays, meanwhile, may soon get some much-needed reinforcements.

Starter Trey Yesavage (knee) was scheduled to throw a bullpen session Sunday. If it goes well, he could return to the rotation next week.

Starter Shane Bieber (shoulder) hopes to throw off the mound during the current six-game homestand.

Slugger Anthony Santander (shoulder) is playing regularly at triple-A Buffalo and could provide some pop to the batting order if he gets back to the big leagues.

The Detroit Tigers will visit Rogers Centre next week ahead of the Blue Jays' six-game road trip to Texas and Baltimore. Toronto will then return home for a season-ending interleague weekend series against the Cincinnati Reds.

A middling campaign still has the potential to be capped in style. It will take a heightened level of play to get there.

"Every game matters and there's still important games that are going to played all the way down the stretch," Schneider said.

Toronto started the day with a 26.5-per cent chance of reaching the playoffs, per FanGraphs.

World.title: 'Canadian renaissance': Stars share their love for homegrown films on the red carpet at TIFF
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This is the opening weekend of the Toronto International Film Festival. And a several big ticket films are making world premiers to kick off the celebration of all things cinema. And that includes a new Canadian film about an underdog 'Evil Knievel' wannabe. CBC's Eli Glasner has more from the red carpet premier of 'The Stunt Driver'.

As tensions between Canada and the U.S. creep into the film industry, Jay Baruchel is more than confident his country can stand toe to toe with its southern neighbour.

"We will be fine," the Ottawa-born actor said on the red carpet Friday ahead of the world premiere of The Stunt Driver at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF).

"We have never done anything but punch above our weight, and our record is pretty bloody strong when it comes to that.… We always find a way through."

He's one of a number of Canadian actors sharing their love of the country's film industry and Canada in general on the TIFF red carpet after the festival kicked off Thursday night.

Baruchel, known for films such as BlackBerry and She's Out of My League, is in the driver's seat of the new underdog film, which is based on the true story of stuntman Ken Carter.

Baruchel portrays Carter, known as The Mad Canadian, who attempted to jump over the St. Lawrence River in a rocket-powered car in the 1970s — partially driven by a desire to outdo his American rival Evel Knievel.

The timing of the film's debut during the ongoing trade war between Canada and the U.S. "added an extra sense of urgency … and a vitality" to the film, Baruchel said.

The cast and director of The Stunt Driver on the red carpet for the film at the Toronto International Film Festival in on Friday. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

"If you've ever been talked down to, if you've ever been dismissed ... you understand where this comes from," he added, calling the story "an indignant middle finger."

The trade war gained took on a cultural dimension ahead of TIFF when, earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump singled out Canada during the announcement of a proposed federal incentive to keep U.S. film productions in the U.S. rather than travelling abroad, stirring up concerns in the Canadian film industry.

The two film industries have long been close.

"It's been over a hundred years that there's been a very solid bridge built between the entertainers and artists and business people of Canada and the U.S. when it comes to making movies," TIFF CEO Cameron Bailey told CBC News on Thursday, noting that the opening film at TIFF, Being Heumann, is a U.S. production that was shot in Toronto.

Members of the production and cast of Below on the red carpet at the Toronto International Film Festival on Thursday. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

At TIFF, Canadian actors and artists say they aren't feeling cowed — but instead feel inspired to champion Canadian art.

"Art can reflect who we are as a country and … who we are as people," Canadian actress Laurence Leboeuf, who plays Carter's wife Gloria in The Stunt Driver, said on the red carpet Friday.

'Canadian renaissance'

Devon Bostick, a Toronto-born actor who co-wrote Closing Night — which also premiered at TIFF — added that he feels "we're part of a Canadian renaissance right now." The film tracks a movie star (Sarah Paulson) as she attempts to connect with her estranged family.

"I live in the States now and from afar I just think Canada's got it going on, and I feel like it's a beacon of light, that what is happening here is thriving and resisting," the Mile End Kicks actor said.

WATCH | Sarah Paulson, Devon Bostick on Canada: Stars at 'Closing Night' red carpet show Canada some love | Duration 0:21 Actor Sarah Paulson and writer Devon Bostick, who's from Toronto, talked about their love for Canada during the world premiere of their new film, Closing Night, at TIFF on Saturday.

When asked if he had any concerns about the Canadian film industry amid trade tensions, he quipped, "I think I'm not afraid for Canada, I’m afraid for the States."

Mary Walsh, a comedian and actress known for her work with This Hour Has 22 Minutes, echoed those sentiments when she arrived on the red carpet for the upcoming Netflix miniseries Below on Thursday.

"The Canadian film industry is bigger than it's ever been, and it's growing. And the more Mr. Trump threatens to attack us, the more we pull together and become stronger," she said.

WATCH | Mary Walsh champions Canada's film industry: Trump's threats only make Canada's film industry stronger: Mary Walsh | Duration 0:24 Comedian Mary Walsh talked about the strength of the Canadian film industry during a TIFF red carpet on Thursday. She's in Toronto promoting Below, a new miniseries filmed in her home province of Newfoundland and Labrador.

Walsh, who hails from St. John's, plays the mayor of a small, shrinking town in Newfoundland in the new horror series.

She said the U.S. upping its aggression against Canada could be the "kick in the arse that the Canadian film industry needed," to back its own artistic works more fully.

"As a country we must support our own … culture, and we do a somewhat good job of that. But at times, you know, Canadians aren't always behind Canadian culture. They've sort of looked to the larger thing to the south, and so I think our eyes are sort of turning back to ourselves.

"If Mr. Trump did only one good thing, only one good thing, it would be that it made us realize that we are a country, and a country worth working together to save and to be."
