World.title: [OPINION] Can young Filipino Catholics spread faith in ‘largest mission land of the world’?
World.content:
The Philippines is Southeast Asia’s oldest Christian nation, having embraced Catholicism over 500 years ago in 1521. Today, nearly 79% of the Philippines’ 118.2 million population is Roman Catholic, making it the third-largest Catholic population worldwide.

The vitality of this faith is sustained by the Philippines’ relatively young population, with a median age of 25.4, and by a Filipino youth population between 15 and 30 years old of approximately 31.4 million.

Acknowledging this reality, Pope John Paul II entrusted the Filipino Catholic youth with the responsibility of spreading the faith in the “largest mission land of the world,” referring to Asia. Furthermore, as recently highlighted in my previous feature of the global “Footprints” study, Pope Francis praised Filipinos’ joy in bringing their faith to other lands and exhorted them to persevere in the work of evangelization.

The huge number of Filipino Catholic youth — estimated at 21 million — underscores the importance of their role in the life of the Church, especially in her missional action. But this raises a crucial question: Are the Filipino youth of today in a position to effectively carry out the evangelizing mission being entrusted to them by the Church? Are they properly equipped with the knowledge and understanding of their faith, and do they possess the values and dispositions needed for missional action?

The survey of 600 Filipino youth – part of the eight-country global study featured last week – reveals a perhaps unsurprising fact: that Filipino youth are deeply spiritual. Over 84% reported that spirituality was either “very present” or “fairly present” in their lives, showing that any decline in spirituality, faith, or religiosity among Filipino youth has been minimal. Interestingly, male respondents reported rates of spirituality virtually identical to females, defying traditional gender gaps in religiosity.

When asked about the attributes they associate with religion, Filipino youth associate it most strongly with attributes tied to mercy — kindness (95%), forgiveness (93.5%), humility (92%), ability to serve (90.5%), and respect for the body and purity (93.3%). Furthermore, an overwhelming majority (96%) affirm the belief that sin exists.

Among young believers, a significant 89% believe in God, overwhelmingly perceiving Him as loving, forgiving, and merciful (95.5%) – a personal Being who relates directly to them. Religion also profoundly shapes their personal lives: 84% claim their religious beliefs influence their daily decisions, 90% admire individuals who live according to their religious values, and 88% believe that belonging to a religious community helps one cope with life’s difficulties.

However, the survey data also reveals notable challenges and limitations in doctrinal formation. For instance, while 93% believe that each person’s conscience determines what is right and wrong, 53% believe it is not necessary to believe in God to have good values. For young Catholics, while 87% affirm Jesus’ true presence in the Holy Eucharist and 70% agree they cannot live without the Eucharist, 64% simultaneously agree they don’t need to go to Mass to be a good Christian. Additionally, while 92% agree the Bible is a sacred text, 62% believe anyone can read Scripture alone without any mediation from the Church, departing from official Catholic teaching.

‘Right living’

The above findings suggest that contemporary Filipino youth place a greater premium on “right living” as a direct consequence of faith rather than “right believing.” However, having to choose between right living and right believing is upholding an unnecessary dualism.

Settling only for right living as if right believing were inferior or unnecessary is settling for an untenable mediocrity. Both are equally crucial because catechesis — the teaching of right believing – is a vital stage in the whole process of evangelization.

The results of our study, thus, give us a basis to suggest that the Filipino youth of today are only partially equipped with the proper knowledge and understanding of their faith and still need more strengthening in the values and dispositions needed for the missional action being entrusted to them by the Church.

Filipino youth show strong engagement with their faith: they are God-centered, prayerful, Bible-engaged, and sacramentally informed. However, to be better equipped at evangelizing, the evangelizers “should be first evangelized themselves.”

Improved catechesis by Christian formators and educators remains vital so that, by addressing gaps in right believing, Filipino youth will be fully equipped to transmit the faith alongside the right living they already emphasize. They may not yet be perfectly prepared for an evangelizing mission, but Filipino youth’s existing foundation positions them to take on this responsibility effectively.

Robert Z. Cortes is assistant professor III in the School of Media and Marketing of the University of Asia and the Pacific, with a PhD in social communication. His areas of study and teaching include communication/media ethics; the dynamics of entertainment, cultures, and societies; philosophy of technology; youth media habits and values. This piece was based on an article published in the journal Church, Communication, and Culture and was written by Robert Z. Cortes and Veronica Ramirez. Download it here.

World.title: How Marcelo del Pilar’s descendant sees the man behind the hero
World.content:
LOLO MARCELO. Pax Pineda poses beside a portrait of his great-great-great grandfather, Marcelo H. del Pilar, at the exhibit 'Lolo Marcelo: The Man Behind the Hero.'

What was Marcelo H. del Pilar like beyond the history books? His great-great-great-grandson, 17-year-old Pax Pineda, hopes to tell a more personal story of the national hero

Marcelo H. del Pilar may be remembered by some Filipinos as a journalist, lawyer, reformist, and propagandist who died in exile in Spain. But for his great-great-great-grandson Pax Pineda, the national hero with the pen name “Plaridel” has always just been “Lolo Marcelo.”

Pax, a 17-year-old senior high school student studying in Hong Kong where he also grew up, learned about the life and times of Plaridel from his family over the years.

At a young age, Pax made it a personal habit to study and tell his friends about his Lolo Marcelo’s story.

“My friends in Hong Kong and all my classmates in Hong Kong are very, very interested in who Lolo Marcelo was and they think it’s a really cool story. So I’m very pleased to have shared that legacy and that story with them,” he said.

An artwork dedicated to Marcelo H. del Pilar at the ‘Lolo Marcelo: The Man Behind the Hero’ exhibit. All photos by Romeo Dio Photography

Pax knows that many Filipinos encounter well-known figures like Del Pilar through history lessons in school, where they learn about their contributions to the Philippines. But rarely do students see them beyond their heroism.

For the young teen, history should be more than names and dates.

“I think the perceived disinterest among the youth regarding Marcelo and other historical figures is based off what they learn in the textbooks,” said Pax.

“It just doesn’t really capture the person these people were. It just turns them into a distant figure that lacks human qualities.”

Family man

Pax shared how Del Pilar’s preserved letters, written when he was in Spain, were documentations of how he expressed love for his family.

“I think even though he did have to leave his family in order to pursue his goals for Philippine independence and pursue trying to fulfill a better country…he still loves his two daughters [Sofia and Anita] and [his wife] Chanay very, very much,” Pax said.

“These artifacts [also show] the man as how he was, not in the exact things he did, but in how he felt, his feelings towards his family, his feelings towards the people of the Philippines.”

This inspired Pax to curate an exhibit for his Lolo Marcelo.

Pax Pineda delivers an inspiring speech, introducing his debut exhibit at the Ayala Museum in Makati City.

“This exhibition is not about a distant monument, it’s about a human character,” Pax said of his debut exhibit, Lolo Marcelo: The Man Behind the Hero, running until October 18 at the Ayala Museum in Makati City.

“His story has always told us to love our nation no matter what and to love our families no matter what.”

Ericsson Dublas, curator of the Museo ni Marcelo H. Del Pilar in Bulacan — the national hero’s home province — also noted how Plaridel wrote about missing his children, often asking them how they were in Epistolario 1 and 2, the two volumes of the hero’s compiled correspondence.

“He mentioned nag-fade na daw ‘yung larawan ng kaniyang mag-iina na palagi niyang hinihimas dahil sa sobrang pagkamiss,” Dublas shared.

(He mentioned that the photo of his family had faded because he constantly caresses it because he misses them so much).

A diorama depicting Plaridel’s longing and love for his family. The quote is about missing his daughters.

Journalist, feminist

On December 15, 1889, Del Pilar became the editor of the La Solidaridad newspaper, which was deemed the principal organ of the Filipino Propaganda Movement.

Unlike his nephew, Gregorio del Pilar, who was known as a general and died in battle, Plaridel used pen and paper as a weapon to fight against injustice amid the Spanish colonization.

“The way he wrote in La Solidaridad was very different,” said Patricio “Blums” Pineda III, Pax’s father. “It was more intellectual, much more about the position because he’s writing for a Spanish audience.”

Del Pilar turned La Solidaridad into the voice of the public, the voice of the Filipino Propaganda Movement in Spain.

At the time, though, it was difficult to sustain the operations of La Solidaridad. But Plaridel used money out of his own pocket.

“That sheer drive he had to get his message out there is an inspiring tale for all journalists everywhere to not let organizations pressure them,” said Pax. “And also just do what you do, always tell the truth, get the truth out there, no matter what, with integrity.”

A bust of Marcelo H. Del Pilar La Solidaridad

In 1888, Spanish Augustinian priest published a pamphlet, Caiñgat Cayo! (Beware), which warned Catholics against reading Rizal’s Noli Me Tangere. In response, Del Pilar wrote a satirical essay titled “Kaiingat Kayo,” which criticized the teachings of the Spanish friars. This was only one of Plaridel’s ways to counter censorship.

Pax shared that many also didn’t know that his Lolo Marcelo was a feminist.

“He wrote constantly about how women should be educated, how women should be almost equal to men,” he said.

Memory project

Pax and his family feel grateful to all those helping keep his Lolo Marcelo’s story alive.

Aside from his own exhibit, the Museo ni Marcelo H. Del Pilar in Bulakan, Bulacan highlights Plaridel’s heroic deeds and contributions to Philippine history.

“In Bulacan, they conducted various projects to evolve this kind of historical knowledge about Del Pilar,” Dublas shared.

“For example, their tourism office, they created or they drafted modules intended for grade schools, specifically learning the Bulacan heroes, specifically headed by Marcelo H. Del Pilar.”

Last July, Del Pilar and other historical figures were also featured in HistoEx 2026 at the SM Mall of Asia.

“Some other collections were digitized from the provincial government of Bulacan, which is already part of the National Memory Project,” Dublas said.

“We have to innovate our ways in order to pass knowledge of our past heritage, including the legacy and works of our heroes, such as the great Marcelo H. Del Pilar.”

Pax (right) with his father Blums Pineda and mother Roslyn Reyes Pineda.

Personally, Pax plans to major in history at the University of California after he graduates senior high school.

Del Pilar’s story continues to fascinate Pax, and if only he could talk to his great-great-great-grandfather, he would like to tell his Lolo Marcelo that he’s “not alone.”

After fleeing to Spain in 1888 to avoid persecution by the Spanish authorities, Del Pilar died in 1896 due to tuberculosis without having the chance to see his family again.

“I know that it must seem difficult and you might feel alone, but you’re not alone,” Pax said, musing what he would have told his lolo.

“We all love you. We all feel for you and we all believe in what you are, and who you are, and what you’re doing. And you will be a massive part in creating something so great for the country of the Philippines.” – Rappler.com

Angel Camille Dio is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at Polytechnic University of the Philippines.

World.title: Who are the retired justices tapped to advise impeachment court on voting threshold?
World.content:
Four retired Supreme Court justices have been invited by the Senate impeachment court to share their views on issue of voting threshold

On Day 23 of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo posed a looming question that could ultimately determine how the Senate impeachment court will deliver its verdict.

Tulfo asked, should the voting basis for Duterte’s acquittal or conviction remain at 24 amid the prolonged absence of some senator-judges?

“When I raised that question, I was not asking for the court to lower the 16-vote threshold. I was asking if we should count the votes of the four senator-judges who were not partaking in the trial,” Tulfo told reporters in a mix of English and Filipino on Friday, September 11.

At the start of the trial in July, impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero set the conviction threshold for Duterte to 16 amid legal interpretations that the two-thirds conviction threshold of the Constitution can mean only 14, as only 21 out of 24 senators can participate in the trial.

But Tulfo’s question at the September 8 trial prompted the court to revisit the ruling and seek the opinion of amici curiae or “friends of the court” in deciding the issue.

The impeachment court set the presentation of the views of the legal experts on September 16. It will be followed by oral arguments between the defense and prosecution, as well as the impeachment court vote the following week, on September 23.

The impeachment court has tapped four retired Supreme Court (SC) justices to share their opinions on the matter and help the impeachment court examine the constitutional question: former chief justices Artemio V. Panganiban, Reynato S. Puno and Hilario G. Davide Jr.; and former associate justice Adolfo S. Azcuna.

Panganiban, Puno, and Azcuna will share their opinion before the impeachment court on September 16, while Davide will submit a legal memorandum instead of appearing in person.

Who exactly are these four legal luminaries and why were they chosen to weigh in on the crucial issue?

Retired chief justice Artemio V. Panganiban

Retired chief justice Artemio V. Panganiban served as the 21st Supreme Court chief justice from 2005 to 2006, after serving as an associate justice for more than a decade.

During his tenure, he penned around 1,200 full-length decisions and separate opinions, including La Bugal v. Ramos, which upheld the constitutionality of the Philippine Mining Act. He is currently an opinion columnist for Philippine Daily Inquirer and works as a consultant for various organizations.

Retired chief justice Reynato S. Puno

Retired chief justice Reynato S. Puno served as the country’s top magistrate from December 2007 to May 2010. He was Supreme Court associate justice from 1993 to 2007.

Under Puno’s leadership, the Supreme Court adopted the writ of amparo, a judicial remedy intended to protect the constitutional rights to life, liberty, and security. He was also one of the legal minds instrumental for the drafting of the interim Constitution under the Cory Aquino administration or the Freedom Constitution.

In 2018, then-president Rodrigo Duterte appointed Puno as the chairperson of the Consultative Committee to Review the 1987 Constitution.

Retired associate justice Adolf S. Azcuna

Retired associate justice Adolf Azcuna, who served as Supreme Court magistrate from 2002 to 2009, is best remembered for championing the writ of amparo, a remedy that serves to protect constitutional rights perceived to be in danger.

Azcuna was a delegate to both the Constitutional Convention in 1971 and the 1986 Constitutional Commission that drafted the 1987 Constitution. He was the presidential legal counsel during the Cory Aquino administration, and had served as chancellor of the Philippine Judicial Academy from 2009 to 2021.

Retired chief justice Hilario G. Davide Jr.

Retired chief justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. was Supreme Court associate justice since 1991 before service as top magistrate from 1998 to 2005. In 2000, Davide presided over the impeachment trial of then-president Joseph Estrada.

Davide was a delegate to the 1986 Constitutional Commission that helped shaped the 1987 Constitution. He served the Cory Aquino administration as Commission on Elections commissioner.

Why were they chosen?

Impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol explained in an online media briefing that the amici curiae were chosen based on their credentials, and were also among those recommended by both the defense and prosecution.

“One of the things that the presiding officer considered is their credentials…. Technically, two of them were framers of the 1987 Constitution and two others were SC chief justices,” he added.

The 1987 Constitution states that no person may be convicted in an impeachment trial without the concurrence of two-thirds of all members of the Senate. But with some senator-judges missing the trial, the dispute lies on whether “all the members of the Senate” should refer to the entire 24-member chamber or only those senator-judges who are legally able to participate in the final vote. – Rappler.com

World.title: 8 independent spaces to experience Manila’s creative scene
World.content:
Manila has always been generous to those who know where to look. Its creative culture has long lived beyond museums and traditional institutions, thriving even in the hidden corners and unexpected pockets of the city.

Many of these places began because someone needed space to create and share their work, until others found their way in and built a community around it. Here are eight independent spaces in the city carving out their own path.

1. Studio Segui

A CREATIVE PLAYGROUND. Studio, coworking space, café, and bar in Mandaluyong City

Studio Segui is the kind of place you visit when working from home starts to feel a little like working alone. Creatives bring their projects here for a day of parallel work without the formality of an office.

Coffee is available during the day. And by evening, the lights dim and the bar takes over — making it easy to wrap up a project and go straight into drinks and conversation.

Before visiting: Check Studio Segui’s social media pages for current hours and events.

2. KalawakanSpacetime

A HOME FOR COUNTERCULTURE. Artist-run gallery and initiative in Quezon City

Dedicated to artists outside traditional gallery walls, KalawakanSpacetime has offered a home for fringe art since 2017. Regular visiting days are quite intimate, giving people time to explore the exhibitions up close — with private viewings available for collectors looking to acquire pieces.

The gallery also hosts an exhibition every two months, filled with music, conversation, and spontaneous performances. As the team puts it, “You’ll get to see the rawest art in the city.”

Address: 2/F Casa Bella Building, 1046 Quezon Avenue corner Roces Avenue, Diliman, Quezon City

Hours: Tuesday to Sunday, 10 am to 7 pm

Admission: Free

Private visits: Contact Dennis Torres at +63 939 877 4407

Instagram: @kalawakanspacetime

3. Bad Student

KEEPING PRINT ALIVE. Independent risograph art press and DIY print and design studio Cainta, Rizal, and Queens, New York City

Bad Student brings a colorful introduction to risograph printing and independent publishing. Visitors can browse its collection of art prints, books, and zines while learning more about the DIY process behind them.

You might also be greeted by their resident “Super Pets” — the studio’s free-roaming pets. Schedule a visit to learn more about the many things you can do with ink and paper, and “be a Bad Student for a day.”

Studio visits: By appointment through Instagram (@_badstudent)

4. Sine Pop

BY THE CINEPHILES, FOR THE CINEPHILES. Microcinema and performance space in Cubao, Quezon City

Sine Pop reimagines the moviegoing experience inside a restored 1948 home, tucked within a bamboo garden in the city. Its intimate 48-seat microcinema offers a tranquil sanctuary for film lovers to watch handpicked cinema and stay for a post-screening debrief.

Beyond film, the space also opens its doors to music recitals and plays, allowing audiences to engage with independent work on a close and personal scale.

Address: 14–16 Saint Mary Street, Cubao, Quezon City

Visiting hours: 6 am to midnight, outside private event hours

Location visits: Free; coordinate with Sine Pop before arriving

5. Studio 1372

ART IN THE HEART OF MANILA. Community art space and studio in Escolta

Behind Studio 1372’s little green door, co-founders Seb and Ruby can usually be found working beside a freshly brewed pot of coffee. Ruby stitches notebooks while Seb prepares layouts and prints their original art. Visitors can explore the works on the walls, use the art bar, or play board games with fellow creatives.

The studio opened in August 2025 as an extension of the family store Kariton by 1372 Designs. Its workshops, community art projects, and monthly mahjong sessions have since turned strangers into regular visitors.

Address: Room 301B, First United Building, 413 Escolta Street, Binondo, Manila

Hours: Weekdays, 2 pm to 6 pm; weekends, 1 pm onwards

Before visiting: Check the Studio 1372’s monthly social media calendar; it closes at least one weekend each month

Events: Available for private bookings; rates depend on event requirements

6. KINKI

NEVER THE SAME NIGHT TWICE. Dance venue and bar in Poblacion, Makati

KINKI is a chic, dance-forward venue where the space changes with every party. The team adjusts the lighting and design for each event while keeping artworks and set pieces from previous nights as personal touches.

Guests may discover a new genre of music or meet new friends on the dance floor. At the bar, try one of the signature cocktails, including the Stoli Vodka-based Carrie Sun.

Address: 2/F 8483 Kalayaan Avenue corner Matilde Street, Poblacion, Makati

Before visiting: Check KINKI’s current lineup and door details.

7. ISTORYA STUDIOS

PAGES & PRESS. Independent bookstore and creative hub in Guiguinto, Bulacan

“Hinto-hinto sa Guiguinto” is how ISTORYA STUDIOS draws its visitors just a couple of hours’ drive outside Manila. Its shelves feature artist-authored titles alongside a growing collection from local Filipino publishers, with open browsing copies for every book so you can read at your own pace.

Between reads, you can also try out the old typewriters, press custom button pins, or make a print at the stamp station — with book readings and workshops hosted on select dates.

Address: 189 San Lorenzo Ruiz Street, Rosaryville Subdivision, Barangay Santa Cruz, Guiguinto, Bulacan

Hours: Tuesday to Friday, 11 am to 8 pm; Saturday and Sunday, 9 am to 8 pm; Closed on Mondays

Admission: Free

8. Sining Shelter

ROOM TO CREATE. Artist-run house venue in Parañaque City

Sining Shelter is a repurposed house run by a close-knit group of artists and friends. Its casual, kitschy space regularly hosts independent DIY gigs in an intimate setting.

The house changes with every event — visitors may find an underground show, a film screening, or a community market. The space also supports emerging artists, with ticket sales directly funding their work and keeping the house open.

Address: 4183 Sun Valley Drive, Sun Valley, Parañaque City

Before visiting: Check Sining Shelter’s event announcements for schedules and ticket information.

These eight spaces offer an intimate look at how Manila’s creative culture builds itself from the ground up. They reflect the raw personality of the city, carved out by the people, subcultures, and passions that bring them to life.

Stepping inside means getting to know Manila through the art made here: in the hum of a printing press, post-film debriefs, or late-night sets on a dance floor. Pick a space that matches your rhythm and see what is happening behind its doors. – Rappler.com

World.title: Why was Martin Romualdez transferred to PGH?

World.title: PMA ends final exam exemption for top-performing cadets
World.content:
EXAMS. Photos of upperclass cadets taking their final exams for 1st Term of academic year 2026-2027.

The Philippine Military Academy says the change is meant to reinforce academic rigor, discipline, preparation, and consistency among cadets

BAGUIO CITY, Philippines — Even the Philippine Military Academy (PMA)’s highest-performing cadets no longer get to skip final examinations.

PMA has ended its practice of exempting cadets with exceptional academic standing from final examinations, requiring everyone to take the same assessment regardless of their grades during the term.

The policy was first implemented during the second semester of Academic Year 2025-2026 and continues this school year. Upperclass cadets are currently taking their final examinations for the first term of the academic year.

The common end-of-term assessment, the academy said, allows faculty to further evaluate how well cadets understand, retain, and apply the knowledge and competencies developed in their courses.

PMA trains cadets to become officers of the Armed Forces of the Philippines. Its four-year program combines academic instruction with military training, physical development, and character formation.

The academy said final examinations are also intended to reinforce discipline, preparation, and consistency alongside the military, physical, and character development expected of cadets.

“Beyond measuring academic performance, final examinations form part of PMA’s continuing efforts to uphold rigorous academic standards and instill discipline, preparation, and consistency among cadets,” PMA Public Affairs Office chief Lt. Cmdr. Jesse Nestor Saludo said.

PMA did not say the policy change was prompted by declining academic performance or a specific problem with the previous exemption system.

The academy has also been reviewing how it prepares future Armed Forces officers for a security environment increasingly shaped by cyber operations, artificial intelligence, information warfare, and other emerging challenges.

PMA said its assessment practices are part of efforts to provide a challenging and globally competitive education, with an emphasis on knowledge, critical thinking, and professional competence.

Cadets who perform well academically can still earn recognition for their grades. But under the new policy, high marks no longer mean they can sit out the final examination. – Rappler.com

World.title: Taal Volcano update: 7 volcanic quakes logged; Alert Level 1 stays
World.content:
INQUIRER.net photo

LUCENA CITY—Taal Volcano in Batangas had seven volcanic earthquakes and a prolonged tremor over the past 24 hours, the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (Phivolcs) reported Sunday morning.

The volcano, however, remains under Alert Level 1 (low level of volcanic unrest).

Phivolcs noted that the volcanic tremor began at 7:10 p.m. on Saturday until the latest monitoring period.

Article continues after this 

Despite the extended duration, Phivolcs clarified that volcanic tremors are standard occurrences at Taal and do not present an immediate cause for concern.

From Sept. 1 to 13, Taal has logged a total of 52 volcanic earthquakes and three tremor episodes.

This reflects a notable decrease in seismic activity compared to the Aug. 20 to 28 monitoring period, which had 229 volcanic quakes and 12 tremor episodes.

Additionally, Phivolcs recorded weak sulfur dioxide (SO₂) emissions averaging 526 metric tons per day since Sept. 1. No upwelling of hot volcanic fluids in the main crater lake or volcanic smog (vog) were observed. /gsg

World.title: Boat operator nabbed for allegedly hiring unlicensed fishers in Mindoro
World.content:
CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Police arrested a fisherman who also operates a fishing vessel for allegedly employing unlicensed fishermen / crewmen in San Jose, Occidental Mindoro on Saturday.

Recovered from the suspect were a fishing vessel, fishing gear and catch worth an estimated P940,000.

The Occidental Mindoro Maritime Police Station (MARPSTA), in coordination with the San Jose Municipal Police Station, apprehended the alleged violator at 9:55 a.m., around 18 kilometers off the shoreline of Barangay San Roque, according to the Police Regional Office (PRO) Mimaropa.

Article continues after this 

Police said the operation was conducted in line with their maritime patrol tasking and resulted in the arrest of the fisherman for alleged violation of Section 113 of Republic Act No. 10654, which prohibits commercial fishing vessel operators from employing unlicensed fisherfolk or crewmen.

The suspect and seized items were brought to the Occidental Mindoro MARPSTA for documentation and proper disposition.

Police said the an appropriate complaint will be filed before the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources Adjudication Board.

World.title: Coast Guard expands search for survivors of Palawan ferry blaze
World.content:
In this photo taken on Saturday, personnel of the Philippine Coast Guard conduct search-and-rescue operations for missing passengers and possible survivors following a fire aboard the passenger vessel MV June Aster off Coron, Palawan. The PCG has expanded its search efforts to coastal communities in Mindoro. (Photo courtesy of PCG)

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) has expanded its search-and-rescue operations to coastal communities in Mindoro for possible survivors of the fire that hit passenger vessel MV June Aster off Coron, Palawan.

The Coast Guard District Southern Tagalog on Sunday said it is coordinating with local disaster risk reduction and management offices, coastal barangays, and local fishermen in Mindoro amid the possibility that some passengers may have drifted or were carried by currents to the area.

Fishermen and coastal residents were urged to remain alert and immediately report any person who may be a survivor or missing passenger.

Article continues after this 

The agency also warned the public against sharing unverified information on social media, saying false reports could cause unnecessary fear and distress among the families of passengers.

Anyone who finds or receives information about possible survivors or missing passengers may report to the nearest Coast Guard station or barangay hall, the PCG said.

The PCG provided the following contact numbers for reports:

Coast Guard Station Batangas: 0956-904-6652

Coast Guard Station Oriental Mindoro: 0975-542-6908

Coast Guard Station Occidental Mindoro: 0945-266-2085

Coast Guard Station Northern Quezon: 0931-764-0859

Coast Guard Station Marinduque: 0930-430-3182

Coast Guard Station Romblon: 0930-137-7821

Coast Guard Station Southern Quezon: 0905-429-8563

The expansion of search operations comes as search and rescue personnel recovered 41 more charred bodies from the fire-struck vessel on Saturday night.

The latest recoveries brought the number of fatalities from the ill-fated ship to 76. The number of survivors remains at 43, while 13 people are still unaccounted for.

Article continues after this 

PCG Spokesperson Commodore Noemi Cayabyab also stated that a casket with remains inside and the cadaver of a dog were among those recovered from the ship.

The retrieved bodies were transferred to PCG vessel BRP Cape Engaño (MRRV 4411) and are scheduled to be transported to Port of Borac for proper disposition and further documentation. /gsg

World.title: Marcos admin extends P154-M aid to 770 Cavite barangays
World.content:
Executive Secretary Ralph Recto leads the distribution of P154 million in direct financial assistance to 770 barangays in Cavite on Sept. 11, 2026, under the Marcos administration’s “Bawat Barangay Makikinabang” program.

MANILA, Philippines — The Marcos administration has released P154 million directly to 770 barangays in Cavite to help fund public safety and development needs and for graduating college students to earn their degrees.

In a statement on Sunday, Executive Secretary Ralph Recto said P77 million would go to 3,850 incoming fourth-year college students in Cavite, with each receiving P20,000.

Another P77 million would fund projects such as solar streetlights, emergency and patrol equipment, and disaster preparedness gear in the province.

Article continues after this 

Recto led the distribution of the funds to barangay officials in Cavite on Sept. 11 under the administration’s “Bawat Barangay Makikinabang” program.

Each barangay received P100,000 for education assistance through the Bagong Pilipinas Barangay Scholars Program. The amount will be divided among five fourth-year college students, with each receiving P20,000.

Another P100,000 per barangay was provided for community development and public safety projects.

The P6.6 million assistance for the 33 barangays of General Trias was handed over by President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. during his visit to the municipality in May.

The funding comes from the Socio-Civic Projects Fund (SCPF), administered by the Office of the Executive Secretary under the Office of the President, to provide a rapid, immediate response to community needs and to continuously implement development projects.

Article continues after this 

READ: Marcos orders release of P8-billion aid for barangays amid crisis

Recto said the President wants the program to help students complete their college education, which he described as key to lifting families out of poverty.

Article continues after this 

“President Marcos believes that education is the key for a family, as well as a country, to rise out of poverty. That is why he wants every barangay to have college graduates,” he added.

He also told barangay officials that the funds were being entrusted directly to them because they were in the best position to identify their communities’ needs.

Recto also reminded local officials to ensure transparency and accountability in using the allocations.

The distribution was witnessed by key provincial and congressional leaders of Cavite, including Governor Abeng Remulla, Vice Governor Ram Revilla, 1st District Representative Ramon “Jolo” Revilla III, 2nd District Representative Lani Mercado-Revilla, 5th District Representative Roy M. Loyola, 7th District Representative Crispin Diego Remulla and Agimat Partylist Representative Bryan Revilla.

World.title: Bulacan logs 5 leptospirosis deaths as cases rise to nearly 400
World.content:
CITY OF MALOLOS, Bulacan—Bulacan has recorded five leptospirosis deaths as cases rose to nearly 400 due to continued flooding, with coastal towns including Hagonoy, Paombong, Calumpit, and this capital city still inundated, data from the Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction Management Office (PDRRMO) on Friday showed.

According to the PDRRMO, the most recent fatality was a 38-year-old male from Muzon Proper in the City of San Jose del Monte who died on August 12, four days after being admitted to the Bulacan Medical Center.

Other recorded deaths include a 60-year-old male from Santa Cruz, Hagonoy, who died on July 24; a 47-year-old female from Barangay Mapulang Lupa in Pandi who died on July 3; a 13-year-old male from Barangay Caysio, Sta. Maria, who died on June 22; and a 53-year-old male from Barangay Tibagan, San Miguel, who passed away on March 23.

Article continues after this 

Dr. Hijordis Marushka Celis, Provincial Health Officer II and Head of the Bulacan Provincial Health Office, reported that total leptospirosis cases in the province have reached 394 since January.

Celis said that symptoms typically appear two weeks after exposure to floodwaters.

With several areas still flooded, health authorities are prioritizing the distribution of doxycycline as prophylaxis to exposed residents through municipal and city health offices.

The PDRRMO said 68 barangays remain flooded with water levels reaching up to 6 feet in Calumpit, Hagonoy, Paombong, and Malolos City.

In Calumpit, Barangay Meysulao remains submerged in 6-foot high floodwaters, while 25 of the town’s 29 villages report floodwaters up to 5 feet.

Article continues after this 

Portions of flooded barangays also face power outages and road closures, leaving boats as the primary mode of transportation in severely affected areas.

High tide levels, which reached 3.94 feet on Friday, continue to aggravate swollen rivers following weeks of sustained monsoon rains.

Article continues after this 

The Calumpit MDRRMO reported that 154,961 individuals (46,770 families) across 29 barangays are affected, with 6,539 residents currently staying in 33 evacuation centers.

Calumpit was placed under a state of calamity on August 10 following rains from typhoons Luis and Maymay and the southwest monsoon.

World.title: Ex-Cavite landfill now a multi-purpose hub, public complex
World.content:
(PHOTO FROM MMDA)

MANILA, Philippines — A 40-hectare former landfill in Carmona, Cavite has been transformed into a multi-purpose public complex focused on disaster preparedness, food security, environmental rehabilitation and clean energy, with the Marcos administration seeking to make it a model for other local government units.

Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, along with Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) Chairman Don Artes and other government officials led the inauguration on Friday of the MMDA Carmona Development Projects at Sitio Paligawan Matanda, Barangay Lantic.

Article continues after this 

It marked the rehabilitation of a site that operated as a sanitary landfill from 1993 to 1998.

The project repurposed the property into a complex that includes disaster-response training facilities, a nature park, modern agriculture facilities and planned renewable energy infrastructure.

“This is how the people’s money should be spent—on projects that our fellow citizens can truly benefit from,” Recto said in a statement on Saturday.

The complex includes a Disaster Preparedness Training Center equipped with a rappelling tower, confined-space structure, wrecked-building and pancake-collapse structures, a fire suppression facility and a crash vehicle extrication area.

Executive Secretary Ralph Recto and other government officials inaugurate the rehabilitated 40-hectare former landfill in Carmona, Cavite, on Sept. 11, 2026. The site now houses a nature park, disaster-response training facilities, modern agriculture facilities and planned clean-energy infrastructure. (PHOTO FROM MMDA)

READ: PH joins India-led coalition to boost disaster-resilient infrastructure

Article continues after this 

The government also plans to add a Swift Water and Flood Training Facility and an MMDA K-9 Training Facility to strengthen the capacity of emergency responders.

The project would help the MMDA expand its disaster preparedness and emergency response capabilities while supporting more sustainable urban development.

Article continues after this 

“The facility is not only for MMDA responders, but is also open to volunteers, partner agencies, local government units, community groups and all those who wish to train and prepare for emergencies,” Artes said.

Recto said the safety of responders should be given priority as the government expands its disaster preparedness capabilities.

“We must ensure that our responders are safe and are able to return to their families,” he added.

The project also includes the MMDA Nature Park, a bamboo pavilion and a seedling nursery, turning portions of the former landfill into green and recreational spaces.

The development of the former sanitary landfill into the MMDA Nature Park was conceptualized by Cabinet Secretary Benhur Abalos during his tenure as MMDA chairman, following the policy direction of President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. to provide additional green and open spaces for public recreation and environmental enhancement.

For food security, the complex houses facilities developed with the Department of Agriculture, including a Kadiwa ng Bayan Store, a smart demonstration agriculture facility featuring hydroponics, and a livestock farm.

A ground-mounted solar photovoltaic farm is also planned for the site as part of efforts to integrate clean energy into the development.

Recto described the complex as a “living ecosystem,” saying food production and clean energy could coexist with environmental protection.

READ: Marcos wants disaster-resilient infrastructure, reform building code law

He also called on other local governments to replicate the Carmona project, which he said could serve as a model for converting underutilized or degraded properties into useful public infrastructure.

The inauguration was also attended by Cavite 5th District Rep. Roy Loyola, Carmona Mayor Dahlia Loyola and Parañaque Mayor Edwin Olivarez, demonstrating strong inter-city cooperation and regional support for sustainable infrastructure development.

Recto also linked the project to the country’s continuing flood-control and environmental challenges, saying infrastructure measures would not be enough without public cooperation in preventing improper waste disposal.

World.title: Final day of 2026 bar exams kicks off
World.content:
Supreme Court building /INQUIRER PHOTO

MANILA, Philippines — The final day of the 2026 bar examinations kicked off in various testing centers nationwide on Sunday, September 13.

The third and final day of the exams will tackle criminal law, remedial law, legal and judicial ethics with practical exercises.

The first day of the examination was held on September 6, which touched on political and public international law, and commercial law and taxation, while the second day, which was held on Wednesday, tackled civil law and land titles and deeds and labor law and social legislation.

Article continues after this 

“It’s not at the level I expected it to be,” a 29-year old bar examinee, who requested anonymity, told Inquirer on the first day of the exam. “It’s difficult, but not extremely difficult.”

“It seems like my efforts to study have paid off,” the examinee, a first-timer, also said.

The examinee said that she is prepared for the final day of the bar exam.

“There’s no feeling that maybe I should stop, maybe I shouldn’t continue during the next days,” she said.

“There’s no such feeling that I can’t handle the following exam days,” she said. “It seems, there’s still that feeling of ‘okay let’s go, we can do this, come on’,” she continued.

Article continues after this 

Reasonable questions

Associate Justice Samuel Gaerlan, who is also this year’s bar exam chairperson, said the questions are “reasonable.”

Article continues after this 

“It’s reasonable because we won’t take questions that are not covered in the syllabus,” Gaerlan said in a press conference last week.

A total of 12,029 examinees showed up in 15 testing centers nationwide on the first day of exams last Sunday, the Supreme Court said.

“There was an increase in the number of examinees this year as compared to other years,” Gaerlan said.

“I think we have the highest number.”

Demographics

Majority of candidates are females (6,773 or 56.3 percent) while males accounted for 5,256 or 43.7 percent of the examinees.

“If I may share, among the most interesting or the numerous requests that we received this year are moms who would wish to bring breast pumps inside the LTC,” bar head Cheska Pazziuagan said last week.

“So, this also shows that we have so many examinees who just gave birth, who are moms, who are wives, and despite those family circumstances and other struggles in life, they still showed up and went to take the bar,” Pazziuagan added.

A total of 304 of examinees are persons with disabilities, while 285 are senior citizens.

World.title: LTFRB summons operator of bus in fatal Manila road crash
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) on Sunday said it summoned the operator of a passenger bus involved in a fatal road crash along España Boulevard in Sampaloc, Manila.

The road crash involving multiple collisions of vehicles last September 11 resulted in the death of a senior citizen while eight other individuals were injured.

LTFRB Acting Chairperson Greg Pua said that the bus operator needs to explain why its Certificate of Public Convenience (CPC) should not be suspended or canceled over the incident.

Article continues after this 

READ: LTFRB opens 8,750 slots for TNVS units in Metro Manila, Ilocos, Bicol

“Both cases are in violation of the existing CPC conditions, one for not ensuring the road worthiness of the public utility vehicle, and the other one is employment of a reckless driver,” Pua said in a statement.

The LTFRB said that the hearing is scheduled on September 17, 2026 to determine possible appropriate sanctions.

Pua said that the operator is expected to bring necessary documents in relation to road worthiness of the public utility vehicle (PUVs) involved.

He added that necessary tests will be conducted to determine if the driver was under the influence of any substance during the incident.

Article continues after this 

READ: LTFRB summons operators of 226 untidy, dilapidated taxis, buses

The Regional Franchising and Regulatory Office of the National Capital Region is also directed to ensure that the victims are covered by insurance.

Article continues after this 

“Each fatality involving PUVs are entitled to P400,000 while injured victims are entitled to P100,000 each,” the LTFRB said. /gsg

World.title: From Bronze Age Settlements to Medieval Cities: New Archaeological Discoveries Across Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA — From Bronze Age settlements to medieval cities, archaeological research across Kazakhstan continues to reveal new details about the societies that once inhabited the Eurasian steppe.

Recent excavations have brought new findings from the ancient settlement of Zhankent in the Kyzylorda Region and a Bronze Age site near Imantau in northern Kazakhstan, while authorities are expanding efforts to protect historical and cultural monuments.

Together, these discoveries highlight the diversity of Kazakhstan’s archaeological heritage and show how excavation, scientific cooperation and modern research methods are helping researchers reconstruct different periods of the country’s past.

Zhankent: 20 years of archaeological research

One of the country’s longest-running archaeological projects is taking place at the ancient settlement of Zhankent in the Kyzylorda Region.

Systematic research at the site began in 2005. Over the past two decades, archaeologists have excavated more than 4,000 square meters and uncovered more than 25,000 artefacts, according to the Ministry of Science and Higher Education of Kazakhstan.

The finds include ceramic, metal, stone, bone and glass objects. They provide researchers with information about the daily life, crafts, economy and cultural connections of the settlement’s inhabitants.

Zhankent is particularly important for studying the history of the Oghuz. Archaeologists have investigated citadel, shahristan, residential quarters and economic structures, gradually reconstructing the layout and development of the medieval city.

The archaeological project has involved researchers from Kazakhstan and several other countries, contributing to a broader understanding of medieval settlements along the Syr Darya and the archaeological landscape of southern Kazakhstan.

Recent work at the site has focused on several areas of the ancient city, including the eastern gate complex and shahristan. Archaeologists have uncovered ceramic fragments, traditional asyks and animal remains, adding to the material evidence of everyday life at Zhankent. The settlement is also part of the Silk Roads: Fergana–Syr Darya Corridor included in Kazakhstan’s UNESCO World Heritage efforts.

Researchers are also using electrical tomography to examine underground layers and identify possible structures without excavating every part of the settlement.

Imantau: a glimpse into Bronze Age life

While Zhankent provides evidence of medieval urban civilization, archaeological research in northern Kazakhstan is taking researchers several thousand years further back. A joint expedition involving the National Museum of Kazakhstan and the National Museum of the People’s Republic of China conducted excavations at a Bronze Age settlement near Imantau in the Aiyrtau district of the North Kazakhstan Region.

According to the National Museum of Kazakhstan, the expedition was held from July 14 to Aug. 16, 2026, as part of cooperation between the two institutions. The researchers are studying the settlement to learn more about the daily life, economy and culture of ancient communities that lived in the region.

The site provides an opportunity to examine a period when communities across the Eurasian steppe were developing new forms of settlement, livestock breeding and metalworking. The expedition is part of longer-term cooperation between the two national museums.

The Imantau project adds another chronological layer to Kazakhstan’s ancient history. Archaeological work elsewhere in the country has similarly revealed evidence from different periods, including Bronze Age settlements and sites connected to the Silk Road.

Protecting what archaeology uncovers

Discovering historical sites is only one part of archaeological research. Protecting the sites themselves is equally important, particularly as ancient settlements and monuments can be vulnerable to construction, land use and natural deterioration.

In the Atyrau Region, protection zones were established for 41 historical and cultural monuments. Specialists also monitored 171 heritage sites and conducted expert assessments of 100 objects. Following the assessments, 80 objects were recommended for inclusion in the list of historical and cultural monuments.

The work covered several districts of the region and included field inspections of the condition of historical sites. The newly established protection zones add to 180 monuments in the Atyrau Region for which such zones had previously been approved.

Such measures are intended to establish clear boundaries around protected sites and reduce the risk of damage from development and other activities.

A wider archaeological picture

The discoveries at Zhankent and Imantau are part of a much broader archaeological effort taking place across Kazakhstan.

At Saraishyk, a medieval settlement associated with the Golden Horde and located in the Atyrau Region, excavations have uncovered hundreds of artefacts and architectural remains, providing new evidence about urban life in the region.

The findings included remains of residential buildings, a citadel and a caravanserai dating to the early 14th century, alongside household and decorative objects made of metal, glass, bone and ceramics.

In southern Kazakhstan, archaeological research has also revealed new evidence of the ancient Kangju state. Excavations at Kultobe have uncovered inscriptions and other artefacts that are helping researchers understand the political and cultural history of the region.

Other recent excavations have focused on earlier periods. Archaeologists in the Kostanai Region have studied Neolithic burials that provide evidence of communities living in northern Kazakhstan thousands of years ago.

These projects demonstrate the chronological depth of Kazakhstan’s archaeological heritage: from early human settlements and the Bronze Age to ancient states, Turkic monuments, Oghuz cities and Golden Horde centres.

Modern archaeology is also increasingly combining traditional excavation with laboratory analysis, geophysical methods and international cooperation. These approaches allow researchers to study not only individual artefacts but also the wider environment in which ancient communities lived.

Pottery can reveal information about technology and cultural contacts, animal remains can provide clues about diet and economic activity, while coins and other objects can help trace trade networks.

World.title: RIKO’s Škrabec: Kazakhstan’s Next Chapter Lies Beyond Resources
World.content:
ASTANA – Director and Partner of Slovenian engineering company RIKO Janez Škrabec has been coming to this part of the world for nearly four decades. His first visit to the Soviet Union was in 1988, when Kazakhstan belonged to a completely different political and economic reality. Today, he is returning to Astana, which is increasingly positioning itself as a regional center of transport, energy, investment and technological cooperation.

There is a certain value in seeing a country not at one particular moment, but across decades. Škrabec’s perspective is therefore more than that of a businessman assessing a market. He has watched the region change, institutions evolve, and Eurasia’s geography take on new economic meaning.

His visit to Kazakhstan comes as Kazakhstan-Slovenia ties build on the momentum of Slovenian President Nataša Pirc Musar’s visit in spring 2025, which placed greater emphasis on practical economic cooperation in trade, investment, energy, transport and technology. Škrabec joined the Slovenian business delegation during that visit and attended the business forum in Astana with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. For RIKO, the visit became a catalyst: the company has since opened a representative office in Astana and is developing projects in energy, water, transport and industrial infrastructure. The next challenge, in Škrabec’s view, is to turn political goodwill into lasting business partnerships.

In an interview with The Astana Times, Škrabec discussed where business can move faster than politics, why energy and infrastructure may become the foundation of a deeper Kazakhstan-Slovenia partnership, and why lasting economic ties ultimately depend not only on capital and technology but also on trust.

From political momentum to practical cooperation

“High-level political visits matter because they open doors, build trust and create the conditions for companies to move toward concrete projects,” Škrabec said.

For him, however, the real test of political goodwill comes after the official meetings end.

“Business can move faster than politics when there is a clear project, financing, technology and a reliable local partner. At that point, political goodwill can quickly become economic reality,” he said.

The next stage of Kazakhstan-Slovenia cooperation, he believes, should therefore focus less on declarations and more on projects in which the two sides can combine their respective strengths. That view comes from a much longer personal history with the region.

“I first came to the then Soviet Union as a young entrepreneur in 1988, and for decades RIKO was active in Russia, Belarus and Ukraine,” he said.

That experience gives Škrabec a perspective that goes beyond assessing Kazakhstan as a market. He has watched the wider region transform over several decades and has seen Astana itself emerge as one of the most visible symbols of Kazakhstan’s transformation. It is a perspective shaped as much by time as by business and one that helps explain why he sees Kazakhstan’s current trajectory not as a sudden opportunity, but as the latest stage in a much longer transformation.

Energy as a test of long-term partnership

Energy is one area where Škrabec believes this principle can be put into practice.

“Kazakhstan needs not only new generation capacity, but also modernization of transmission and distribution networks, stronger grid reliability, digitalization, integration of renewables and energy-storage solutions,” he said.

He sees opportunities across a broad part of the energy system, including “transformer and traction substations, grid modernization, hydropower, renewables, battery storage and energy efficiency.”

For Slovenian companies, Škrabec believes the opportunity lies in combining specialized engineering with technology integration and project implementation.

“Slovenian companies are strong in specialized engineering, technology integration and project implementation. RIKO, for example, has references in photovoltaics, hydropower, substations and battery energy storage,” he said.

But he also places a strong emphasis on localization, noting that the most sustainable model is not simply to export European solutions to Kazakhstan.

“For us, localization is essential. We want to work with Kazakh engineers, contractors and manufacturers and, where economically justified, develop local production or joint ventures.”

He also sees potential in the European Union’s Global Gateway initiative, “especially where Kazakhstan’s development priorities can be combined with European engineering and financial instruments.” The approach reflects a broader idea running through Škrabec’s thinking: the strongest partnerships create capacity on both sides rather than simply completing individual contracts.

What still holds European investors back

Kazakhstan, in his assessment, has become increasingly interesting to European capital for reasons that extend well beyond raw materials.

“Kazakhstan offers a powerful mix of advantages: natural resources, strategic geography, growing infrastructure and a clear ambition to modernize its industrial and technological base,” Škrabec said.

He believes European investors are increasingly looking at Kazakhstan “not only as a resource market, but as a place for infrastructure, logistics, industry, energy transition and higher-value technology.” For Slovenian companies, another advantage is familiarity with the wider region.

“Many of us have decades of experience in the wider post-Soviet region. We understand technical standards, institutional structures and the organization of large infrastructure projects,” he said.

At the same time, Škrabec is frank about what European investors continue to watch closely.

“European investors still pay close attention to regulatory predictability, procurement transparency, administrative efficiency, investment protection and geopolitical risk,” he said, noting that progress on those fronts could have a direct economic effect.

Beyond trade: building joint capabilities

Škrabec sees the greatest long-term potential in a relationship that goes beyond traditional trade statistics. The strongest model, in his view, is based on complementarity.

“Slovenian companies can bring specialized technology, engineering expertise, project management and access to European know-how and financing. Kazakh companies bring local market knowledge, industrial capacities and strong regional connections,” he said.

That combination, Škrabec said, creates opportunities in “energy, water, railways, logistics, environmental technologies and industrial infrastructure.” There is also a regional dimension. According to him, there is a strong potential for joint ventures, localization and, eventually, expansion into third-country markets across Central Asia. For RIKO, this is particularly relevant because its model integrates technologies, financing and partners into complete project solutions.

Such a model could change the very definition of economic cooperation between Kazakhstan and Slovenia. Instead of asking only what one country can export to the other, businesses can begin to consider what they can build together and where those combined capabilities might travel next.

A Kazakhstan beyond resources

That question becomes even more important when Škrabec looks five to ten years ahead.

“I believe it would be a mistake to see Kazakhstan ten years from now primarily as a supplier of natural resources,” he said.

Resources will remain important, but in his view, the key question is how much value Kazakhstan can create domestically. He expects continued growth in manufacturing, energy, logistics, transport, digital industries and advanced technologies. The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route will add another layer to that transformation.

“The Trans-Caspian, or Middle Corridor, will also strengthen Kazakhstan’s role as a bridge between Asia and Europe,” Škrabec said.

But even the word “bridge” may ultimately be too narrow.

“The real opportunity is for Kazakhstan to become not only a transit and resource country, but a place where industrial value, technology and expertise are created,” he noted.

That is where he sees the strongest basis for European and Kazakh cooperation: European companies can contribute technology, engineering and investment, and Kazakhstan offers scale, location, resources and regional connectivity. The relationship, therefore, could evolve from a connection between markets into a partnership between capabilities.

The role of trust and of people

For Škrabec, however, economics alone cannot sustain a relationship over decades.

“I would add one more dimension: long-term partnerships are not built only through trade and investment. Culture and trust matter too,” he said.

This is not simply a philosophical observation. RIKO has already supported Kazakh cultural initiatives in Slovenia, including the Astana Opera’s Spartacus performance and an evening of Kazakh culture. The company is also developing an initiative for a memorial to Abai Kunanbayev in Slovenia. These efforts sit alongside a longer tradition of cultural diplomacy.

For the past 26 years, Škrabec’s Lions Club has organized an annual evening in Ljubljana dedicated to one country, presenting its art, cuisine, history, traditions, natural beauty and economy. RIKO has traditionally been the main sponsor. This year, the evening focused on Kazakhstan.

“The event takes place in the Slovenian capital, on one of Ljubljana’s most prestigious stages, and has long been regarded as one of the city’s leading social events,” Škrabec said.

He recalls the response to the Kazakhstan evening as exceptional. He also singled out Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Slovenia, Altay Abibullayev, whose role went beyond formal diplomatic representation.

“Ambassador Altay Abibullayev proved to be an excellent host. At the end of the evening he presented me with a traditional Kazakh shapan (a coat). I received it as a great honor and a beautiful symbol of friendship between our two countries.” Škrabec said

It is a fitting detail in a relationship that Škrabec increasingly sees as being built on more than economic calculation. A representative office, a tender, a joint venture or a logistics project can create the infrastructure of a partnership. But people create memories.

And perhaps this is where Škrabec’s nearly four decades of experience matter most. He has seen the political map change, economies transform, and Astana grow from a very different place into the capital it is today. His assessment of Kazakhstan’s future is therefore not simply an investor’s forecast. It is also the perspective of someone who has seen how quickly a country can change when its ambitions, geography and institutions begin moving in the same direction.

For Kazakhstan and Slovenia, the next stage may be about turning that accumulated political goodwill into something more permanent: industrial partnerships, shared technologies, new transport links, local capabilities and, ultimately, a relationship in which economic cooperation becomes as natural as diplomatic dialogue.

As Škrabec put it, the most durable foundation is not trade alone, but “that combination of economic interest, cultural understanding and personal trust.”

World.title: Foreign Digital Firms Pay Kazakhstan Nearly $390 Million in Tax Since 2022
World.content:
ASTANA – Foreign digital companies have paid Kazakhstan 178.8 billion tenge ($390.2 million) in value-added tax since 2022, with annual collections rising more than fivefold over three years under the country’s so-called Google tax.

The figures show the growing fiscal contribution of international platforms serving consumers in Kazakhstan. They do not, however, directly measure the country’s total digital consumption or cross-border e-commerce, because the mechanism covers both digital services and goods sold through online platforms.

Kazakhstan introduced VAT rules for foreign internet companies, commonly known as the Google tax, in 2022. The mechanism requires international companies providing digital services or selling goods online directly to consumers in Kazakhstan to register and pay VAT.

Taxpayers include companies providing software, entertainment, gaming, education and other digital services, alongside businesses selling goods through online platforms.

How much did companies pay

As of Aug. 1, 133 foreign companies were registered as taxpayers, according to the State Revenue Committee of the Ministry of Finance, as reported by Kazinform.

Annual collections increased substantially through 2025. Foreign companies paid 10.4 billion tenge (US$22.7 million) in VAT in 2022, the first year of the mechanism. Payments increased to 24.3 billion tenge (US$53 million) in 2023 and 35 billion tenge (US$76.4 million) in 2024.

In 2025, the figure reached 57.6 billion tenge (US$125.7 million), more than five times the amount collected in 2022. Foreign companies paid 51.5 billion tenge ($112.4 million) during the first seven months of 2026, nearly 90% of the full-year amount collected in 2025.

Who are the largest taxpayers

The largest taxpayers illustrate the range of activities covered by the mechanism. The list spans physical goods, gaming, entertainment, software, communications and online education, underscoring that the mechanism extends well beyond online shopping.

In 2025, Singapore-registered Elementary Innovation Pte. Ltd., associated with the Temu marketplace, paid 13.3 billion tenge (US$29 million) in VAT. Apple paid 11.2 billion tenge (US$24.4 million), while Valve Corporation, the company behind the Steam gaming platform, paid 10.3 billion tenge (US$22.5 million).

Google contributed 7.3 billion tenge (US$15.9 million) and iHerb paid 4.9 billion tenge (US$10.7 million).

Netflix paid 353.9 million tenge (US$772,333), Spotify paid 293.1 million tenge (US$639,646), Zoom paid 183.2 million tenge (US$399,806) and Coursera paid 33.2 million tenge (US$72,454).

Expanding e-commerce market

The trend comes as Kazakhstan’s e-commerce sector continues to expand. Retail e-commerce reached nearly 3.8 trillion tenge (US$8 billion) in 2025, with marketplaces accounting for 86% of online retail sales, according to the Bureau of National Statistics. Together, these developments point to a broader shift in how Kazakh citizens purchase goods and access services, with both domestic and international digital platforms playing an increasingly important role.

The expansion of e-commerce has coincided with the widespread adoption of digital payments. Cashless payments account for 98% of transactions by number and 87% by value.

The tax receipts do not represent the total value of Kazakhstan’s digital consumption or measure cross-border e-commerce alone. Taken together with rising online retail sales, however, they indicate the growing presence of foreign platforms in the country’s consumer economy.

World.title: Almaty Museum of Arts Opens Exhibition Tracing Seven Decades of Kazakh Sculpture
World.content:
ASTANA – The Almaty Museum of Arts has opened a major exhibition exploring the development of Kazakh sculpture over seven decades.

The exhibition, titled “Müsinder: Sculpture in Kazakhstan from the 1950s to the Present Day,” opened on Sept. 8 in the museum’s Saryarka Hall and brings together more than 50 works by several generations of Kazakh artists, reported the museum’s press office. The project is curated by art historian Aliya Tiesenhausen and is part of the museum’s first-anniversary programme.

Among the artists represented are Kha­kimzhan Nauryzbayev, Isaac Itkind, Erkin Mergenov, Madina Zholdybek, Rysbek Akhmetov, Moldaqul Narymbetov, Yerbossyn Meldibekov and Aruzhan Zhumabek.

Rather than presenting a strictly chronological history, the exhibition examines how the language of sculpture has changed from the Soviet period to contemporary Kazakhstan. The works explore themes including the human body, memory, family, identity and social change.

The title refers to the Kazakh word “musin,” which can mean both “sculpture” and “human figure.” The human body therefore becomes a central element of the exhibition, allowing artists from different periods to reflect on society and personal experience.

The exhibition is divided into four thematic sections. One of them, “Game of Opposites?”, focuses on sculpture from the late 1950s through the early 1990s and examines the tension between officially accepted artistic practices and more individual approaches developed by artists in their studios. Works by Isaac Itkind and Erkin Mergenov demonstrate the emergence of more personal forms of sculptural expression during the Soviet period.

Later sections turn to contemporary approaches to the human body and its relationship with politics, culture, gender and personal experience. The exhibition thus connects works created under very different historical circumstances, highlighting changes in artistic materials, techniques and interpretations of the human figure.

According to curator Aliya Tiesenhausen, the exhibition presents sculpture as a “living artistic process” rather than simply a historical record. Soviet-era academic works are placed in dialogue with contemporary pieces to show how both artistic language and perceptions of sculpture have evolved.

“The history of sculpture is at the same time a history of society, memory, and the human being,” said Tiesenhausen.

The exhibition will run from Sept. 8 through May 2027. An illustrated catalogue accompanying the exhibition will be published in Kazakh, Russian and English, featuring scholarly texts by Tiesenhausen and art historians Valeria Ibrayeva and Alexandra Tsai.

The exhibition is also part of the Almaty Museum of Arts’ broader effort to study and present Kazakhstan’s artistic heritage. The museum, which opened in September 2025, was established as a major platform for Kazakh, Central Asian and international contemporary art.

In an earlier interview with The Astana Times, the museum’s artistic director Meruert Kaliyeva described its mission as combining the study and preservation of regional art with greater public access to international contemporary art. The museum was featured in an episode of The Astana Times exploring Almaty’s major cultural landmarks.

World.title: Kazakhstan Sets Out Priorities Ahead of BRICS Summit in India
World.content:
NEW DELHI – Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev is expected to participate in the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on Sept. 12-13, with Kazakhstan seeking to advance cooperation in energy, critical minerals, transport connectivity and global water security.

India is hosting the summit under the theme Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability. BRICS is a group of eleven major emerging markets and developing countries of the world. They include Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates, representing almost half of the world’s population and 40% of the global GDP.

Priorities of Kazakhstan, which joined the group as a partner country in 2025, were presented by Kazakh Ambassador to India Azamat Eskarayev at the BRICS Energy Partnerships for Progress and Prosperity diplomatic dialogue in New Delhi on Sept. 3.

Energy security was among the central topics of the meeting. Participants discussed traditional and renewable energy, new technologies, infrastructure, investment and critical minerals. Particular attention was given to resilient supply chains and emerging energy and transport corridors.

For Kazakhstan, the agenda closely aligns with its efforts to strengthen its role in Eurasian transport and energy connectivity. Eskarayev emphasized the country’s potential in traditional energy, renewable energy and critical minerals.

The discussion was not focused on a single project or agreement but on areas Kazakhstan intends to promote through the BRICS partnership.

Water initiative adds another dimension

Separately, Yeskarayev highlighted Tokayev’s initiative to establish an International Water Organization under the auspices of the United Nations.

The initiative calls for stronger international coordination on water resources and seeks to bring greater political attention to global water security. Kazakhstan has previously presented the proposal in other international forums, including the United Nations.

According to Aidar Kurmashev, head of the Asian Studies Department at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies under the President of Kazakhstan (KazISS), the initiative could gain practical value if it is accompanied by cooperation on water technologies and management.

He suggested that Kazakhstan could develop pilot projects for arid regions involving satellite monitoring of water resources, digital irrigation management, wastewater reuse and specialist training.

“Kazakhstan could offer its territory for pilot projects involving Indian, Chinese and Emirati companies. Then the idea of an international water organization will gain a practical dimension, and potential partners will see specific facilities, technology needs and a possible financing model,” Kurmashev told The Astana Times.

From critical minerals to concrete projects

Kurmashev noted that in critical minerals, Kazakhstan should promote projects focused on domestic processing, component manufacturing and modern exploration technologies, Kurmashev said.

He emphasized that projects should have a clearly defined resource base, site, energy and water requirements, technology partner, potential buyer and financing model. The same approach should apply to transport and digital projects.

“Tokayev’s participation in the summit could help present Kazakhstan as an independent Eurasian participant with a practical agenda covering transport, energy, water and food security and technology,” Kurmashev said.

“The Indian context is also important. India’s chairmanship makes South Asia, sustainable supply chains and technological cooperation issues more prominent,” he added.

However, he noted that the value of Kazakhstan’s participation should ultimately be measured by what follows the summit.

“Political presence should be assessed by the continuation: whether there are bilateral agreements, responsible operators and projects with certain deadlines after the summit,” Kurmashev said.

BRICS as a tool for economic diversification

For Kazakhstan, BRICS can provide an additional platform for expanding economic ties beyond its traditional partners, particularly with major economies in Asia, the Middle East, Africa and South America.

The grouping was established in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China, with South Africa joining in 2011. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Indonesia have since joined as members.

Kazakhstan is not a BRICS member but became one of the group’s partner countries in 2025. It participated in the 2025 BRICS Summit in Brazil as a partner country.

According to Kurmashev, the partner-country format gives Kazakhstan flexibility to advance its interests without making BRICS an exclusive foreign policy platform.

“Kazakhstan has a dense network of bilateral and multilateral channels with Russia and China. These are the Eurasian Economic Union and the the Commonwealth of Independent States with Russia, the the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and Confidence Building Measures in Asia, the Central Asia-China format and regular high-level meetings,” Kurmashev said.

“Therefore, the additional value of BRICS lies primarily in reaching a wider audience. On the same platform, Kazakhstan gets access to the leadership and business circles of India, Brazil, South Africa, the United Arab Emirates, Indonesia, Egypt and other countries with which the intensity of economic contacts still varies,” he said.

Kurmashev emphasized that BRICS membership or partnership does not automatically increase trade. The grouping is not a customs union and does not create a common market or uniform tariffs.

Its practical value lies in bringing governments, companies and development institutions closer together, helping them identify partners and address barriers.

For Kazakhstan, the success of economic diversification should therefore be measured not simply by total trade with BRICS countries, but by increased trade with countries such as India, Brazil, Indonesia, the UAE, Egypt and South Africa, the emergence of new export categories and a broader investor base.

Kurmashev suggested that government agencies along with QazTrade, a state-owned agency aimed at promoting trade, develop individual country strategies, organize trade missions and support companies through the contracting process.

Can BRICS strengthen transport links with India?

Transport connectivity is another area where Kazakhstan sees potential for BRICS cooperation, although the grouping itself does not manage transport corridors.

The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route links Kazakhstan through the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Türkiye with European markets. For connections with India, the International North-South Transport Corridor, Iranian ports such as Chabahar, and the Kazakhstan-Turkmenistan-Iran railway offer potential links.

According to Kurmashev, a possible long-term route could connect India, Iran, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan, with onward access through the Kazakh ports of Aktau and Kuryk to the Trans-Caspian route.

However, he noted that political declarations alone would not make such a route commercially viable. Stable cargo volumes would be needed to support regular container trains and shipping services, reduce empty runs and distribute fixed costs.

“At the BRICS Summit, Kazakhstan could propose preparing a pilot container shipment involving Indian, Iranian, Turkmen and Kazakh operators. Such a project could help identify actual transit times, tariffs and bottlenecks at each stage of the route,” he said.

At the same time, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Türkiye remain essential to the Trans-Caspian route, meaning key decisions on its operation would need to be coordinated outside the BRICS framework.

“Payments, insurance, sanctions risks around Iran and the number of transshipment points will remain important constraints. Therefore, BRICS can bring together interested parties, but the commercial viability of the route must ultimately be confirmed by carriers and shippers,” Kurmashev said.

World.title: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Economic Transformation, AIFC and Rybakina’s Rise to World No. 1
World.content:
