World.title: NT Labor celebrating win, but there's still much trust to earn back
World.content:
The ranks of the Northern Territory parliament feature a grab bag of different backgrounds.

Over the years, the building known as "the wedding cake" has welcomed a school principal, commercial lawyer, AFL players, Aboriginal elders and an Oxford-educated migration expert.

NT Labor scored a new entry into this field overnight with the election of a man with one of the more extraordinary backstories of any politician entering the legislative assembly.

Labor has picked up 77.5 per cent of first preferences in Mulka with 36.2 per cent of votes counted, easily defeating independent Andrew Blamey. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Registered nurse and Yolŋu man Yiwarr McGrath won the Mulka by-election in remote north-east Arnhem Land and will take over from retired independent MLA Yiŋiya Guyula.

As Mr McGrath told the ABC in Nhulunbuy last night, he grew up in the north-east Arnhem Land electorate in poverty, as "an orphan child … not knowing when the next meal is".

"So, I'm going to come here to the parliament with real life experiences and influence policy for my people and everyone else in this region," he said.

In Mulka, Mr McGrath's story is not an isolated one.

Yiwarr McGrath has spoken about his childhood growing up in Arnhem Land. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Australian Bureau of Statistics data shows east Arnhem Land remains one of the nation's 10 most disadvantaged local government areas.

A 35-year-old father-of-three, a health professional and a former NT Young Australian of the Year, Mr McGrath will now take his people's plight into the halls of power.

Six seats and celebrating

NT Labor celebrated Mr McGrath's victory in Nhulunbuy on Saturday night after he swept up the majority of votes against sole challenger, independent Andrew Blamey.

Mr McGrath's victory sees NT Labor hit six seats in parliament, and restores the seat of Mulka — formerly named Nhulunbuy — to the party that held it between 1980 and 2016.

Selena Uibo says Labor's focus is now on ensuring the party "can make a strong alternative government come 2028". (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

There was little doubt NT Labor would reclaim Mulka at the by-election.

The well-resourced party rolled out its biggest players on the campaign trail, from a sitting federal MP and a government minister to former local MLAs and even an ex-NT chief minister.

At the by-election after-party in Nhulunbuy, an elated Opposition Leader Selena Uibo said the win was a "huge boost for our Labor caucus, and of course our Labor party".

"We want to show Territorians we are there to do the heavy lifting … that we've learned from the past," she said.

Questions around Territory Labor's chances at the next general election linger following the party's victory in Mulka. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"We want to make sure that we can make a strong alternative government come 2028.

" And having six members now in the Labor caucus in the NT parliament will show that we're a force to be reckoned with. "

NT Labor's six members — five Aboriginal members from the bush, and one MLA in Darwin — will now come up against the Country Liberal Party (CLP) government's 17 seat majority.

But with the loss of an independent member following Mr Guyula’s retirement, some fear the major parties aren’t serving the NT community’s best interests.

Loss of crossbench voice

NT Labor's only challenger for Mulka, Mr Blamey, spoke during the campaign of how he believed Labor and the CLP had continuously let the region down.

"The two major parties have really lost their way [in the NT]," he said.

Andrew Blamey says the major parties are too focused on each individual electoral cycle. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"When you actually take a step back and look at it, our debt is spiralling out of control, there's issues throughout the NT … and politicians don't necessarily have all the answers.

" We need to listen to those voices in our communities. "

Mr Blamey, a father-of-two and human services worker, has lived in the NT for almost 20 years.

He said he was driven to run for Mulka after watching the NT parliament constantly "yo-yo" between Labor and CLP governments, with vastly different agendas and "short-term vision".

His bid for parliament, if successful, would have kept an independent voice on the crossbench, which after two resignations, has now dwindled to just two independent members.

Uphill battle to win back trust

NT Labor has also recently been mired in issues largely of its own making, including the unceremonious dumping of its deputy leader and an undisclosed speeding ticket scandal.

The party is also yet to put forward any meaty policy positions ahead of the 2028 election, although Ms Uibo insists it is "doing a lot of the background work on policy development now".

Labor still has work to do to build on the momentum from this weekend's success. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

In 2024, the party was decimated by Darwin and Palmerston voters at the NT general election over its handling of high crime rates and the territory's languishing economy.

Labor wins Mulka by-election NT Labor has won the by-election for the seat of Mulka in Arnhem Land, the first time for the party since 2016.

So with ambitions to claw back ground in those areas, how will it handle those issues now?

With a caucus mainly from Labor's left faction, will the party shift away from the tough-on-crime approach under the CLP that has seen a spike in Indigenous incarceration?

Or will it stay the course to try to convince suburban voters it won't lose control once again?

With Labor's policy platform still under development, it's hard to guess exactly which route the party will take, but whichever way it goes, the party has a lot of trust to win back — even with six seats.

World.title: Netball team's emotion-filled win after player killed in car crash
World.content:
The Navarre Grasshoppers have triumphed in a scenario no sporting team should ever have to face.

One of their most talented young players, 23-year-old Zanaiya Bergen, died on Thursday evening when her car hit a tree after training.

She and her teammates were on the verge of making history, after snapping Avoca's 69-game winning streak in a thrilling Maryborough Castlemaine District Netball League (MCDNL) preliminary final just days earlier.

In what was Zanaiya's debut season in the MCDNL, the goal shooter was one of five Navarre players named in the team of the year.

Zanaiya Bergen was named in the 2026 MCDNL team of the year. (Facebook: Navarre Football Netball Club)

Her unexpected death cast doubt on whether her team would even play on Saturday.

Do it for Zee

Zanaiya, or Zee as she was affectionately known, had played 18 games for her new club, scoring 664 goals across the 2026 season.

Zanaiya Bergen played for the Rupanyup Football Netball Club for three years. (Facebook: Rupanyup Football Netball Club)

She had previously featured in A-grade matches for Stawell in the Wimmera Football Netball League, and Rupanyup in the Horsham District Football Netball League.

MCDNL netball coordinator Katrina Turner said the league had spent most of Friday speaking with the Navarre Football Netball Club about whether the finals would go ahead.

"Whatever they decided, we would fully support them with what they wanted to do," Ms Turner said.

"When they called and said they wanted to play, I called their opponents in the A-grade and C-grade to let them know."

Zanaiya's name remained on the scoresheet for Saturday's grand final, and a minute's silence was held at the start of the game.

Purple ribbons and black arm bands were worn to mark the tragedy.

As the day went on, a significant crowd surrounded the Princes Park netball court at Maryborough to witness an A-grade match which was tense, competitive, and above all, highly emotive.

Zanaiya's teammates were doing all they could to win in honour of their teammate.

Emotion overcame some players as the game neared its end, and despite the heartbreaking circumstances, as the final whistle was blown the Navarre Grasshoppers came away with the win, 58-51.

Navarre's A-grade netball team beat Carisbrook 58-51 on Saturday. (Facebook)

Video of the match showed some players overwhelmed with tears the moment the game finished.

Members of the Navarre Football Netball Club have been offered counselling.

A premiership medal will go to Zanaiya's family.

Tributes far and wide

Zanaiya has been remembered as a funny, energetic, loyal and kind person.

Outside of her netball accolades, she spent five and a half years as a personal aged care worker at Eventide Homes in Stawell.

Her employer posted a social media tribute, which said Zanaiya brought warmth, laughter, kindness and genuine connection to every interaction.

Zanaiya Bergen's aged-care employer says it will miss her kindness, patience and infectious smile. (Facebook: Eventide Homes Stawell)

"Zee leaves behind an enormous hole in our workplace and, most importantly, in the hearts of the residents and people she cared for so deeply," the post read.

"We will miss her more than words can express and will forever be grateful that she was part of our Eventide family."

World.title: Some migrants are open to One Nation if it passes an important test
World.content:
Charanjit Singh believes One Nation deserves a chance to govern Australia.

The Melbourne-based business owner supports its promise to cut net overseas migration, which he believes would relieve pressure on the cost of living, infrastructure and public services.

"With the two major parties, they tried everything. They tried all their cards," he said.

" Now let someone else try their own cards. "

Mr Singh, an Australian citizen who migrated from India more than 20 years ago, first became interested in One Nation because he supported its opposition to vaccine mandates during the COVID pandemic.

While he has previously voted Labor, he is now a member of the One Nation party and attends its events.

"I was not their supporter from day one. But then I said, 'OK, let's go watch [a One Nation event],'" he said.

One Nation has surged in national polling and the party this year won its first federal by-election, as well as state seats in South Australia and Western Australia.

Among those expressing support, polling suggests, are some culturally diverse Australians.

Recent polling from research company Roy Morgan indicates pockets of support for One Nation among voters born in India, China and the Philippines, among other countries, while other pollsters have reported the same among people who speak a language other than English at home.

What is 'monoculturalism' and what does it look like in practice? Pauline Hanson has called for Australia to reject multiculturalism and be "monocultural". So what does it involve and are there any nations overseas that show what it might look like in Australia?

Even within communities, there are diverse views.

Some of those voters open to One Nation have told the ABC they were concerned about migration levels and security, worried about inflation, and had been disappointed with the major parties.

Manju, an Indian Australian voter who asked to be identified only by her first name, said she supported One Nation's immigration policy.

"The criteria should be restricted to skilled migrants according to our actual requirements, and restrictions must be placed on those who pose a national security threat," she said.

Hanson steps in after Farley interview One Nation MP David Farley told Insiders One Nation would pursue cuts to migration "not too different" to Labor. Pauline Hanson has stepped in to say the party's policy would actually slash immigration by about half current rates.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has said the party would cut Australia's net overseas migration, which was about 300,000 last year, to 130,000.

She said it would do this by reducing the number of international students and temporary graduate visas, and through "a much more targeted skilled migration program".

One Nation also intends to restrict migration from countries on the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade's "do not travel" list.

While he did not directly refer to One Nation's policies, former prime minister John Howard, speaking at an ANU event last week, questioned whether there was strong evidence that terrorists had entered Australia through migration.

He acknowledged the public mood was strongly focused on stopping terrorism from entering "under the cover of immigration", but argued this could not be addressed simply by stopping migrants from particular countries.

He said that type of approach to national security was "very hard" and could "be a lot more limiting than … people imagine".

However, like some other Australians the ABC spoke to, Manju said One Nation had not secured her support just yet.

Some are still grappling with the party's positions on migrants and religion, as well as Senator Hanson's recent call for Australia to embrace "monoculturalism".

Pauline Hanson called for Australia to reject multiculturalism and pursue "monoculturalism" at her NPC address. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Before deciding whether to support One Nation, Manju wants to hear Senator Hanson respond to anti-Indian racism on social media, including racist comments about Australians who were missing in the Nepal-Tibet flash floods.

"The extreme hatred directed at any brown-skinned person makes me sick," Manju said.

"How does she handle this group of people with this mindset?"

Migrants have questions for Hanson

Hindu Council of Australia vice president Surinder Jain said some migrants were also concerned about religious extremism following the Bondi attack and believed One Nation would "make Australia safe" by rejecting people known to support terrorism.

But Mr Jain said some of Senator Hanson's recent statements had put migrant voters off, including her call for Australia to be "monocultural".

"We are seeking a meeting with her to understand what is her stand on migrants, not on migration," he said.

"The freedom of speech, freedom of religion, that is such an important part of Australian values."

He said leaders should not use divisive rhetoric, which he feared could fan anti-Indian hatred on social media, and ensure what they say aligned with "the best interests of Australia".

Edgar Lu, a Sydney-based social media influencer who posts on YouTube as "Sydney Daddy", said he once volunteered for One Nation in 2019.

He also posted a Mandarin-subtitled video of Senator Hanson's National Press Club speech to his 360,000 followers.

YouTuber Edgar Lu said he is undecided about endorsing One Nation. (Supplied: Edgar Lu)

Mr Lu said One Nation's Chinese Australian supporters were older migrants who held politically conservative views.

While he also supported cutting net overseas migration levels, he said he had not endorsed One Nation yet and was unsure whether Senator Hanson had a strong team to help run the country.

"I am still observing," he said.

Mr Lu said he would also like Senator Hanson to clarify comments she made at the National Press Club criticising the number of people who spoke Mandarin at home.

Among her controversial statements on race and religion in the past 30 years, Senator Hanson has said Australia was at risk of being "swamped by Asians", described Islam as a "disease" that Australia needed to be "vaccinated against", and more recently suggested there were no "good" Muslims — all remarks that were widely condemned.

Protesters condemned Pauline Hanson's views after her maiden speech to parliament criticising Asian immigration. (Reuters)

The Federation of Ethnic Communities' Councils (FECCA), the peak body representing culturally diverse community groups, said multiculturalism and migrants should not be made scapegoats for issues facing the country.

"Blaming one group for complex problems does nothing to help everyday Australians and will only create and deepen divisions," FECCA's chief executive Prerana Mehta said.

FECCA chief executive Prerana Mehta. (Supplied: FECCA)

"We can have serious debates about migration, housing and infrastructure without questioning whether some Australians belong more than others.

"National unity does not require us to be the same. It requires a shared belief that we all belong and have something to contribute."

The ABC put detailed questions to One Nation but received no response.

Is Hanson courting culturally diverse voters?

Senator Hanson drew attention earlier this month when she posted a photo with the Indian Australian owner of Harold's Seafood, a fish and chip shop in Townsville.

"I'm still a sucker for fish and chips … Battered mackerel and chips. 10/10," the post said.

Pauline Hanson, a fish and chip shop owner before entering politics, at Harold's Seafood with business owner Pankaj Patel. (Facebook: One Nation)

Australia's Indian Sun magazine, which reported on the post with the headline "One Nation courts multicultural Australia on its own terms", saw it as a move to build support among culturally diverse voters.

Jill Sheppard, an Australian National University (ANU) researcher on political participation among migrants, said the photo served two purposes for One Nation.

"They're trying to cultivate this idea of a good migrant who assimilates to Australian culture, who cooks and eats fish and chips, and who can be accepted into a mainstream 'monocultural' Australia, given that's apparently Pauline Hanson's preference," she said.

One Nation was also trying to broaden its appeal to win seats in parliament, she said.

"Running as a very strongly anti-migration single-issue party will only get One Nation so far," Dr Sheppard said.

"They're going to have to diffuse their messaging a little bit and that means that we're going to see Pauline Hanson turn up in more culturally and linguistic diverse areas talking to voters from all walks of life."

Mabil says monoculture debate 'bulls***' as Socceroos land home The Socceroos star says anyone "trying to divide" the community is "probably not Australian themselves."

But if polls indicate some support among culturally diverse Australians, they also reflect a massive electoral barrier for the party.

Kos Samaras, a pollster and director at the Redbridge Group, said its polling showed most were shunning One Nation.

"They're choosing not to vote with them purely because of One Nation's position on race or perceived position on race and migration," he said.

Poll analyst Kevin Bonham also said he would not expect One Nation to win Labor-held outer-suburban seats with large culturally diverse populations at the next federal election.

"Some of the frontline seats that One Nation is looking at are rural seats where they can take a huge amount of support from the National Party and outer suburban seats that are not so historically Labor-friendly and perhaps less diverse," he said.

Ms Mehta, from FECCA, said the diversity of multicultural Australians meant there was no "catch-all migrant vote".

"Like every other Australian, their support has to be earned by understanding what matters to them," she said.

Culturally diverse Australians were dealing with many of the same pressures as the rest of the country, including cost of living, housing, healthcare and secure work, she said.

"There are additional barriers for some communities, including recognition of overseas qualifications, discrimination, being apart from their families, access to services and navigating complex systems," Ms Mehta said.

"Where people feel they are working hard but not getting ahead, or that institutions don't understand their frustrations and the obstacles they face. That weakens the trust and belonging they have in that system.

"That should matter to every political party."

World.title: WorkSafe investigates shovel fire at Kalgoorlie Super Pit
World.content:
WorkSafe WA is investigating after a fire engulfed the driver's cab of a heavy-duty mining shovel at one of Australia's biggest gold mines.

The incident occurred last Wednesday during the night shift while the 750-tonne Komatsu PC8000 shovel was working in the Oroya Brownhill section of Kalgoorlie's Super Pit, about 600 kilometres east of Perth.

The Super Pit's owner, gold miner Northern Star Resources, confirmed no one was injured in the incident.

The cause of the fire has not been disclosed at this stage.

A Komatsu PC8000 shovel operating at Kalgoorlie's Super Pit gold mine. (Supplied: Northern Star Resources/Dianne Newell)

'No disruption' to mine

In a statement to the ABC, Northern Star said the mine operator Kalgoorlie Consolidated Gold Mines (KCGM) immediately activated its emergency response team, which extinguished the fire.

A Northern Star spokesperson said there has been no material interruption to Super Pit operations.

"KCGM has initiated contingency plans to cover for the damaged excavator, which in any event was due to be retired in November 2026 and replaced by a new excavator," they said.

"In line with our normal processes, the KCGM team is carrying out a thorough assessment of the incident so that we can apply learnings, strengthen our processes and continue safe and reliable operations."

WorkSafe WA said it was aware of the incident and was investigating the circumstances surrounding the fire.

The Super Pit gold mine has been operating since 1989. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

According to Northern Star, the PC8000 is one of the biggest mechanical shovels in the world and has an estimated replacement cost of $18 million.

Its fuel tank has a capacity of 13,900 litres of diesel, and one full bucket of material is equal to 68.5 tonnes.

The damaged machine is one of four PC8000 shovels in the open pit fleet at the Super Pit, which also includes 45 Caterpillar 793F trucks with a 226-tonne payload and five newer 793NG trucks.

New shovel on the way

The fire comes just weeks after Northern Star put a retired PC8000 shovel on display at the Super Pit's public lookout, which attracts thousands of locals and tourists every year.

The company has ruled out returning that shovel to service.

Mining equipment supplier Liebherr delivered a new 600-tonne R9600 excavator to the Super Pit in July, with a second shovel due to arrive in October.

A decommissioned PC8000 shovel was put on display at the Super Pit public lookout in August. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

The Super Pit employs more than 1,200 workers, and has had about 600 contractors on site during the past three years to complete a $1.7 billion expansion of the Fimiston Mill, which is now being commissioned.

After a two-year ramp-up of the new mill, the Super Pit is forecast to grow production from 480,429 ounces in the 2025-26 financial year to 900,000 ounces a year from 2028-29.

If it hits that mark, it would reclaim the title of Australia's biggest producing gold mine from Boddington in WA's South West.

World.title: How Bryce Dessner juggles orchestral concertos with indie rock stardom
World.content:
Bryce Dessner has always lived across two worlds.

He is the guitarist and keyboardist in The National, one of indie rock's most successful and prestigious acts, which he co-founded in 1999.

At the same time, he was a classically trained Yale graduate who composed and performed experimental music around Brooklyn into the early 2000s.

He has won Grammys for both alternative and chamber music albums, earned a Best Original Song Oscar for Train Dreams, co-written with Nick Cave, collaborated with minimalist masters Philip Glass and Steve Reich, and penned orchestrations for Paul Simon, Bon Iver and Taylor Swift (on albums produced by his twin and The National bandmate Aaron Dessner).

This month, he teams with the Sydney Symphony Orchestra for the first solo Australian tour of his orchestral work.

Bryce Dessner with his band mates in indie rock darlings, The National (Supplied: Graham MacIndoe)

Dessner views both disciplines as complementary.

"They're actually kind of similar," he tells Double J. "They're this collaborative, very human archetype of people who work together week in, week out on music."

The big difference? The National composes together whereas, with an orchestra, "I have to show up with a fully completed score. It doesn't mean the collaboration is any less deep or important; it's just a different process".

Then there is the grander scale an orchestra provides: "I can really dig in deeper, and there's lots of colours to explore."

He compares it to writing poetry versus an epic novel. This month he'll showcase his newest musical chapter: the Australian debut of his cello concerto Trembling Earth

The political and the pastoral

Trembling Earth was inspired by an Oslo exhibition of landscape paintings by Edvard Munch.

"They were pre-World War I, probably a similar time [to now] in terms of the intensity of situations playing out on a global scale," says Dessner, who grew up in Ohio surrounded by maple and cedar trees.

"I found it so moving.

"He's painting these old oak woods … so full of emotion and tragedy."

It recalls a quote from German painter Anselm Kiefer: "There is no such thing as an innocent landscape."

"Trembling Earth is like a pastoral symphony but reflecting on the state of the human condition," Dessner says.

" I didn't necessarily want to make a really political piece, but obviously the times we're living in are so difficult, traumatic and full of conflict. "

As the Czech Philharmonic's inaugural composer-in-residence, Dessner wrote Trembling Earth for Russian cello virtuoso Anastasia Kobekina.

He calls Kobekina a "force of nature" who can play all the classics ("Dvorak, Elgar, Tchaikovsky") but also loves new music "like Radiohead and Aphex Twin".

Loading Instagram content

Kobekina is the concerto's axis, animating its melodic, lyrical moments and bringing a forceful intensity that evokes the rhythmic power of Shostakovich or Stravinsky.

"She's one of the premier soloists in the world, so it's a big deal for Australian audiences to hear her," Dessner says.

Landscape is a unifying force in Dessner's music.

Impermanence, an award-winning work commissioned by the Australian String Quartet and Sydney Dance Company, was written in response to Australia's devastating Black Summer bushfires.

Set to Rafael Bonachela's visceral choreography, it juxtaposes beauty and devastation. Those themes extend to Trembling Earth, where calamity and renewal co-exist.

"The way the Earth bears witness to the effects of humanity's bad decision-making," explains Dessner. "And that, despite its fragility, spring does come. There's a sense of renewal and hope in these pieces."

St Carolyn By The Sea, another Australian premiere, features two electric guitars that function like harps, overlapping in waves against strings ranging from soft to frenzied.

Loading Instagram content

It was inspired by Jack Kerouac's 1962 novel Big Sur, written while the author battled alcoholism and declining mental health.

"He wrote it about the west coast and the Pacific Ocean," Dessner says. "But also mentioning Stravinsky, John Coltrane and Beethoven. It just felt vast and orchestral.

"This endless sky, the sense of the ocean – the orchestral sound can really do that."

The concert hall vs the algorithm

The orchestra's size and scope allow Dessner to translate landscape into sound. But both his classical and rock backgrounds serve similar artistic impulses: capturing emotion and the fragility of the human condition.

In the age of what he calls "algorithmic culture", feeds bombarded by "AI and computer-driven music, where we don't even know if it's a human being behind it", Dessner argues live music and human connection matter more, not less.

"The concert hall itself has become this kind of haven, this human temple of creativity," he says.

"Let's get off our phones and listen to live music, not be filming it. Just be in the space with sound, with musicians who spent their lives playing these instruments.

"It's an interesting time. People are freaking out about seeing AI artists on Spotify. I don't think we're going to see that in the concert hall; robots on stage playing Beethoven or something.

Bryce Dessner now lives in southern France with wife Pauline (aka artist Mia Tindle) and children. (Supplied: Anne Mie Dreves)

Dessner remains busy. He recently finished his first opera, Herakles Mad, "which I'm really happy about," that opens next year.

Next month, The National reunite for a one-off show; their first since a "good, healthy break" from intense touring supporting back-to-back 2023 albums First Two Pages of Frankenstein and Laugh Track.

The National & Fleet Foxes are a perfect double bill. But too much of a good thing? A back-to-back evening of prestige indie rock, with Fleet Foxes' majestic folk complementing The National's artfully maudlin poetry.

It is not too soon to talk about a follow-up.

"We never turn it off. Matt [Berninger, vocalist] sent me something last week," Dessner reveals.

"We don't have a deadline or a plan necessarily, but we're starting to veer back towards each other."

It is a wonder Dessner finds time to sustain his many creative threads.

"There's seasons of things … moving calendars," he says.

"It can get lonely. And writing a concerto can feel like climbing Mount Everest.

"I told myself, 'You know what? I do this because I love it'. I try to keep track of that … that I'm enjoying doing it. That keeps me grounded."

Turning 50 prompted reflection on his achievements – and his shrinking bucket list.

"There was a time when I was like, 'Oh god, I really want to write a string quartet or orchestral piece'. I've done quite a few of these things now, and I'm proud of the music," he says.

"It really becomes a choice of, 'What am I most excited to do?' And keeping track of what I have to say, and enjoying that time."

Bryce Dessner's Trembling Earth, with Anastasia Kobekina and Umberto Cleriici, is at the Sydney Opera House on September 19 and 20.

Bryce Dessner and The Sydney Symphony's A Portrait In Music, September 24 at Sydney City Recital Hall and September 25 at Melbourne Recital Centre.

World.title: AFLW round five: Hawks star suffers a serious knee injury; weekend results as they happen
World.content:
Hawthorn coach Daniel Webster hailed his players’ ability to dig deep for an 11-point AFLW win over the Western Bulldogs after losing captain Emily Bates to a suspected serious knee injury.

Bates will have scans on her right knee in coming days after the leg twisted underneath her in a tackle at the Kennedy Community Centre on Saturday.

Umpires held up play for several minutes before Bates was taken off the field on a stretcher as teammates showed support for their much-loved skipper.

Hawthorn’s Emily Bates goes to ground with a knee injury. AFL Photos

The Hawks also lost Laura Stone (concussion) after an early head clash with an opponent and were 11 points down at halftime.

But they piled on five unanswered goals in the third quarter - four of those before Bates’ injury - to set up their 6.5 (41) to 4.6 (30) victory.

It lifted Hawthorn (3-2) into the top eight, leapfrogging the Bulldogs (3-2) on percentage.

Three-time All-Australian Bates reached her 100-game milestone a week earlier, but is now set for a lengthy period on the sidelines.

Webster said he was proud of his players’ response to the injury.

“It’s incredibly difficult [to remain focused]. I’ve seen numerous times in AFLW different ways where this has really impacted groups,” he said.

“Credit to our players, they kept their minds on the job, as challenging as that was, and were able to dig deep and finish the game off.

“Now we’ll get around Batesy once we work out what’s going on with it and support her as best we can.”

Hawthorn’s Irish key forward Aine McDonagh fired in attack with a career-best four majors, extending her lead at the top of this season’s goal-kicking list.

McDonagh has kicked 16 majors in five outings this season.

Eliza West (24 disposals), Tamara Smith (20) and Jasmine Fleming (19) also shone for the Hawks, as did ruck Lucy Wales.

Isabelle Pritchard had game-high tallies of 31 disposals and eight clearances for the Bulldogs, with Elisabeth Georgostathis (19 touches) also busy.

The Dogs kicked three of the first four goals but were held scoreless in the third quarter as Hawthorn took control of the contest.

AAP

World.title: The new terror stalking Kyiv day and night
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war The new terror stalking Kyiv day and night David Crowe Updated September 13, 2026 — 3:45pm ,first published September 13, 2026 — 9:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kyiv, Ukraine: The shocking new weapons in the war on Ukraine are deepening fears over civilian deaths when major cities seem defenceless against the speed and scale of the latest Russian attacks. Drones fitted with jet engines are radically changing the war, slamming into targets at speeds of about 600km/h and outrunning the interceptors designed to stop them. Loading The result is a new terror for Kyiv and other cities, according to the Ukrainian officers who defend the nation against relentless missile and drone attacks. “Kyiv is being terrorised day and night with the jet-powered drones from Russia,” said Colonel Skurativskyi, chief of the air defence directorate of Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Response Corps.



Russia unleashed the new drones in massive numbers over the past month, setting off air raid alerts throughout the day and changing the tempo of a war once dominated by overnight missile strikes. Ukraininan police officers carrying the wreckage of a Russian drone in Kharkiv last month. The strike that killed a 40-year-old man and injured five others was carried out by a Russian Geran-4 jet-powered drone equipped with a camera. Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Daily life continued on the streets of Kyiv in recent days, as many residents chose to stay out at a bar or cafe while checking their social media channels to gauge the scale of the danger, particularly if the attack was likely to be a ballistic missile rather than a drone. The alert on Friday night, for instance, did not stop young people gathering in a park for drinks. The alert on Saturday morning did not deter an old man from walking his dog in the light rain on the streets near the city’s historic Saint Sophia cathedral. But the danger was real, and deadly, in other parts of the city and country. On Friday, Russian drones hit two petrol stations in Kyiv, killing two people and wounding six. A drone strike on an apartment building in Zaporizhzhia injured two civilians, including a young boy. An attack in Dnipro wounded a dozen people.



On Saturday, a Russian strike ​on a grocery store in the town of Zvyahel, west of Kyiv, killed two people. In the southern city of Odesa, the local governor said 37 were injured in overnight strikes. Earlier drones, including the Shahed models designed in Iran and shared with Russia, came with propeller engines, enabling them to reach speeds of about 180km/h. Men stand near a fire after a jet-powered drone struck an office building in the Podilskyi district of Kyiv on Friday (Ukrainian time). SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Firefighters work near the scene of a fire after a jet-powered drone struck an office building in Kyiv’s Podilskyi district, on Friday (Ukrainian time). NurPhoto via Getty Images Ukraine developed drones to counter these threats, although the country remains desperately short of the Patriot interceptors it needs to stop Russian missiles.



Now the jet-powered drones are finding a way through Ukraine’s air defence – and forcing a debate over how quickly the armed forces can develop faster interceptors to destroy the flying bombs before they kill. Related Article War Are we in World War III, and just don’t know it? Russia is intensifying the danger on a rapid scale, with the Ukrainian armed forces telling the BBC that jet-powered drone attacks rose from 350 in June to 1600 in July and 2800 in August. Skurativskyi expressed confidence on Saturday that Ukraine would find a way to counter the danger. Speaking to the Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference in Kyiv, he said the danger was not restricted to Ukraine alone. “Jet-powered drones are not just a problem for Ukraine but for the entire civilised world,” he said.



“They [Russia] have this lethal tool, this kind of weaponry, that they can apply not just against us but against other countries as well. “The good news is that Ukrainian Armed Forces are on alert all the time.” Skurativskyi argued that other countries should be concerned about the new jet-powered design after Romania, Poland and Moldova experienced Russian drone incursions in recent weeks. German authorities named Russia as the source of an explosive drone at Leipzig airport that failed to detonate when it struck a transport aircraft on August 4. Behind the shift to the faster drone is a Russian deal to buy small jet engines from Chinese suppliers in massive volumes.



The main supplier of the turbojet engines is said to be Telefly Telecommunications Equipment, based in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, according to The Wall Street Journal. The impact is felt across Ukraine because people know their armed forces lack the technology to stop jet-powered drones and do not have enough Patriot interceptors to bring down ballistic missiles. “Ukraine badly needs air defence,” admitted Yuriy Fedorenko, a commander of the Achilles drone unit in the Ukrainian Armed Forces and a member of the Kyiv City Council. Air defence officer Artem Skurativskyi (right), a colonel in the Armed Forces of Ukraine, speaks at the Yalta European Strategy conference in Kyiv on Saturday (Ukrainian time). Victor Pinchuk Foundation Fedorenko told the YES conference that this danger intensified the need for international help, especially with the supply of missile interceptors.



“Ukraine lives on the brink,” he said. “Please help us to survive.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, addressing the conference by video on Friday, said the country was working with European governments to develop air defence systems that could reach test mode as soon as December. Loading Even so, the immediate need is the supply of more Patriot systems, given that it can require two interceptors to take down one ballistic missile. “Today, Russia produces 140 ballistic missiles per month. According to NATO standards, to down 140 missiles you use 280 anti-ballistic interceptors,” Zelensky posted on X.



“But you will never get 280 Patriot missiles per month. Even getting 100 missiles is a huge challenge. And this is what I want – to have 100–120 interceptors for the difficult, cold months ahead.” But global stocks are low because of the Ukraine and Iran wars. Defence giant Lockheed-Martin produces about 600 Patriot interceptors per year and is scaling this up to 2000 over the next seven years. Related Article Analysis

World elections Election shockwave: Meet the smiling new leader set to bring hard-right upheaval to Germany Ukrainian company Fire Point, which developed the successful Flamingo missile now striking targets deep inside Russia, is cautious about when it can produce a missile defence system to fill the gap. The company’s chief executive, Iryna Terekh, announced the Freyja project for a missile interception system with European partners in July, but it would take until next year to reach the test phase for the prototypes.



“Hopefully, the first test interception will be conducted by the end of next year,” Terekh told the conference. For the people of Ukraine, the advent of new Russian weaponry brings more fear and suffering, but there is no easy solution to the shortage of Patriots, the time required to develop the Freyja and the immediate threat of the jet-powered drones. Related Article Opinion

Russia-Ukraine war Putin will not win: My encounter with Europe’s new-found optimism George Brandis Former high commissioner to the UK and federal attorney-general For now, the answer in Kyiv is to escalate missile and drone strikes on Russian facilities that help produce Russian weapons – such as chemical plants and warehouses. Ukraine also targets oil refineries, forcing a supply crisis at petrol stations. Kyrylo Budanov, the top aide to Zelensky and a key negotiator on potential peace deals, said the long-range strikes would continue to put pressure on Russia. The objective, he told the YES conference, was to ensure Russian President Vladimir Putin would eventually accept the need for a peace agreement.



“Sooner or later, it will bring the desired effect,” said Budanov. Meanwhile, high-speed drones will menace Ukrainian skies. And the air raid alerts will continue to go off, day and night. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Harrowing Israeli documentary pipped by Danish war drama at Venice Film Festival awards
World.content:
CultureMoviesCinema Harrowing Israeli documentary pipped by Danish war drama at Venice Film Festival awards Stephanie Bunbury September 13, 2026 — 3:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There was widespread surprise when NAZA, an Israeli documentary that had a record-breaking 25-minute standing ovation at the 83rd Venice Film Festival, won the special jury prize at the awards ceremony on Saturday. Director May el-Toukhy, left, with Mathilde Arcel at the Venice Film Festival. AP Photo/Scott A Garfitt That early award meant Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s harrowing documentary, which features testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders whose insights into the war in Gaza include what they say is the systemic killing of Palestinian civilians, could not win the Golden Lion later in the ceremony. Three days earlier, NAZA had left many viewers winded and speechless. For this viewer, it made everything else at the festival pale into unimportance. Shot on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night in extreme secrecy over three years by two of the filmmakers behind the Oscar-winning No Other Land, the documentary is named after the acronym used for non-combatants killed when the Israeli army targets suspected Hamas operatives.



Related Article ★★★½

Review Israeli and Palestinian journalists mine the horrors of the West Bank Wreathed in shadows, soldiers tell how the blanket hacking of phones means they know where everyone is and what they’re saying. Linked numbers create suspects who may be taken out with family groups or as entire streets of houses, the exact number of expected dead already noted. One soldier remembers pushing the button while listening to a baby crying in the target house; another remembers wondering, on a school trip to Auschwitz, how the Germans could have done such terrible things. “I still think the Nazis were evil,” he says, pondering what that now made him. “It’s honestly not very easy to stand here, thinking of all the people, the Israeli politicians, the journalists back home who are attacking this film, denying it without even seeing it,” Abraham said after winning the award. “It is really, really especially important to us that Israelis watch this film.” If NAZA had not been in the mix, the Golden Lion winner, Danish director May el-Toukhy’s A Woman Unknown, would have been beyond dispute. Set in Denmark immediately after World War II, it begins as a live-in nanny, played by Mathilde Arcel, prepares to marry her older employer. But a secret past relationship with a German soldier threatens to upend her reputation.



Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor with the special jury prize award they won for Naza at the Venice Film Festival. Getty Images Austere, tight with tension and rich with social history, A Woman Unknown was considered a safe bet for a jury led by actor-director Maggie Gyllenhaal, whose own films The Lost Daughter and The Bride revolve around disruptive women. El-Toukhy, who was the only woman to have solely directed a film in the main competition this year, became just the eighth woman to win the festival’s top prize. “To me personally, Woman Unknown is about the female body as a battleground,” she said. “At the same time the film tells the tale of women who are unseen, invisible and voiceless.” Arcel was a popular winner of the Volpi Cup for best actress. “This is my first lead role in a movie and my first time at a film festival,” she said. “I’m extremely honoured.”



John Malkovich won best actor for his performance in Martin McDonagh’s dark CIA comedy Wild Horse Nine. “I am humbled to be chosen for this award which has been given to so many wonderful actors,” he said in a video message, explaining that he was shooting in Montreal. Korean slow cinema doyen Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love, on the relationship between a working-class woman whose husband has lost his job and a rich film-maker documenting dismissed workers’ lives, won the Silver Lion, the festival’s second-biggest honour. Naza was shot on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night in extreme secrecy. Venice Film Festival via AP Thoughtful and punctuated by small but sharp plot twists, Lee’s unpacking of Korea’s high-voltage economic miracle – and its winners and losers – was a critical favourite. “We are living in an era where the meaning of labour is fading and human connections are increasingly becoming severed,” Lee said through a translator. “I made this film to ask what cinema can and should do in times like these. I take this award as a sign that you want me to keep asking these questions.”



Related Article Entertainment Moss Moore’s murder was never solved. A Brisbane Festival show reopens the case Stephane Brize’s A Good Little Soldier, an angry French film about a human resources manager (Alba Rohrwacher) trying to paper over systematic bullying within a company, won best screenplay. The Silver Lion for directing went to Russian-born Ilya Khrzhanovsky for DAU, an epic three-hour-plus film which has been described as loose biopic of the Soviet Nobel Prize-winning physicist Lev Landau. Taking more than 20 years to make, it took two years to film with actors living around the clock as their characters in a purpose-built complex that included laboratories, kitchens and a newspaper office. The prize for the best new young actor went to the unknown Malou Khebizi from French director Cedric Khan’s A Place to Heal, about a juvenile care hostel for troubled young people. With AP

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share License this article More: Cinema Stephanie Bunbury is a film and culture writer for The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald.

World.title: Australian tourist dies after falling from cliff at famous beach near Bali
World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaTragedy Australian tourist dies after falling from cliff at famous beach near Bali Ellen Connolly and Ashleigh McMillan Updated September 13, 2026 — 3:33pm ,first published September 13, 2026 — 3:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An Australian tourist has died after falling about 80 metres from a cliff at Kelingking Beach in Nusa Penida near Bali. The incident unfolded after 8am on Saturday when tourists alerted a lifeguard to a woman who appeared to be stranded on a cliff at the popular beach, about 20 kilometres off the south-eastern coast of Bali. Local authorities recover the woman’s body. Basarnas Bali (search and rescue agency) Emergency services rushed to the scene, but she fell further before they could reach her. The woman, named as Brianna Lani Cronin, 29, was from Queensland and visiting the area on holiday, Nusa Penida police said.



“The victim is estimated to have fallen around 9am,” Nusa Penida Alert Unit co-ordinator Cakra Negara said in a statement. “At the time, she was seeking an independent path toward the edge of the cliff before slipping and falling into the ravine. The body of the young Australian woman killed in a fall in Bali is recovered. Basarnas Bali (search and rescue agency) “When found, the victim had sustained several fractures; we secured her onto a stretcher to facilitate the evacuation process.” Cronin had already died from her injuries by the time rescuers reached her, a spokesperson for the Indonesian Navy said.



Search and rescue agency Basarnas Bali said attempts to retrieve her body by boat were unsuccessful because of large waves. Related Article Kelingking Beach, Bali: The hidden beach overrun by Instagram tourists Instead, rescuers had to place Cronin’s body on a stretcher and carry her up a steep and narrow staircase for 1½ hours. A Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade spokesperson confirmed the government was providing consular assistance to the woman’s family, who had requested privacy. Queensland Premier David Crisafulli described the death as tremendously sad.



“To have a life taken away in a heartbeat like that ... it’s just incredibly, incredibly sad,” he told reporters on Sunday. “I just express my sympathies to her family and those loved ones with her and back at home. I think all of Queensland collectively looks at that and just feels ... just a huge degree of sorrow.” Kelingking Beach sits on the southwest coast of the island of Nusa Penida, which is about 20 kilometres off the main island of Bali. The beach is best known for its headland nicknamed “T-Rex Bay”, named for a massive, emerald-green cliff formation that twists out into the Indian Ocean in the shape of a dinosaur. An aerial view of Kelingking Beach on Nusa Penida.



It is widely celebrated as one of the most Instagrammable beaches in Asia, and tourists line up for an hour along the cliffside edge to snap selfies against the stunning backdrop. Swimming at the beach is banned year-round due to dangerous currents. The trek down to the beach can take two hours on a path described as perilous. Work on a panoramic glass lift to carry visitors down to the beach was started in 2024, but after fierce opposition from locals and tourists the project was halted in October 2025. Investigations are continuing into the circumstances that led to the woman’s fall. With AAP Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: It’s not ending with Trump. Now we’re under attack from his clones
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's America Opinion It’s not ending with Trump. Now we’re under attack from his clones Melanie La'Brooy Writer September 13, 2026 — 3:21pm

September 13, 2026 — 3:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Of all the weird things occurring in the US right now (Measles are back! Cold War with Canada!) one of the strangest has been the rise of the Trump clones. Their origin dates back to 2016. As the then Republican front-runner for the presidential nomination, Trump infamously declared that “I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody and I wouldn’t lose any voters. It’s, like, incredible.” US President Donald Trump. AP Marvelling at the prospect of engaging in criminal behaviour while retaining electability, Trump went on to prove his hypothesis, notching up convictions for sexual assault and defamation and 34 counts of falsifying business records in a hush money case involving his affair with a porn star. He was then elected president again. Now, as the US heads towards November midterm elections, Trump’s revelation that acts of violence, immorality and criminality no longer preclude running for public office has seemingly become normalised. It’s now incredible if a candidate running for office in the US doesn’t have a skeleton in the closet. Or tattooed to his chest, as in the case of the former Democratic Senate candidate for Maine, Graham Platner, whose skull-and-crossbones tattoo, which closely resembled the Nazi Totenkopf, caused a minor furore. Fortunately for Platner, these days there’s a higher tolerance for white supremacist-adjacent tattoos among holders of high office in the US, (as evinced by Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth’s ink), so it wasn’t until allegations of sexual assault were made against him that Platner finally exited the race in July.



Referring to the situation in Maine, conservative commentator Greg Price, wrote on X: “It’s truly hysterical how Democrats can’t seem to find one normal dude to run for office”, which would have been a solid partisan burn about the importance of candidate quality control in the midterm elections, if only Brandon Herrera and Ken Paxton didn’t exist. Herrera is a Republican candidate running for congress in Texas. A gun influencer who boasted about owning a copy of Mein Kampf, Herrera has made jokes about using homeless people for target practice and has referred to women as “fat bitches” and “whores”. In a video, Herrera refers to the Nazi submachine gun he is wielding as the “original ghetto blaster” and “Hitler’s street sweeper”. He also coined a vulgar epithet for children, which is unprintable. It’s a measure of the current “When he goes low, we go lower” standard set by Trump that Herrera is running as the Trump-endorsed candidate for the GOP: the same party that only days ago at the Republican convention in Dallas, Vice President JD Vance positioned as the champion of family values. Donald Trump speaking at the wedding reception of Max Miller and Emily Moreno in 2022. X Meanwhile, Ken Paxton, the Republican Texas Attorney General and Trump-endorsed Senate candidate, is facing a formidable opponent; not the Democrat candidate, James Talarico, but rather himself. As The New York Times reported, Paxton has been “indicted on charges of felony securities fraud and impeached ... [on allegations] of bribery, dereliction of duty, obstruction of justice and abuse of the public trust, and other misdeeds.” Paxton’s wife has accused her conservative Christian husband of adultery and filed for divorce on “biblical grounds”. If that’s not enough, Talarico’s team turned security footage of Paxton stealing a $US1000 Montblanc pen into a campaign ad. When asked by a New York Times reporter why he thought voters stuck with him, given he’s been indicted, impeached and accused of adultery, Paxton invoked the Fifth Avenue amendment, replying: “Why does the base stick with President Trump, when you can say all those same things?”



Paxton’s touching “Whither thou goest, I will go” declaration of fealty to the dishonourable example set by Trump reveals just how deep the rot has gone. US politicians are no longer required to deny, explain or even blush when accused of immoral or criminal behaviour. The “Trump did it first” defence works for almost any situation an ethically compromised politician might find themselves accused of: racism, misogyny, lying, corruption, sexual abuse, colonising Venezuela or unauthorised building works. Ken Paxton’s win was welcomed by Donald Trump, who said Paxton would “become a fantastic, common-sense senator”. AP However, Trump’s ability to defy political gravity doesn’t appear to work for all of his would-be mini clones, as illustrated by the growing roll-call of candidates from both sides who have slunk away in shame during this scandal-plagued electoral cycle. Related Article Opinion

Immigration How a conspiracy theory embraced by Trump became mainstream in Australia Melanie La'Brooy Writer Sexual misconduct claims forced Democrat congressman, Eric Swalwell to drop out of the California governor’s race in April. The same day, Republican Texas congressman, Tony Gonzales resigned, after admitting to an affair with a staffer, who had later died by suicide. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, a Democrat congresswoman from Florida, also resigned after being indicted on embezzlement charges. In August, North Carolina Republican, Chuck Edwards, dropped his re-election bid following allegations of sexual harassment by his young female staffers.



Grimly hanging on is Republican Ohio congressman, Max Miller, who is still running for re-election despite horrific domestic violence allegations against him. Miller’s ex-wife is the daughter of Republican senator, Bernie Moreno who wrote on X: “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them.” Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump is using a secret code to motivate extremists. It’s everywhere, if you know where to look Melanie La'Brooy Writer Herein lies the pre-eminent problem of the Trumpian age: no-one appears to know any more what the basic standards of character required to hold elected office are. From the top down, this is no longer politics as public service. Instead, it’s a permission structure for the unscrupulous to act with impunity. It’s dire news for those hoping that the malfeasance of the Trump era will end when he leaves office in 2029. Whether Republican or Democrat, every US politician attempting to wield dissolute power without consequence continues his legacy. As the attack of the clones continues, it’s hard not to think wistfully of a former US president who stated: “Character is the most important qualification the president of the United States can have.”



Well said, Richard Nixon. Melanie La’Brooy is a novelist who writes on politics and social justice issues. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: ‘Unsafe staffing, unmanageable workloads’: Thousands of Queensland nurses quit
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Health ‘Unsafe staffing, unmanageable workloads’: Thousands of Queensland nurses quit Courtney Kruk September 13, 2026 — 3:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Crisafulli government has defended its efforts to increase frontline health workers after data showed thousands of nurses had quit crucial positions at public hospitals in recent years. Figures obtained by News Corp through Right to Information indicated more than 2400 nurses left hospitals in 2024–25, the worst departure of nursing staff in four years. Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls has defended the Crisafulli government’s efforts to grow frontline healthcare workers after data showed thousands of nurses had left the sector. Courtney Kruk A total of 10,824 nurses left Queensland hospitals in the past five years, according to the data provided. Health Minister Tim Nicholls admitted the statistics were concerning, but said attrition across Queensland Health had dropped under the Crisafulli government, from 6.54 per cent under Labor, to 5.42 per cent, and efforts were underway to grow and maintain nursing staff across the sector.



“[We’ve reduced attrition] by hiring 10,000 more employees in Queensland Health. More than 7000 of those have been frontline and frontline support [staff],” Nicholls said. Related Article Queensland Health Nearly half of all Queensland doctors at risk of burnout, survey finds “We are working very hard to reduce those numbers [of nurses leaving] … I don’t think anyone could raise any quibbles about the amount of time, energy, and effort that’s being put into retaining staff as well as bringing on new staff.” The Crisafulli government has pledged 46,000 additional healthcare workers – including doctors, nurses and paramedics – by 2032, but has yet to detail how such figures will be achieved. A workforce gap analysis of Queensland Health was released in November, and a follow-up plan – initially promised by July – will be released later this year, Nicholls said.



Queensland Nurses and Midwives’ Union (QNMU) secretary Sarah Beaman said staffing issues continue to plague hospitals across the state, and were contributing to the recent exodus of workers. “After years of ‘hanging in there’ because they love what they do, growing numbers of public nurses and midwives are leaving, or considering leaving, because they can no longer absorb unsafe staffing, unmanageable workloads or feeling unsupported by management,” Beaman said. “It is important to note there will always have some natural workforce movement such as retirement or relocation. We also need to distinguish between leaving an employer and leaving their professions. Queensland Nurses and Midwives’ Union (QNMU) Secretary Sarah Beaman said a growing number of nurses were leaving the profession due to unsafe staffing and unmanageable workloads. Courtney Kruk “The big concern is when nurses and midwives who want to keep working feel they can’t due to unsafe conditions.”



A recent survey of QNMU members found 15.6 per cent of shifts in wards covered by legislated ratios were still below the minimum staffing requirement. On wards without legislated ratios, nearly 60 per cent of shifts did not meet the same minimum staffing threshold. Related Article Queensland Health Shocking video of patient assaulting nurse prompts union call for safer conditions The same Grow Your Voice survey found 84 per cent of respondents had recently experienced violence at work, with nearly a third experiencing three or more types of violence. “People are not walking away because they have stopped caring about nursing or midwifery. They are reaching a point where the job is unsustainable,” Beaman said. Shadow health spokesperson Mark Bailey accused the LNP of being combative towards health workers and said issues raised during wage negotiations and hospital planning had caused many to lose confidence in the government’s approach to recruitment and retention.



“There’s no doubt that our nurses are being overworked and are feeling burnt-out … because the government is not backing them in with extra capacity in our system,” Bailey said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘It is a beautiful property’: No bids for $4m renovated Rosebery house
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions ‘It is a beautiful property’: No bids for $4m renovated Rosebery house Elizabeth Redman September 13, 2026 — 3:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An architecturally renovated family home in Rosebery is still available after passing in at an auction on Saturday at which nobody bid. The transformed four-bedroom bungalow at 24 Morley Avenue has leadlight windows, high ceilings, glass sliding doors, a gourmet kitchen with striking Avocatus Quartzite bench, covered barbecue area and swimming pool. It was listed with a price guide of $3.95 million. The property was one of 706 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 53 per cent from 410 reported results throughout the week, while 133 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. The early read is slightly lower than last week’s preliminary result of 57 per cent. But Sydney’s monthly auction clearance rate has edged up for the last two months as sellers realise they need to meet the market to sell. Sydney remains a buyer’s market, below the threshold of 60 per cent considered balanced between buyers and sellers.



The Rosebery home attracted three registered bidders. The potential buyer demographic was largely young professional couples from the surrounding suburbs and inner city, plus some downsizers. Related Article Auctions ‘State of inaction’: Inner west home sells for $2.59m as buyers go MIA But on the auction floor, none of the potential buyers raised their hands and the home was passed in. “It was just one of those auctions where people did all their diligence,” The Agency selling agent Chris Skarlatos said, “And no-one put their hand up. They all sat there and looked at each other.” He is now working with a few potential buyers and hopes it will sell soon.



“It is a beautiful property,” he said. “The cost of buying an unrenovated home – it makes sense to just buy this.” The reserve was $4 million. The vendors are moving to be closer to family. He described the market as “very patchy. You get the odd property that goes very well.” There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide.



On the north shore, a young family paid $3,755,000 for a brick family home in Roseville, beating two others. The four-bedroom house at 44 Moore Street has an open-plan extension at the rear and was listed with a price guide of $3.7 million. Three parties registered to bid, all young families, some of whom had been looking to buy for some time. But Ray White Upper North Shore selling agent Jessica Cao described the auction as “very slow”.



“This is just the perfect location, perfect size, ready to move into, no work needs to be done,” she said. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Former Mirvac boss to sell $11m Killara home with tennis court Bidding began at $3.49 million, below the price guide, and then climbed to $3.55 million where the bidding stopped again before the third family entered the fray. The price rose to $3.7 million but was still short of the reserve price of $3.75 million. Cao was then able to secure a winning bid of $3,755,000 to get the deal done. The marathon auction took about 40 minutes.



“No one wants to overpay,” Cao said. “The good thing is, auctions, you can see who wants it.” The winners are an upsizing family of six who have sold their home on the lower north shore. The sellers are a young family moving overseas who bought the home four years ago for $3.36 million. “I do feel there is more energy in the market,” Cao said. “The turnkey properties in a good location with a scarcity of listings still can reach a good result in this market.” In the inner west, a possible duplex development site in Ashfield is also still available after it did not reach its reserve at auction.



The four-bedroom house at 51 Palace Street is on a block of about 697 square metres and was for sale for the first time in 70 years. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Downsizer pad of late Katies co-founder listed for around $20 million It was listed with a price guide of $2.8 million and attracted interest from builders. One potential bidder, a builder, attended the auction but did not bid. A vendor bid was placed at $2.85 million but with no further offers, the home passed in. The reserve was $3 million. The builder has indicated interest at around the $2.7 million to $2.75 million mark.



Rich & Oliva selling agent Marco Errichiello said buyers are interested and builders are asking questions such as about settlement, but the home has not yet sold. “Buyers, if they see really good value, they will buy, but it has got to be really good value,” Errichiello said. “They are almost predicting what it will be worth in a couple of months, after a rate rise,” he added, alluding to economist forecasts of another likely cash rate hike by the end of this year. “The only thing that speeds up buyers is a lack of stock.”

World.title: AFLW round five: Hawks star suffers a serious knee injury; weekend results as they happen
World.content:
Hawthorn coach Daniel Webster hailed his players’ ability to dig deep for an 11-point AFLW win over the Western Bulldogs after losing captain Emily Bates to a suspected serious knee injury.

Bates will have scans on her right knee in coming days after the leg twisted underneath her in a tackle at the Kennedy Community Centre on Saturday.

Umpires held up play for several minutes before Bates was taken off the field on a stretcher as teammates showed support for their much-loved skipper.

Hawthorn’s Emily Bates goes to ground with a knee injury. AFL Photos

The Hawks also lost Laura Stone (concussion) after an early head clash with an opponent and were 11 points down at halftime.

But they piled on five unanswered goals in the third quarter - four of those before Bates’ injury - to set up their 6.5 (41) to 4.6 (30) victory.

It lifted Hawthorn (3-2) into the top eight, leapfrogging the Bulldogs (3-2) on percentage.

Three-time All-Australian Bates reached her 100-game milestone a week earlier, but is now set for a lengthy period on the sidelines.

Webster said he was proud of his players’ response to the injury.

“It’s incredibly difficult [to remain focused]. I’ve seen numerous times in AFLW different ways where this has really impacted groups,” he said.

“Credit to our players, they kept their minds on the job, as challenging as that was, and were able to dig deep and finish the game off.

“Now we’ll get around Batesy once we work out what’s going on with it and support her as best we can.”

Hawthorn’s Irish key forward Aine McDonagh fired in attack with a career-best four majors, extending her lead at the top of this season’s goal-kicking list.

McDonagh has kicked 16 majors in five outings this season.

Eliza West (24 disposals), Tamara Smith (20) and Jasmine Fleming (19) also shone for the Hawks, as did ruck Lucy Wales.

Isabelle Pritchard had game-high tallies of 31 disposals and eight clearances for the Bulldogs, with Elisabeth Georgostathis (19 touches) also busy.

The Dogs kicked three of the first four goals but were held scoreless in the third quarter as Hawthorn took control of the contest.
