World.title: The new terror stalking Kyiv day and night
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war The new terror stalking Kyiv day and night David Crowe Updated September 13, 2026 — 3:45pm ,first published September 13, 2026 — 9:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kyiv, Ukraine: The shocking new weapons in the war on Ukraine are deepening fears over civilian deaths when major cities seem defenceless against the speed and scale of the latest Russian attacks. Drones fitted with jet engines are radically changing the war, slamming into targets at speeds of about 600km/h and outrunning the interceptors designed to stop them. Loading The result is a new terror for Kyiv and other cities, according to the Ukrainian officers who defend the nation against relentless missile and drone attacks. “Kyiv is being terrorised day and night with the jet-powered drones from Russia,” said Colonel Skurativskyi, chief of the air defence directorate of Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Response Corps.



Russia unleashed the new drones in massive numbers over the past month, setting off air raid alerts throughout the day and changing the tempo of a war once dominated by overnight missile strikes. Ukraininan police officers carrying the wreckage of a Russian drone in Kharkiv last month. The strike that killed a 40-year-old man and injured five others was carried out by a Russian Geran-4 jet-powered drone equipped with a camera. Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Daily life continued on the streets of Kyiv in recent days, as many residents chose to stay out at a bar or cafe while checking their social media channels to gauge the scale of the danger, particularly if the attack was likely to be a ballistic missile rather than a drone. The alert on Friday night, for instance, did not stop young people gathering in a park for drinks. The alert on Saturday morning did not deter an old man from walking his dog in the light rain on the streets near the city’s historic Saint Sophia cathedral. But the danger was real, and deadly, in other parts of the city and country. On Friday, Russian drones hit two petrol stations in Kyiv, killing two people and wounding six. A drone strike on an apartment building in Zaporizhzhia injured two civilians, including a young boy. An attack in Dnipro wounded a dozen people.



On Saturday, a Russian strike ​on a grocery store in the town of Zvyahel, west of Kyiv, killed two people. In the southern city of Odesa, the local governor said 37 were injured in overnight strikes. Earlier drones, including the Shahed models designed in Iran and shared with Russia, came with propeller engines, enabling them to reach speeds of about 180km/h. Men stand near a fire after a jet-powered drone struck an office building in the Podilskyi district of Kyiv on Friday (Ukrainian time). SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Firefighters work near the scene of a fire after a jet-powered drone struck an office building in Kyiv’s Podilskyi district, on Friday (Ukrainian time). NurPhoto via Getty Images Ukraine developed drones to counter these threats, although the country remains desperately short of the Patriot interceptors it needs to stop Russian missiles.



Now the jet-powered drones are finding a way through Ukraine’s air defence – and forcing a debate over how quickly the armed forces can develop faster interceptors to destroy the flying bombs before they kill. Related Article War Are we in World War III, and just don’t know it? Russia is intensifying the danger on a rapid scale, with the Ukrainian armed forces telling the BBC that jet-powered drone attacks rose from 350 in June to 1600 in July and 2800 in August. Skurativskyi expressed confidence on Saturday that Ukraine would find a way to counter the danger. Speaking to the Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference in Kyiv, he said the danger was not restricted to Ukraine alone. “Jet-powered drones are not just a problem for Ukraine but for the entire civilised world,” he said.



“They [Russia] have this lethal tool, this kind of weaponry, that they can apply not just against us but against other countries as well. “The good news is that Ukrainian Armed Forces are on alert all the time.” Skurativskyi argued that other countries should be concerned about the new jet-powered design after Romania, Poland and Moldova experienced Russian drone incursions in recent weeks. German authorities named Russia as the source of an explosive drone at Leipzig airport that failed to detonate when it struck a transport aircraft on August 4. Behind the shift to the faster drone is a Russian deal to buy small jet engines from Chinese suppliers in massive volumes.



The main supplier of the turbojet engines is said to be Telefly Telecommunications Equipment, based in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, according to The Wall Street Journal. The impact is felt across Ukraine because people know their armed forces lack the technology to stop jet-powered drones and do not have enough Patriot interceptors to bring down ballistic missiles. “Ukraine badly needs air defence,” admitted Yuriy Fedorenko, a commander of the Achilles drone unit in the Ukrainian Armed Forces and a member of the Kyiv City Council. Air defence officer Artem Skurativskyi (right), a colonel in the Armed Forces of Ukraine, speaks at the Yalta European Strategy conference in Kyiv on Saturday (Ukrainian time). Victor Pinchuk Foundation Fedorenko told the YES conference that this danger intensified the need for international help, especially with the supply of missile interceptors.



“Ukraine lives on the brink,” he said. “Please help us to survive.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, addressing the conference by video on Friday, said the country was working with European governments to develop air defence systems that could reach test mode as soon as December. Loading Even so, the immediate need is the supply of more Patriot systems, given that it can require two interceptors to take down one ballistic missile. “Today, Russia produces 140 ballistic missiles per month. According to NATO standards, to down 140 missiles you use 280 anti-ballistic interceptors,” Zelensky posted on X.



“But you will never get 280 Patriot missiles per month. Even getting 100 missiles is a huge challenge. And this is what I want – to have 100–120 interceptors for the difficult, cold months ahead.” But global stocks are low because of the Ukraine and Iran wars. Defence giant Lockheed-Martin produces about 600 Patriot interceptors per year and is scaling this up to 2000 over the next seven years. Related Article Analysis

World elections Election shockwave: Meet the smiling new leader set to bring hard-right upheaval to Germany Ukrainian company Fire Point, which developed the successful Flamingo missile now striking targets deep inside Russia, is cautious about when it can produce a missile defence system to fill the gap. The company’s chief executive, Iryna Terekh, announced the Freyja project for a missile interception system with European partners in July, but it would take until next year to reach the test phase for the prototypes.



“Hopefully, the first test interception will be conducted by the end of next year,” Terekh told the conference. For the people of Ukraine, the advent of new Russian weaponry brings more fear and suffering, but there is no easy solution to the shortage of Patriots, the time required to develop the Freyja and the immediate threat of the jet-powered drones. Related Article Opinion

Russia-Ukraine war Putin will not win: My encounter with Europe’s new-found optimism George Brandis Former high commissioner to the UK and federal attorney-general For now, the answer in Kyiv is to escalate missile and drone strikes on Russian facilities that help produce Russian weapons – such as chemical plants and warehouses. Ukraine also targets oil refineries, forcing a supply crisis at petrol stations. Kyrylo Budanov, the top aide to Zelensky and a key negotiator on potential peace deals, said the long-range strikes would continue to put pressure on Russia. The objective, he told the YES conference, was to ensure Russian President Vladimir Putin would eventually accept the need for a peace agreement.



“Sooner or later, it will bring the desired effect,” said Budanov. Meanwhile, high-speed drones will menace Ukrainian skies. And the air raid alerts will continue to go off, day and night. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Harrowing Israeli documentary pipped by Danish war drama at Venice Film Festival awards
World.content:
CultureMoviesCinema Harrowing Israeli documentary pipped by Danish war drama at Venice Film Festival awards Stephanie Bunbury September 13, 2026 — 3:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There was widespread surprise when NAZA, an Israeli documentary that had a record-breaking 25-minute standing ovation at the 83rd Venice Film Festival, won the special jury prize at the awards ceremony on Saturday. Director May el-Toukhy, left, with Mathilde Arcel at the Venice Film Festival. AP Photo/Scott A Garfitt That early award meant Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s harrowing documentary, which features testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders whose insights into the war in Gaza include what they say is the systemic killing of Palestinian civilians, could not win the Golden Lion later in the ceremony. Three days earlier, NAZA had left many viewers winded and speechless. For this viewer, it made everything else at the festival pale into unimportance. Shot on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night in extreme secrecy over three years by two of the filmmakers behind the Oscar-winning No Other Land, the documentary is named after the acronym used for non-combatants killed when the Israeli army targets suspected Hamas operatives.



Related Article ★★★½

Review Israeli and Palestinian journalists mine the horrors of the West Bank Wreathed in shadows, soldiers tell how the blanket hacking of phones means they know where everyone is and what they’re saying. Linked numbers create suspects who may be taken out with family groups or as entire streets of houses, the exact number of expected dead already noted. One soldier remembers pushing the button while listening to a baby crying in the target house; another remembers wondering, on a school trip to Auschwitz, how the Germans could have done such terrible things. “I still think the Nazis were evil,” he says, pondering what that now made him. “It’s honestly not very easy to stand here, thinking of all the people, the Israeli politicians, the journalists back home who are attacking this film, denying it without even seeing it,” Abraham said after winning the award. “It is really, really especially important to us that Israelis watch this film.” If NAZA had not been in the mix, the Golden Lion winner, Danish director May el-Toukhy’s A Woman Unknown, would have been beyond dispute. Set in Denmark immediately after World War II, it begins as a live-in nanny, played by Mathilde Arcel, prepares to marry her older employer. But a secret past relationship with a German soldier threatens to upend her reputation.



Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor with the special jury prize award they won for Naza at the Venice Film Festival. Getty Images Austere, tight with tension and rich with social history, A Woman Unknown was considered a safe bet for a jury led by actor-director Maggie Gyllenhaal, whose own films The Lost Daughter and The Bride revolve around disruptive women. El-Toukhy, who was the only woman to have solely directed a film in the main competition this year, became just the eighth woman to win the festival’s top prize. “To me personally, Woman Unknown is about the female body as a battleground,” she said. “At the same time the film tells the tale of women who are unseen, invisible and voiceless.” Arcel was a popular winner of the Volpi Cup for best actress. “This is my first lead role in a movie and my first time at a film festival,” she said. “I’m extremely honoured.”



John Malkovich won best actor for his performance in Martin McDonagh’s dark CIA comedy Wild Horse Nine. “I am humbled to be chosen for this award which has been given to so many wonderful actors,” he said in a video message, explaining that he was shooting in Montreal. Korean slow cinema doyen Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love, on the relationship between a working-class woman whose husband has lost his job and a rich film-maker documenting dismissed workers’ lives, won the Silver Lion, the festival’s second-biggest honour. Naza was shot on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night in extreme secrecy. Venice Film Festival via AP Thoughtful and punctuated by small but sharp plot twists, Lee’s unpacking of Korea’s high-voltage economic miracle – and its winners and losers – was a critical favourite. “We are living in an era where the meaning of labour is fading and human connections are increasingly becoming severed,” Lee said through a translator. “I made this film to ask what cinema can and should do in times like these. I take this award as a sign that you want me to keep asking these questions.”



Related Article Entertainment Moss Moore’s murder was never solved. A Brisbane Festival show reopens the case Stephane Brize’s A Good Little Soldier, an angry French film about a human resources manager (Alba Rohrwacher) trying to paper over systematic bullying within a company, won best screenplay. The Silver Lion for directing went to Russian-born Ilya Khrzhanovsky for DAU, an epic three-hour-plus film which has been described as loose biopic of the Soviet Nobel Prize-winning physicist Lev Landau. Taking more than 20 years to make, it took two years to film with actors living around the clock as their characters in a purpose-built complex that included laboratories, kitchens and a newspaper office. The prize for the best new young actor went to the unknown Malou Khebizi from French director Cedric Khan’s A Place to Heal, about a juvenile care hostel for troubled young people. With AP

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share License this article More: Cinema Stephanie Bunbury is a film and culture writer for The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald.

World.title: Australian tourist dies after falling from cliff at famous beach near Bali
World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaTragedy Australian tourist dies after falling from cliff at famous beach near Bali Ellen Connolly and Ashleigh McMillan Updated September 13, 2026 — 3:33pm ,first published September 13, 2026 — 3:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An Australian tourist has died after falling about 80 metres from a cliff at Kelingking Beach in Nusa Penida near Bali. The incident unfolded after 8am on Saturday when tourists alerted a lifeguard to a woman who appeared to be stranded on a cliff at the popular beach, about 20 kilometres off the south-eastern coast of Bali. Local authorities recover the woman’s body. Basarnas Bali (search and rescue agency) Emergency services rushed to the scene, but she fell further before they could reach her. The woman, named as Brianna Lani Cronin, 29, was from Queensland and visiting the area on holiday, Nusa Penida police said.



“The victim is estimated to have fallen around 9am,” Nusa Penida Alert Unit co-ordinator Cakra Negara said in a statement. “At the time, she was seeking an independent path toward the edge of the cliff before slipping and falling into the ravine. The body of the young Australian woman killed in a fall in Bali is recovered. Basarnas Bali (search and rescue agency) “When found, the victim had sustained several fractures; we secured her onto a stretcher to facilitate the evacuation process.” Cronin had already died from her injuries by the time rescuers reached her, a spokesperson for the Indonesian Navy said.



Search and rescue agency Basarnas Bali said attempts to retrieve her body by boat were unsuccessful because of large waves. Related Article Kelingking Beach, Bali: The hidden beach overrun by Instagram tourists Instead, rescuers had to place Cronin’s body on a stretcher and carry her up a steep and narrow staircase for 1½ hours. A Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade spokesperson confirmed the government was providing consular assistance to the woman’s family, who had requested privacy. Queensland Premier David Crisafulli described the death as tremendously sad.



“To have a life taken away in a heartbeat like that ... it’s just incredibly, incredibly sad,” he told reporters on Sunday. “I just express my sympathies to her family and those loved ones with her and back at home. I think all of Queensland collectively looks at that and just feels ... just a huge degree of sorrow.” Kelingking Beach sits on the southwest coast of the island of Nusa Penida, which is about 20 kilometres off the main island of Bali. The beach is best known for its headland nicknamed “T-Rex Bay”, named for a massive, emerald-green cliff formation that twists out into the Indian Ocean in the shape of a dinosaur. An aerial view of Kelingking Beach on Nusa Penida.



It is widely celebrated as one of the most Instagrammable beaches in Asia, and tourists line up for an hour along the cliffside edge to snap selfies against the stunning backdrop. Swimming at the beach is banned year-round due to dangerous currents. The trek down to the beach can take two hours on a path described as perilous. Work on a panoramic glass lift to carry visitors down to the beach was started in 2024, but after fierce opposition from locals and tourists the project was halted in October 2025. Investigations are continuing into the circumstances that led to the woman’s fall. With AAP Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: It’s not ending with Trump. Now we’re under attack from his clones
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's America Opinion It’s not ending with Trump. Now we’re under attack from his clones Melanie La'Brooy Writer September 13, 2026 — 3:21pm

September 13, 2026 — 3:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Of all the weird things occurring in the US right now (Measles are back! Cold War with Canada!) one of the strangest has been the rise of the Trump clones. Their origin dates back to 2016. As the then Republican front-runner for the presidential nomination, Trump infamously declared that “I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody and I wouldn’t lose any voters. It’s, like, incredible.” US President Donald Trump. AP Marvelling at the prospect of engaging in criminal behaviour while retaining electability, Trump went on to prove his hypothesis, notching up convictions for sexual assault and defamation and 34 counts of falsifying business records in a hush money case involving his affair with a porn star. He was then elected president again. Now, as the US heads towards November midterm elections, Trump’s revelation that acts of violence, immorality and criminality no longer preclude running for public office has seemingly become normalised. It’s now incredible if a candidate running for office in the US doesn’t have a skeleton in the closet. Or tattooed to his chest, as in the case of the former Democratic Senate candidate for Maine, Graham Platner, whose skull-and-crossbones tattoo, which closely resembled the Nazi Totenkopf, caused a minor furore. Fortunately for Platner, these days there’s a higher tolerance for white supremacist-adjacent tattoos among holders of high office in the US, (as evinced by Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth’s ink), so it wasn’t until allegations of sexual assault were made against him that Platner finally exited the race in July.



Referring to the situation in Maine, conservative commentator Greg Price, wrote on X: “It’s truly hysterical how Democrats can’t seem to find one normal dude to run for office”, which would have been a solid partisan burn about the importance of candidate quality control in the midterm elections, if only Brandon Herrera and Ken Paxton didn’t exist. Herrera is a Republican candidate running for congress in Texas. A gun influencer who boasted about owning a copy of Mein Kampf, Herrera has made jokes about using homeless people for target practice and has referred to women as “fat bitches” and “whores”. In a video, Herrera refers to the Nazi submachine gun he is wielding as the “original ghetto blaster” and “Hitler’s street sweeper”. He also coined a vulgar epithet for children, which is unprintable. It’s a measure of the current “When he goes low, we go lower” standard set by Trump that Herrera is running as the Trump-endorsed candidate for the GOP: the same party that only days ago at the Republican convention in Dallas, Vice President JD Vance positioned as the champion of family values. Donald Trump speaking at the wedding reception of Max Miller and Emily Moreno in 2022. X Meanwhile, Ken Paxton, the Republican Texas Attorney General and Trump-endorsed Senate candidate, is facing a formidable opponent; not the Democrat candidate, James Talarico, but rather himself. As The New York Times reported, Paxton has been “indicted on charges of felony securities fraud and impeached ... [on allegations] of bribery, dereliction of duty, obstruction of justice and abuse of the public trust, and other misdeeds.” Paxton’s wife has accused her conservative Christian husband of adultery and filed for divorce on “biblical grounds”. If that’s not enough, Talarico’s team turned security footage of Paxton stealing a $US1000 Montblanc pen into a campaign ad. When asked by a New York Times reporter why he thought voters stuck with him, given he’s been indicted, impeached and accused of adultery, Paxton invoked the Fifth Avenue amendment, replying: “Why does the base stick with President Trump, when you can say all those same things?”



Paxton’s touching “Whither thou goest, I will go” declaration of fealty to the dishonourable example set by Trump reveals just how deep the rot has gone. US politicians are no longer required to deny, explain or even blush when accused of immoral or criminal behaviour. The “Trump did it first” defence works for almost any situation an ethically compromised politician might find themselves accused of: racism, misogyny, lying, corruption, sexual abuse, colonising Venezuela or unauthorised building works. Ken Paxton’s win was welcomed by Donald Trump, who said Paxton would “become a fantastic, common-sense senator”. AP However, Trump’s ability to defy political gravity doesn’t appear to work for all of his would-be mini clones, as illustrated by the growing roll-call of candidates from both sides who have slunk away in shame during this scandal-plagued electoral cycle. Related Article Opinion

Immigration How a conspiracy theory embraced by Trump became mainstream in Australia Melanie La'Brooy Writer Sexual misconduct claims forced Democrat congressman, Eric Swalwell to drop out of the California governor’s race in April. The same day, Republican Texas congressman, Tony Gonzales resigned, after admitting to an affair with a staffer, who had later died by suicide. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, a Democrat congresswoman from Florida, also resigned after being indicted on embezzlement charges. In August, North Carolina Republican, Chuck Edwards, dropped his re-election bid following allegations of sexual harassment by his young female staffers.



Grimly hanging on is Republican Ohio congressman, Max Miller, who is still running for re-election despite horrific domestic violence allegations against him. Miller’s ex-wife is the daughter of Republican senator, Bernie Moreno who wrote on X: “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them.” Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump is using a secret code to motivate extremists. It’s everywhere, if you know where to look Melanie La'Brooy Writer Herein lies the pre-eminent problem of the Trumpian age: no-one appears to know any more what the basic standards of character required to hold elected office are. From the top down, this is no longer politics as public service. Instead, it’s a permission structure for the unscrupulous to act with impunity. It’s dire news for those hoping that the malfeasance of the Trump era will end when he leaves office in 2029. Whether Republican or Democrat, every US politician attempting to wield dissolute power without consequence continues his legacy. As the attack of the clones continues, it’s hard not to think wistfully of a former US president who stated: “Character is the most important qualification the president of the United States can have.”



Well said, Richard Nixon. Melanie La’Brooy is a novelist who writes on politics and social justice issues. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: ‘Unsafe staffing, unmanageable workloads’: Thousands of Queensland nurses quit
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Health ‘Unsafe staffing, unmanageable workloads’: Thousands of Queensland nurses quit Courtney Kruk September 13, 2026 — 3:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Crisafulli government has defended its efforts to increase frontline health workers after data showed thousands of nurses had quit crucial positions at public hospitals in recent years. Figures obtained by News Corp through Right to Information indicated more than 2400 nurses left hospitals in 2024–25, the worst departure of nursing staff in four years. Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls has defended the Crisafulli government’s efforts to grow frontline healthcare workers after data showed thousands of nurses had left the sector. Courtney Kruk A total of 10,824 nurses left Queensland hospitals in the past five years, according to the data provided. Health Minister Tim Nicholls admitted the statistics were concerning, but said attrition across Queensland Health had dropped under the Crisafulli government, from 6.54 per cent under Labor, to 5.42 per cent, and efforts were underway to grow and maintain nursing staff across the sector.



“[We’ve reduced attrition] by hiring 10,000 more employees in Queensland Health. More than 7000 of those have been frontline and frontline support [staff],” Nicholls said. Related Article Queensland Health Nearly half of all Queensland doctors at risk of burnout, survey finds “We are working very hard to reduce those numbers [of nurses leaving] … I don’t think anyone could raise any quibbles about the amount of time, energy, and effort that’s being put into retaining staff as well as bringing on new staff.” The Crisafulli government has pledged 46,000 additional healthcare workers – including doctors, nurses and paramedics – by 2032, but has yet to detail how such figures will be achieved. A workforce gap analysis of Queensland Health was released in November, and a follow-up plan – initially promised by July – will be released later this year, Nicholls said.



Queensland Nurses and Midwives’ Union (QNMU) secretary Sarah Beaman said staffing issues continue to plague hospitals across the state, and were contributing to the recent exodus of workers. “After years of ‘hanging in there’ because they love what they do, growing numbers of public nurses and midwives are leaving, or considering leaving, because they can no longer absorb unsafe staffing, unmanageable workloads or feeling unsupported by management,” Beaman said. “It is important to note there will always have some natural workforce movement such as retirement or relocation. We also need to distinguish between leaving an employer and leaving their professions. Queensland Nurses and Midwives’ Union (QNMU) Secretary Sarah Beaman said a growing number of nurses were leaving the profession due to unsafe staffing and unmanageable workloads. Courtney Kruk “The big concern is when nurses and midwives who want to keep working feel they can’t due to unsafe conditions.”



A recent survey of QNMU members found 15.6 per cent of shifts in wards covered by legislated ratios were still below the minimum staffing requirement. On wards without legislated ratios, nearly 60 per cent of shifts did not meet the same minimum staffing threshold. Related Article Queensland Health Shocking video of patient assaulting nurse prompts union call for safer conditions The same Grow Your Voice survey found 84 per cent of respondents had recently experienced violence at work, with nearly a third experiencing three or more types of violence. “People are not walking away because they have stopped caring about nursing or midwifery. They are reaching a point where the job is unsustainable,” Beaman said. Shadow health spokesperson Mark Bailey accused the LNP of being combative towards health workers and said issues raised during wage negotiations and hospital planning had caused many to lose confidence in the government’s approach to recruitment and retention.



“There’s no doubt that our nurses are being overworked and are feeling burnt-out … because the government is not backing them in with extra capacity in our system,” Bailey said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘It is a beautiful property’: No bids for $4m renovated Rosebery house
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions ‘It is a beautiful property’: No bids for $4m renovated Rosebery house Elizabeth Redman September 13, 2026 — 3:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An architecturally renovated family home in Rosebery is still available after passing in at an auction on Saturday at which nobody bid. The transformed four-bedroom bungalow at 24 Morley Avenue has leadlight windows, high ceilings, glass sliding doors, a gourmet kitchen with striking Avocatus Quartzite bench, covered barbecue area and swimming pool. It was listed with a price guide of $3.95 million. The property was one of 706 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 53 per cent from 410 reported results throughout the week, while 133 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. The early read is slightly lower than last week’s preliminary result of 57 per cent. But Sydney’s monthly auction clearance rate has edged up for the last two months as sellers realise they need to meet the market to sell. Sydney remains a buyer’s market, below the threshold of 60 per cent considered balanced between buyers and sellers.



The Rosebery home attracted three registered bidders. The potential buyer demographic was largely young professional couples from the surrounding suburbs and inner city, plus some downsizers. Related Article Auctions ‘State of inaction’: Inner west home sells for $2.59m as buyers go MIA But on the auction floor, none of the potential buyers raised their hands and the home was passed in. “It was just one of those auctions where people did all their diligence,” The Agency selling agent Chris Skarlatos said, “And no-one put their hand up. They all sat there and looked at each other.” He is now working with a few potential buyers and hopes it will sell soon.



“It is a beautiful property,” he said. “The cost of buying an unrenovated home – it makes sense to just buy this.” The reserve was $4 million. The vendors are moving to be closer to family. He described the market as “very patchy. You get the odd property that goes very well.” There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide.



On the north shore, a young family paid $3,755,000 for a brick family home in Roseville, beating two others. The four-bedroom house at 44 Moore Street has an open-plan extension at the rear and was listed with a price guide of $3.7 million. Three parties registered to bid, all young families, some of whom had been looking to buy for some time. But Ray White Upper North Shore selling agent Jessica Cao described the auction as “very slow”.



“This is just the perfect location, perfect size, ready to move into, no work needs to be done,” she said. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Former Mirvac boss to sell $11m Killara home with tennis court Bidding began at $3.49 million, below the price guide, and then climbed to $3.55 million where the bidding stopped again before the third family entered the fray. The price rose to $3.7 million but was still short of the reserve price of $3.75 million. Cao was then able to secure a winning bid of $3,755,000 to get the deal done. The marathon auction took about 40 minutes.



“No one wants to overpay,” Cao said. “The good thing is, auctions, you can see who wants it.” The winners are an upsizing family of six who have sold their home on the lower north shore. The sellers are a young family moving overseas who bought the home four years ago for $3.36 million. “I do feel there is more energy in the market,” Cao said. “The turnkey properties in a good location with a scarcity of listings still can reach a good result in this market.” In the inner west, a possible duplex development site in Ashfield is also still available after it did not reach its reserve at auction.



The four-bedroom house at 51 Palace Street is on a block of about 697 square metres and was for sale for the first time in 70 years. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Downsizer pad of late Katies co-founder listed for around $20 million It was listed with a price guide of $2.8 million and attracted interest from builders. One potential bidder, a builder, attended the auction but did not bid. A vendor bid was placed at $2.85 million but with no further offers, the home passed in. The reserve was $3 million. The builder has indicated interest at around the $2.7 million to $2.75 million mark.



Rich & Oliva selling agent Marco Errichiello said buyers are interested and builders are asking questions such as about settlement, but the home has not yet sold. “Buyers, if they see really good value, they will buy, but it has got to be really good value,” Errichiello said. “They are almost predicting what it will be worth in a couple of months, after a rate rise,” he added, alluding to economist forecasts of another likely cash rate hike by the end of this year. “The only thing that speeds up buyers is a lack of stock.”

World.title: Mining company's equipment targeted in Panguna arson attack
World.content:
Reports from Bougainville say heavy machinery and vehicles belonging to a foreign mining company were destroyed in an arson attack at the Panguna mine site.

Armed men are alleged to have entered the site in the autonomous Papua New Guinea region this morning, and set fire to heavy haul trucks and other equipment stationed near the large open pit mine.

The machinery is understood to belong to Indian company Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited.

Lloyds was selected by the Autonomous Bougainville Government as one of the developers involved in plans to assess the future rehabilitation and possible reopening of the copper and gold mine.

The company has been in Bougainville advancing feasibility studies and exploration work.

Conflict over the former mine operations at the Panguna sparked Bougainville's civil war in 1989 - since then the mine has been closed for industrial mining.

Panguna and its large reserves of copper are seen by the ABG and others as critically important to Bougainville's aim to develop its economy as it seeks independence from Papua New Guinea.

The mine's potential rehabilitation has remained at the centre of debate in Bougainville over ongoing discussions about resource ownership and development.

But this weekend's unrest has raised concerns about security at the mine site and the future of proposed exploration and rehabilitation activities.

Details surrounding the attack, including the identities and motives of those responsible and the full extent of the damage, remain unclear.

PNG's Post Courier reports that police in Bougainville are investigating the incident.

World.title: Women's health advocates questions waitlist discrepancies
World.content:
Women's Health Action is questioning why colposcopy - or cervix scans - has seen significantly less improvement in wait times than other diagnostic services.

Colposcopy is a procedure to check the cervix for signs of precancerous or cancerous tissue.

Yesterday, Minister of Health Simeon Brown announced that waitlists for diagnostic services had reduced 21 percent overall.

Waitlists from June 2025 to June 2025 have fallen 9 percent for colposcopy and echocardiography. While CT waitlists were down 48 percent and MRI down 33 percent.

Manager of the action group, Isis McKay said, "Why has the reduction in the colposcopy waitlist been considerably smaller than the reductions seen in services such as CT and MRI scanning or coronary angiography?"

She questioned to what extent the use of private health providers contributed to the improvement.

Urgent colonoscopy services was the only service where waitlists had gotten worse, increasing two percent since June 2025.

"Understanding why some services are improving more quickly than others is crucial if we are to ensure equitable and timely access to care across the system."

McKay asked the Government for transparency around the changes, saying this will help improve trust that it can be maintained long term.

"These details matter because there is no quick fix to the challenges facing our health system.

World.title: National to set up Auckland Transport police team if re-elected
World.content:
The National Party will set up a dedicated Auckland Transport police team if re-elected.

The policy announcement coincides with the opening of the City Rail Link (CRL) on Sunday morning, which is expected to increase peak commuter capacity through the city centre by around 50 percent.

National would recruit 50 new officers for the team and police would received $7 million per year from Budget 2027.

Police spokesperson Mark Mitchell said the team would boost the visible police presence in trains, buses, ferries, stations and transport hubs.

"Police should be where people are. As more Aucklanders use public transport, it makes sense to have more police on the network.

"A visible police presence helps deter offending before it occurs, reassures passengers and transport staff, and ensures rapid intervention when something does go wrong," he said.

A policy statement released by the party said the team would focus on preventing anti-social behaviour, protecting passengers and staff, and responding quickly to incidents.

It said the team would be established in Auckland first, but could be expanded to other cities if successful.

Mitchell said it would be up to police to decide which services the team would patrol.

"They're very used to working in a way where they identify where the need is and then putting resources there.

"That's BAU (Business As Usual) for police, they gather intelligence, they look at where the work is, and then they put resources in there," he said.

New Zealand Police Association president Steve Watt said it was always good to have more police but pointed out the government had failed to meet past promises when it came to policing numbers.

"The irony behind it all is, however, is that we're still waiting for this government to fulfil its promise of 500 extra cops.

"So an extra 50, you know, who knows when that's going to actually happen."

New Zealand First and National's coalition agreement included a promise that by November 2025 the number of police officers in the force would be increased by 500.

However, the government conceded last year that the target would be missed.

Watt said it was always difficult to choose where to increase police presence but a boost in policing numbers was always a good thing.

Asked if the government had met its target of 500 new police officers, National Leader Christopher Luxon said he was confident that commitment would be met.

"We'll be delivering on that 500 extra police officers, and that's why we're confident we can push on and recruit another 50.

"With extra funding coming out of budget next year, we'll be able to get the police operationalising that funding." he said.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said National could not fulfil its promise of 500 extra officers, let alone 50 for a new transport beat.

"Why should New Zealanders believe that they're somehow going to magic up more police when they can't even fulfil the commitment they've already made?

"More police on the beat's a good thing, it would be good if this government showed up with the 500 extra police they promised to have delivered by now," he said.

Meanwhile, ACT leader David Seymour said National were trying to "solve the right problem", but more efficiencies could be found.

World.title: How world media reacted to All Blacks' loss against South Africa
World.content:
Heartbreak.

The All Blacks have suffered their third straight loss after being beaten by the Springboks 43-28 in Baltimore.

The loss concludes the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series, with world media highlighting South Africa's dominant performance.

However, the All Blacks also received much recognition for the "pulsating, breathless and unpredictable nature" of the past six weeks.

Here's how world media reacted to the All Blacks vs Springboks series closer.

The Telegraph

"Springboks look like World Cup champions... again," The Telegraph's headline reads.

The post-match article angles in on the "long shadow" that has been cast over the All Blacks ahead of next year's World Cup in Australia.

"At key moments [the All Blacks] were let down by their discipline and turnovers in attack to gift the Springboks' transition ball, and their directness, backed by their power both in collisions and set piece, enabled them to pick up points much more easily than their opponents," the article reads.

It acknowledged the All Blacks' attempts to claw their way back into the game, but said the reality was the "Springboks always had another gear".

The Guardian

The Guardian continued with that sentiment, describing the All Blacks' loss as a thrashing.

Codie Taylor, Will Jordan, Ethan Blackadder and Beauden Barrett received honourable mentions, but the post-match article made it clear they were no match for "South Africa's total dominance at the breakdown, set piece and aerial battle".

The article acknowledged the controversy in the first half when play was held up for more than eight minutes after a failure in communication equipment between the match officials.

However, the newspaper said the Springboks "produced a devastating second-half display" to seal the Rivalry series victory.

Will Jordan of New Zealand tackled by Springboks, fourth Test, Baltimore, 2026. Dylan Davies / www.photosport.nz

RugbyPass

RugbyPass angled in on All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie's post-game heartbreak.

"Yeah, look, the boys put in a massive shift again," Rennie is quoted as saying.

"You look at all the numbers, and everything's very even, but they were electric, and when they got their opportunities, and we were trying to chase the game late and put ourselves under a bit more pressure."

The 62-year-old said coming to South Africa and the US to play the Springboks in a four-Test series wasn't easy.

"Tonight will hurt, but you know we'll wake up tomorrow, and I think be moving in the right direction."

The South African

What a game. What a series. What a tour. That is how the South African online newspaper The South African concluded the four-Test series.

The newspaper's post-match article said although the Springboks dominated the series, the All Blacks "contributed immensely to the pulsating, breathless and unpredictable nature of the past six weeks".

"Many, if not all, other Test teams would have crumbled under the sheer pressure and intensity of a tour like this; and yet, these two sets of players just kept at it and at each other for four consecutive matches."

The All Blacks will take on Australia next, in a battle for the 2026 Bledisloe Cup.

World.title: 'Gutted': All Blacks coach Dave Rennie feels the pain as Springboks win series 3-1
World.content:
All Blacks coach Dave Rennie feels the All Blacks are making making good progress, but says the loss of Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series hurts.

The Springboks rejoiced with the series trophy after beating the All Blacks 43-28 in Baltimore, taking the four-match series 3-1, with victory in the final three matches after the All Blacks won in Johannesburg.

It has been a bruising eight-match tour over more than six weeks for the New Zealanders, who were hoping to unseat the South Africans as world number one, albeit with a revamped side after skipper Ardie Savea, Luke Jacobson and Quinn Tupaea returned home injured after the third test loss.

But they could not match the Springboks' firepower and clinical approach.

The All Blacks made too many mistakes to be able to foot it with the Boks at M&T Bank Stadium, the home of NFL side the Baltimore Ravens, where nearly 70,000 people turned up. A win would have drawn the series and the Greatest Rivalry trophy would have been split in half.

When asked for his initial reaction, Rennie replied: "Gutted."

"We were confident that if we got a few things right tonight, we'd have a good chance of winning and fell short."

Siya Kolisi holds up Rugby's Greatest Rivalry Trophy Getty Images via AFP

"So, yeah, disappointing from that perspective. From a tour point of view, you know, I think I said three, four or five months ago whenever I got appointed that I was really excited about the tour coming here because we knew it was going to be tough, but we'd learn a lot about ourselves and we'd leave with a better understanding of our game model and tighter as a group.

"And we're definitely in that position. It's been awesome for us."

Rennie has found the Boks the big stumbling block in his first season as All Blacks coach, after the New Zealanders beat France in his initial test in charge on 4 July, then Italy and Ireland. Hopes were high after the All Blacks won the first test 33-16 in Johannesburg, but the wounded Springboks rebounded with victories in the next three tests.

Rennie said they were a great side.

"I thought South Africa were very good, they were electric and really clinical when they got their opportunities," said at the press conference after the Baltimore test.

"That was probably a key point tonight."

'Really excited' despite loss

Rennie said the result hurt, but with an eye on next year's Rugby World Cup in Australia he was pleased with his side's progress.

"Really excited about where our game's heading and knowing that we need to be better when you play a great side like the Springboks.

He thought on the match numbers that it was "a very even game tonight, bar the score".

"We probably conceded a little bit chasing the game late, but felt even with 15 to go we were right in it. So, yeah, disappointed, but still really proud of the effort and feel that we're tracking in the right direction.

Of areas that stung the All Blacks, he was disappointed with the performance under the high ball, saying the South Africans put them under more heat again.

"We couldn't grab a lot of those."

But he was pleased with the set pieces.

As to the near nine-minute break in the first half when officials tried to work out how to fix the broken communications system used by referee Karl Dickson and the Television Match Official, Rennie said it did not have an impact, but it should not have happened.

"I'm not sure. If comms gear goes down, you pull out of the spare set, surely. So, yeah, I'm not sure why it took so long," Rennie said.

One discipline area the All Blacks will have to work on is at the breakdown where they were pinged for illegal cleanouts and holding players down. Rennie conceded as much calling the illegalities "dumb".

Beauden Barrett has late say with try

Rennie also complimented veteran Beauden Barrett on his efforts for the team. The 35-year-old came on at fullback as a late replacement for his 145th cap and had the final say in the game, dancing in for a nifty try.

"Yeah, we're really happy with Beauden. Yeah, I mean, you guys just get to see the game. We get to see his contribution daily in meetings and in training and in leadership."

He said Barrett had been excellent in the matches he played on tour, while halfback Kyle Preston, who played in all eight tour matches, had been a strong performer who "suited our game".

World.title: ACT unveils party list, Paul Henry could enter Parliament on current polling
World.content:
Broadcaster turned political candidate Paul Henry has debuted at number four on the ACT Party list, making it likely he will enter Parliament next term on current polling.

The party released its full candidate list ranking on Sunday, with fellow newcomer James Christmas debuting at seven.

Biosecurity Minister Andrew Hoggard has jumped from fifth to third while Children's Minister Karen Chhour has gone up one ranking to replace him at number five on the list.

However, MPs Todd Stephenson, Parmjeet Parmar and Cameron Luxton have all fallen in rank; Luxton form 11th to 12th, Parmer from ninth to 10th and Stephenson, who has dropped from fourth on the list to sixth.

The party's new deputy leader Nicole McKee has taken second on the list, following the departure of out-going MP and deputy leader Brooke van Velden.

Speaking to media, leader David Seymour said he felt an "awesome responsibility" and he "must get these people elected to Parliament".

"The biggest stories today is the ACT Party is planning to re-elect every one of its incumbent MPs - except two who have retired for understandable reasons."

"All of them will be re-elected on current polling and then a couple more." he said.

He said has was "absolutely confident" Henry would perform will in Parliament, despite having no prior experience.

"The thing about Paul is that a lot of New Zealanders know Paul for about two minutes of video that lingers on YouTube 15 years later."

"I know Paul from sitting down with him in the office, at his house, having a wine. He's a deeply patriotic, sincere and conscientious New Zealander who's doing this for his grandkids who he loves deeply." he said.

Seymour said both Hoggard and Stephenson also debuted high on the list without prior experience, so the move was not "unprecedented".

Seymour denied ACT was "making room" for Henry and Christmas.

"We get a list; we take into account every aspect of a person's performance [and] obviously some of our candidates are experienced MPs."

"I wouldn't say that we've made room, I would say that we have ranked our list on all of their attributes, including their parliamentary experience."

Far North councillor Davina Smolders - a vocal opponent of unelected iwi and hapū representation on councils - is ranked 18 on the list.

Asked about Smolder's position on the list, Seymour said he had nothing against "controversial figures".

"I've actually got quite some sympathy for them, to be honest."

"Davina Smolders has stood up to anti-democratic practices... there's three Māori in this front row here who very strongly believe in democracy and support Davina."

World.title: 'We could have saved more': Vanuatu MP criticises 30-hour search delay after ferry sinking
World.content:
A Vanuatu MP says it took more than 30 hours for a boat search to begin after an inter-island ferry sank in rough seas, saying more lives might have been saved if information about the incident had been provided sooner.

The MV Matui was carrying 45 people when it sank between the islands of Santo and Ambae on Friday morning.

Luganville MP Matai Seremaiah said the vessel left Santo at 6am (local time) and sank at about 9.30am.

"What we now know is that the vessel capsized at 9.30am."

But Seremaiah said those on the ground did not begin their own search until about 4pm on Saturday - more than 30 hours after the vessel sank.

He said there was confusion and misinformation about what had happened, including reports the vessel was drifting.

"We were awaiting for coordinates, but nothing came through until one of surviving crew swarm ashore and alerted us that the ship has capsized."

Seremaiah said the government had conducted aerial searches because it believed the ship was still adrift.

"We were not given any instructions at the time, and in the end, I and, other people went out to search," he said.

He said a local pilot spotted survivors and provided vessels with the coordinates needed for the rescue.

The Vanuatu government said 15 people have been accounted for alive and one body has been recovered, with more than 30 people still missing at sea.

Seremaiah said the 15 survivors had been taken to the main hospital in Luganville.

He said another body was spotted but could not be recovered because of bad weather.

The delayed search was made more difficult by rough conditions, Seremaiah said.

"Yesterday, during the search, the weather was really bad, swells were up to 2.5 to 3 metres, and again, because we left late, 4pm yesterday, and only a few hours before dark set in, it made it really difficult with the weather conditions."

Families of people who were on the ferry have gathered in Santo seeking answers, he said.

Seremaiah said many of those who went out to search were private citizens.

The Vanuatu government has said an investigation will examine why the vessel sailed despite strong marine wind warnings issued by the Vanuatu Meteorology and Geo-hazard Department on Friday.

Prime Minister's public relations officer Kiery Mannaseh told local broadcaster VBTC News the government was concerned the vessel had not heeded the warnings.

The government has said the sinking appeared to have resulted from strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded, with possible negligence including overloading of the vessel.

Mannaseh said the government would prioritise search and rescue before conducting its investigation.

World.title: Labour to make employer contributions to KiwiSaver compulsory if elected
World.content:
Labour will make employer contributions to KiwiSaver compulsory, as well as raise the minimum to 6 percent even when employees reduce or pause their own, with the party saying it wants to make the retirement savings scheme "work harder for more New Zealanders".

The party will also set the default employee rate at 4 percent, extend employer contributions to workers over 65, maintain contributions while parents are on parental leave, and ban new total remuneration contracts that absorb KiwiSaver contributions from employers into salaries, if elected.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said KiwiSaver was one the party's "proudest legacies", as he announced the policy at the Sharesies office in Wellington on Sunday.

"We created it, and now we're going to make it work better for people," Hipkins said.

He said Labour was the party of KiwiSaver, and believed every New Zealander should have the opportunity to build a secure future.

"Sir Michael Cullen turned that belief into KiwiSaver, while National voted against it," Hipkins said, adding that under National "too many New Zealanders are struggling to pay the bills, let alone save for tomorrow".

Hipkins referenced the 83,400 people who were currently on a savings suspension because times were tough, with more than a million working-age KiwiSaver members not contributing at all.

New Zealand First and National were first off the blocks with KiwiSaver policies this year, both proposing automatic enrolment at birth and compulsory contributions from employees.

Labour's finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds said on Sunday National was making it harder for Kiwis to save and now wanted to "force" workers to put more in.

"Labour will require employers to contribute at the same amount as National is proposing but give workers more flexibility when money is tight.

"We'll also make KiwiSaver fairer for parents, older Kiwis and broaden who benefits - working with self-employed New Zealanders on more flexible ways to build their savings in the scheme."

From 1 July 2028, employer contributions would become compulsory and extend to paid parental leave and workers over 65. The minimum contribution rate from employers would be lifted to 6 percent by 2032.

Edmonds said the changes across Labour's KiwiSaver policy would be phased in carefully, "giving workers and businesses certainty".

The full policy proposal looks to:

Make employer contributions compulsory, and lift to 6 percent by 2032, including when employees reduce or pause their own contributions.

Set the employee default at 4 percent, remove the minimum contribution rate, and give employees more flexibility to choose their rate as circumstances change.

Ban new total remuneration contracts that absorb employer KiwiSaver contributions into salaries.

Extend employer contributions to workers over 65.

Keep KiwiSaver growing for parents while they're on paid parental leave.

Explore more flexible KiwiSaver options for self-employed New Zealanders.

The party explained that making the employer contribution compulsory and increasing the employer contribution to 6% over time would increase revenue from the Employer Superannuation Contribution Tax.

It said that would help fund government contributions to paid parental leave recipients and meet the government's higher costs as an employer. That would be managed through the Budget process, the party added.

National "ankle-tapped" Labour - SImplicity founder

Simplicity founder Sam Stubbs said National seemed to be offering a more comprehensive KiwiSaver policy and had "ankle-tapped" Labour into making their own policy.

"I was actually sort of personally disappointed that their policy wasn't like everything that National had promised and a little bit more because, you know, KiwiSaver was invented by the Labour Party."

Stubbs said the Labour policy was a step in the right direction with compulsory contributions but had missed the mark when it came to children.

"We should be having KiwiSaver accounts at birth and the member tax credit that people get at the moment should be redirected towards children."

He also said the combined total amount that people could get with KiwiSaver under various scenarios would not be enough.

World.title: I'm ready to be Swans captain, says Gulden
World.content:
Sydney superstar Errol Gulden says he is prepared to step up as captain to help the Swans pursue an AFL premiership bid without the injured Callum Mills.

The 24-year-old has thrown his hat in the ring to deputise for skipper Mills after his midfield performance led the Swans to a stirring qualifying final win over Brisbane.

Sydney coach Dean Cox also has an experienced leader in former co-captain Dane Rampe, as well as fellow veteran Jake Lloyd, midfielder James Rowbottom and Tom Papley at his disposal.

Whoever Cox lands on could also play a key leadership role next year, with Mills facing the possibility of missing the entire 2027 season after tearing the anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee.

Swans vice-captain Isaac Heeney is among five players serving club-imposed bans after last month's post-match incident at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne.

Star defender Mills had earned significant praise for leading the Swans through the turmoil, which past players said shattered the club's famed "Bloods culture".

Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice are the other Swans who will not play again this season.

Gulden rallied the Swans after Mills went down late in the first quarter against the back-to-back reigning premiers, finishing with one goal, 34 disposals and eight clearances.

"If it [the captaincy] was offered to me, I would love to," Gulden told AAP.

"I would feel like I'd be ready. I wouldn't change anything that I'm doing. I don't think any of us need to change anything that we're doing.

"But you're just so shattered for the person. He's [Mills] just an amazing leader.

"He is the best human being at the club. It's just not fair.

"We've just got to keep going, and it's going to be next man in."

Gulden said the 53-point qualifying final win left him with the most pride he has ever felt in the Swans across six seasons at the club.

The two-time All-Australian has played in two losing grand finals (2022, 2024), with last year's 10th-placed finish the first time he had missed finals in his career.

"I love playing with this team. The last couple of games have been so fun as a player to be a part of," Gulden said.

"There's something in having your back against the wall and trying to fight your way out of it.

"The weekend [against the Lions] was easily the most rewarding game.

"The most pride I've felt to be a part of this team in my career.

"There was obviously some respect lost for the club. It's completely fair enough.

Scans confirm ACL rupture for Swans skipper Callum Mills will be sidelined for the remainder of Sydney's finals campaign and possibly all of next season after scans revealed an ACL tear in his right knee.

"All we can focus on as players is what we can control, and that's going out there and representing the club the best way we can on and off the field.

"I'm really proud of the club and the team, everyone involved, because the last few weeks have been really difficult."

Sydney will continue its unlikely flag push by hosting minor premiers Fremantle at the SCG on Friday.

"A premiership would mean the absolute world to me," Gulden said.

"Even if what happened hadn't happened, it still would mean the world to me."

AAP

World.title: Warriors moved to Eden Park for Knights finals showdown
World.content:
The Warriors will make history when they host their first NRL final at Eden Park after the governing body announced the venue for the club's elimination final.

The NRL confirmed the Warriors would play Newcastle at Eden Park next Sunday at 6:05pm (4:05pm AEST) in week two of the finals.

The Warriors' first preference is to play at Mt Smart Stadium where their support is through the roof.

Eden Park holds 50,000 people, however, and is a more modern stadium compared to Mt Smart, where a sold-out crowd of 26,131 created a cauldron-like atmosphere in the Warriors' 26-16 loss to the Dolphins in Saturday night's qualifying final.

The Warriors have hosted five finals in their history in Auckland, but all at Mt Smart.

The Warriors have injury concerns ahead of the clash with the Knights, who they beat 46-32 in Auckland in round 25.

They lost strike centre Leka Halasima in the warm-up to the Dolphins clash with the Tonga international clutching at his right leg.

Trindall returns from shoulder dislocation to lead Sharks in finals win Four weeks after dislocating his shoulder, Braydon Trindall has returned to lead the Cronulla Sharks to a 26-16 win, advancing to the second week of the NRL finals while knocking out the North Queensland Cowboys.

"It was a hamstring in the warm-up, nothing related to what he's been having, which was an ankle injury," coach Andrew Webster said.

"He just felt his hamstring in the first stride out and reported it straight away. Yeah, couldn't go.

"I don't know any more than that right now."

Halasima is set to miss the Newcastle clash amid fears that prop Jackson Ford's injury comeback will be short-lived.

Ford, on return after a 12-week pectoral tear lay-off, limped off against the Dolphins with an ankle complaint.

"Not good," Webster said, when asked about the nature of the injury.

"We don't know much more."

The Warriors were never in full cry in attack against the Dolphins, with five penalty goals edging them to a 16-8 lead, but also denying them the chance near the opposition tryline to perhaps put the game to bed.

"We didn't get the opportunity to get a flow in to our attack," Webster said.

"That's the negative side of taking the penalty goals. But to stretch the lead out to eight points, we had to do it. It's a no-brainer.

"The negative side is there, but the eight-point gap is what every team should take."

Webster said the Warriors were in a strong position when leading 12-8 at half-time, but were unable to contain Dolphins centre Herbie Farnworth in particular as their tackles failed to stick.

"We were trying so hard … chasing contact and collision, and they were pinballing. We have to be more efficient next week."

AAP

World.title: Root says England's back from 'chaos' after Pakistan series sweep
World.content:
Joe Root admits England descended into "chaos" before he returned as the Test captain and believes things are back on track after sealing a cricket series whitewash over Pakistan on Saturday.

England survived a scare before Root and Jordan Cox scored unbeaten half-centuries to knock off the target of 130 and win the third Test at Edgbaston by eight wickets with five sessions to spare.

The dramatic retirement of Ben Stokes in June followed by coach Brendon McCullum being stripped of his red-ball responsibilities briefly left the Test side with a worrying leadership vacuum.

Root, who served as skipper for five years before standing down in 2022, accepted the captaincy again and, in concert with interim coach Marcus Trescothick, brought a hat-trick of comfortable wins at Leeds, Lord's and now Edgbaston.

The partnership steadied the ship ahead of Stephen Fleming's arrival as McCullum's long-term successor.

The Kiwi is due to arrive in the country in the coming days and Root believes he will find a team that has put its turbulent recent past to one side.

"There's been a lot of chaos around this series before a ball was bowled," Root said.

"The way we've handled it on and off the field, the way everyone understands what is expected of them, both as a player and how we want to carry ourselves, is a really good thing.

"It's been a very unusual summer, hasn't it? We had a resignation mid-series, there has been a few off-field incidents and we've got a new coach. Whether you call it chaos, whether you call it unusual, whether you call it unsettling, all of those are fair.

Root fuming after Carse nightclub incident England captain Joe Root opens up on his disappointment after finding another teammate involved in an alcohol-fuelled off-field incident.

"But ultimately, the thing that I care about and the most important thing is what happens from that. The way that we've responded to that has been excellent. And the fact that there's now clarity in what is expected of the group moving forward is quite evident. We build on that now."

Pakistan finally put England under some pressure in Birmingham after flaccid efforts in the first two games.

A stunning 81-run cameo from debutant Razaullah Khan on Friday left England chasing 130.

In Saturday's first over, the host was reduced to 2-2 when Mohammad Abbas got Ben Duckett to edge behind and Emilio Gay lbw.

"We thought this morning that anything is possible," Abbas said. "My specialty is taking wickets with the new ball … and we tried our best."

England could have been 3-35 when Root dragged on but Mohammad Ali overstepped.

Root and Cox shared an unbeaten stand of 128 with Root finishing on 62 and Cox 59 when they won at 2-133 just before lunch.

Seam bowler Ollie Robinson was named the player of the series for taking 21 wickets at an average of 8.76.

AP

World.title: New world number one Rybakina dethrones Sabalenka in US Open final
World.content:
Elena Rybakina has won her first US Open title, ending Aryna Sabalenka's hopes of a hat-trick of wins at Flushing Meadows in New York.

Rybakina controlled the first set, then was put in danger in the second, defending two set points before losing a third to allow Sabalenka back into the match.

However, the Kazakh player held her nerve, taking an early break in the third set and holding on for her third major title win, 6-4, 5-7, 6-2.

The win marked a second major triumph for Rybakina this year, after her Australian Open final victory over Sabalenka in January.

Sabalenka's loss ended her hopes of winning a third US Open crown in a row, emulating tennis great Serena Williams, who was undefeated between 2012 and 2014.

Sabalenka was increasingly frustrated through the match, smashing a couple of racquets as she struggled to find a way past her opponent.

Aryna Sabalenka's inability to crack Elena Rybakina left her frustrated at the US Open final. (Getty Images: Sarah Stier)

Rybakina stopped Sabalenka's 19-match winning streak at the US Open, where she had not lost since falling to Coco Gauff in the 2023 final.

The WTA Tour leader in aces got less than half of her first serves in but instead put Sabalenka under constant pressure with a strong return game, racking up 12 break chances and converting three, which was all she needed.

Rybakina earned $US5.5 million ($7.67 million), the largest prize in grand slam history, and tied Sabalenka and French Open winner Mirra Andreeva with a tour-high three titles this season.

Sabalenka took home $US2.8 million ($3.9 million) but it was clear how little that meant to her, as she smashed her racquet after a brief hug with Rybakina at the net.

A devastated Sabalenka found it hard to talk at the trophy presentation.

"That's the last thing I want to do now is giving a speech," she said.

"Obviously, I'm disappointed but I want to say congratulations Elena, it's a great win.

"I wish I could perform a little better, but maybe next year," she said as tears fell.

Rybakina was overjoyed and a little overwhelmed.

"It's tough to find words right now," she told the crowd.

"I didn't expect anything like this coming to this tournament. I've been dealing with an injury but somehow everything aligned together on my side.

"I want to say to Aryna, you are a great champion. It's so difficult to play you. I was diving around on court trying to get balls [back]."

Rybakina also thanked the crowd for their support, adding: "I'm falling in love with New York more and more."

It was celebration time for Elena Rybakina at the US Open after she won her second major title of 2026. (Getty Images: Julian Finney)

The second seed drew first blood to go ahead 3-2 following a Sabalenka double ⁠fault, with the frustrated Belarusian earning a code ‌violation immediately afterwards for launching ‌a ball high into the stands of the main showcourt.

A sudden drop-off in Rybakina's level midway through the second set gave the 28-year-old Sabalenka hope, and she produced a delicate drop shot and a stunning backhand crosscourt winner en route to forcing a deciding set.

However, Rybakina's quality ‌shone through as she took a commanding 5-2 lead and then ​closed out a famous triumph to leave her Belarusian rival without any major silverware in 2026.

ABC/wires

World.title: Wallaroos scare England but fail 'mission impossible'
World.content:
Australia's rugby women have given England's world champions a run for their money by leading sensationally at half-time, but the Wallaroos' dream of downing the Red Roses crumbled as they ended up losing 48-15 in Salford.

The English were stunned in the first 40 minutes of their WXV Global Series opener on Saturday (Sunday AEST) as the Australians went in to the break with a 10-5 lead but any hopes of handing the hosts their first defeat after 38 straight victories was buried after the break.

The John Mitchell-coached world champs, initially rusty in their first outing since being crowned European grand slam champions in May and struggling to adapt to the new smaller size 4.5 ball being trialled, ran in eight tries in total as their set-piece finally began to tick over to their normal high efficiency.

But Australia could be proud of their efforts, deserving their half-time lead as they controlled the breakdown and defended stoically even after being reduced to 14 for 10 minutes in the first period when halfback Samantha Wood was sin-binned for a deliberate knock-on.

Still, they went in to the break with the lead thanks to barnstorming prop Faliki Pohiva rumbling her way over for a try after Michaela Leonard's stolen lineout on England's five-metre line, but the world champions were hardly inconvenienced, despite their initial rustiness.

"It is an absolute joke if you are worried about being down 10-5," said Mitchell afterwards and the response of his team demonstrated they were surely never really concerned.

"More important is how we worked our way back into it."

In front of a crowd of 9,251, England did indeed begin to turn it on, with May Campbell, captain Meg Jones, Bryony Field, Mia Venner and Sadia Kabeya all crossing for tries in a 20-minute spell to add to player-of-the-match Abi Burton's first-half score.

Lucy Packer and Claudia Moloney-MacDonald also then went over, with Asoiva Karpani scoring a second for the Wallaroos late on in a show of defiance amid the hammering.

Loading Instagram content

Wallaroos skipper Siokapesi Palu Sekona was proud of her "super-stoked" side's efforts.

"Unfortunately, I don't think that score is a reflection of the game we produced," she said.

"I know that we didn't finish the way we wanted to but we're going to take a lot of positives.

"That's the first time England have trailed at half-time since 2019, I believe, and so we'll take a lot of confidence.

"Against a world-class team like that we can actually give it, so for us it's about stringing it for a full 80-minute game now."

The Wallaroos travel to Marseille for their next assignment against France next weekend.

Flanker Lily Bone failed a HIA midway through the first half while Palu Sekona (knee) and debutant Amelia Whitaker will both be monitored after suffering knocks.

Meanwhile, Scotland were swept aside 64-26 in Edinburgh as Canada warmed up in style for their World Cup final rematch against England in Exeter next weekend.

AAP

World.title: More F1 pain for Piastri after 'pretty shocking' qualifying in Spain
World.content:
Oscar Piastri's increasingly underwhelming Formula 1 season has taken another bad turn in Madrid with a "pretty shocking" qualifying lap at the Spanish Grand Prix.

The Australian's hugely disappointing seventh-place finish in qualifying on the new Madring street circuit came as teammate Lando Norris delivered a pole-grabbing lap hailed by McLaren's team boss as a "masterpiece".

The world champion produced his dazzling lap in the sunshine seemingly from nowhere, clocking a 1 minute 31.82 seconds circuit to edge Mercedes's championship leader Kimi Antonelli by just 0.011 of a second, with Red Bull's Max Verstappen third and Ferrari's ‌Lewis Hamilton fourth.

But while a "shocked" Norris was hailing what he called "probably one of the best laps I've done", it was back to the drawing board for Piastri, who was disappointed to finish in 1:32.294 — remarkably, nearly half a second behind his teammate.

"The first lap wasn't too bad but the second lap was pretty shocking. Disappointing," said the 25-year-old, who could find it difficult to make much headway from seventh on Sunday on an unforgiving, tight circuit where, he admitted, overtaking "will be difficult".

He is keeping up a brave face, though, still talking up how he hopes to earn a victory somewhere this year to set himself up for a realistic crack at the title in 2027.

Piastri has not won a race since the Dutch Grand Prix now over a year ago when he was leading the 2025 championship, but he is adamant his dramatic fall-off was not a factor in his disappointing 2026 campaign.

"Of course, I would love to win a race ‌or two this year, ‌or more if I can. But for me, honestly, the biggest thing, the end goal is to ​try and win championships," he said.

"And if I can't do that this year, then I want to make sure I'm as best prepared as I can for next year."

For the moment, though, that still seems a long way off as his smooth driving style just doesn't seem to be suited to the vast changes to the 2026 F1 cars.

F1 debuts new track with Monumental corner Formula 1 debuts a new circuit to its calendar, and despite no grand prix raced yet, the Madring already boasts a corner that is poised to become an iconic scene in motorsport.

"It's all to do with ‌technically driving the car. There's nothing to do with a hangover from last year … it's very much a technical thing," he explained.

"It's not like I'm slow, feeling sorry for myself or thinking about last year. It's just that a few of the weekends I've had to drive the car in a different way that just hasn't really worked for me.

"The biggest thing this year has been the cars are very different to drive, both from a power unit point of view but also the car itself is fundamentally very ​different and the tyres also.

"You've got to drive it ​very differently and I would say it's not ⁠necessarily in the way that I would choose to drive a race car. So there's just been some struggles getting ​to grips with that."

Meanwhile, though, Norris does seem to be getting to grips with it, producing "one of those laps where everything pretty much worked perfectly".

The champion's 19th career pole and third of the season was hailed by McLaren team boss Andrea Stella as a "masterpiece", which could only have been bettered if he had not made a mistake at the very last corner that possibly cost him 0.3 of a second.

Norris had been only sixth after the first run in the third qualifying session but he diced daringly with the wall during the breathtaking final lap, and declared over the radio at the end: "Oh, what a lap, gorgeous … oh, that might be my best one."

AAP/Reuters

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Formula 1 Spanish Grand Prix from 9pm AEST on Sunday, September 13.

World.title: Sharks hand Dragons NRLW wooden spoon and Eels down Cowboys
World.content:
Parramatta has scored a thrilling 33-28 come-from-behind victory over the Cowboys, and the Sharks have handed the Dragons the wooden spoon with a 16-8 win in the final round of NRLW action.

None of Saturday's teams were in finals contention, but pride was still on the line, and both games were genuine contests.

The matches were played under the experimental rule that allows the side conceding a try to choose whether to kick off or receive, and both games saw teams use the latter option and score shortly after.

In the day's first game, the Eels scored five second-half tries and overcame a 16-point deficit to win a thriller at Western Sydney Stadium.

After losing their opening six matches of the season, the Eels ended 2026 with four wins from their last five starts.

The Cowboys' Charlize Lloyd-Phillips got the scoring under way after just four minutes, but suffered a suspected ACL injury in the process.

Parramatta took less than three minutes to reply, strike centre Rory Owen crossing for her sixth try in four games, before former Wallaroos star Ash Marsters posted the only other try of the half to see the Cowboys up 10-6 at the break.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au
